23:43 The new rules put renting first in the withdrawal order
This revision adjusts 20 clauses in total. First, renovating an owner-occupied home and paying property fees on an owner-occupied home are included as withdrawal purposes for the first time; the fund no longer serves only loan-financed home purchases. Second, renting used to require that rent exceed a set proportion of household wage income; this version removes that restriction, and renting is placed first in the withdrawal order. Third, flexible-employment workers are formally brought into the system for the first time: self-employed individuals and part-time workers may contribute voluntarily and apply for provident fund loans. In addition, the management centre must reply to withdrawal applications within three days and to loan applications within ten days, and nationwide mutual recognition of contribution records is being pushed forward.

30:18 The share of contributions lent out has fallen from 70% to 30%
The figure Lao Qian saw: this year the proportion of provident fund contributions lent out is as low as just over 30%, against more than 70% at the peak — a steady decline in just a few years. In other words, the theoretically most stable, lowest-rate, highest-quality lending channel is actually used by only a bit over 30% of people. That directly reflects how low the willingness to buy is. Lao Qian also points out the new rules aim at housing consumption rather than leverage: renting moved to first place, property fees and renovation both withdrawable, thresholds sharply lowered — supporting measures as the property market shifts from an incremental to a stock phase, and also echoing the ageing trend: the month when the withdrawal ratio turned up was 2023, exactly when the post-1960 cohort retired.

32:20 If you want to buy, be careful about withdrawing
Yubai warns: the provident fund loan amount is tied to the account balance — in some cities you can borrow 16 times the balance, in others 20 times, varying by city. Guangzhou has several caps, and at application the smallest of the standards applies: for a first or second owner-occupied home the minimum down payment is 20%, so on a 1 million yuan home the loan cannot exceed 800,000; and a monthly repayment exceeding 50% of monthly income also fails. So before taking the fund out as living expenses, check your city's lending rules. Yubai is also cautious about the buying logic of ‘rent-to-price ratio close to the provident fund rate, only a down payment short’: you still have to weigh depreciation, price swings, and how to withstand risk once a 600,000 down payment is locked up.

44:05 Flexible-employment contributors carry the full amount alone
For flexible-employment workers the contribution base and rate are calculated the same way as for employees, but no employer pays half, so one person bears the full 10% to 24%. The base must be self-declared: below 10,000 no proof is needed, above 10,000 you must log into the individual income tax app and pull your tax details as documentation, to prevent inflating the base to extract a higher loan amount. Zhou Yi ran the numbers: 10,000 at 10% to 24% is 1,000 to 2,400 yuan, and this money is not counted in individual income tax, but it is a loss if you never use it. In addition, most pilot cities require 6 to 12 consecutive months of contributions before you can apply for a provident fund loan, and most do not allow one-off back payments.

47:33 In the public sector the fund is an invisible benefit
Zhou Yi asked a friend with a public-institution post back home, who readily showed a screenshot of her provident fund account: the monthly credit is more than twice Zhou Yi's, and the balance already exceeds her savings. The friend lives at home with no need to rent, so the fund just accumulates as forced savings or future loan capacity, plus she has an occupational annuity, and the contribution base counts bonuses and allowances in full. Lao Qian adds: the provident fund is tax-free, and with private pensions capped at 12,000 yuan a year and taxed at 3% on withdrawal, the public sector already has an extra layer of tax advantage. On the data: in 2025 the average annual wage of urban non-private unit employees nationwide was 129,441 yuan, against 71,590 yuan for private units — while working hours run the other way.

52:44 Full provident fund contributions are a slice for judging a company
Lao Qian's judgment on ‘is a company that pays the provident fund a better choice’ has not changed at all: a company that contributes in full respects its employees and respects the rules, which means it is probably well-run in every respect, rather than finding workarounds for every policy. He goes further: this points to not making profit maximisation the first goal, to treating people as people, and the invisible returns show up elsewhere. Zhou Yi has run the numbers: on a wage base of 100, you actually take home just over 70, but the boss pays out over 130, and everyone along the chain feels aggrieved. Lao Qian cites Ford's pay raise on the Model T — letting workers afford a car and have time to use it was not the capitalist having a conscience, it was simply a better utility function.

item.title: AI Executives Line Up to Ask for Regulation: Even the Accelerationists Are Getting Spooked
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-hardfork-ai-高管集体求监管-连加速派也开始发怵/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-hardfork-ai-高管集体求监管-连加速派也开始发怵/
item.description: Dario Amodei calls for embedded evaluators inside AI companies, and Altman, Musk and Hassabis follow — competitors who agree on almost nothing are, for the first time, saying publicly what they have said privately for years.
item.content:encoded:
Dario Amodei calls for embedded evaluators inside AI companies, and Altman, Musk and Hassabis follow — competitors who agree on almost nothing are, for the first time, saying publicly what they have said privately for years.

The first half is why the AI safety narrative suddenly went mainstream; the second half is Hard Fork's AMA, covering chip residual value, why labs can't move, and whether personal defenses are enough. Medium information density; the AMA portion is more casual chat.

4:05 The resignation post tore open an internal consensus
Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic and OpenAI, saying publicly that neither company is acting responsibly and that they are ‘racing straight to self-improving super intelligence’. What actually made Casey realize he was inside a bubble was the reply from Anthropic employee Evan Hubinger: he too believes AI could kill all humans, and puts the probability above 10%. Casey's reaction was ‘that's it?’ — among the lab researchers he talks to, a 10% PDOOM counts as optimistic. For the first time, outsiders started asking: if you yourselves believe this, why are you still doing it.

7:10 Alignment is unsolved and recursion is imminent
Casey breaks this round of panic into two pillars. The first is the alignment problem exposed by the Hugging Face incident: researchers had assumed that kind of dangerous behavior between agents — mutual sacrifice, mutual cooperation — would show up much later, but they saw it in very primitive models. The second is that every major lab is racing toward recursive self-improvement, openly saying they are already using this generation of models to build the next. An unsolved alignment problem plus imminent recursive self-improvement is what makes the resignations look reasonable rather than a cult shouting apocalypse.

9:14 Even the accelerationists are getting spooked
The mood inside the companies has shifted too. Three or four months ago, the same company held both a safety and alignment team worried about risk and a team that just pushed model capabilities and chased new breakthroughs, and the two sides were opposed. What changed in the past few weeks: even the optimists, the accelerationists, the capability people started being frightened by the pace of system progress. That is what makes this round different from past AI risk narratives — not more external critics, but the least worried people inside starting to worry.

10:17 Dario wants to put regulators inside the companies
Dario Amodei published a 3,800-word piece, ‘We Must Pace the Frontier’, calling for globally coordinated AI slowdown and proposing a concrete mechanism: embedded evaluators placed inside major AI companies, given employee-level access, sitting in the office continuously to monitor whether systems develop dangerous capabilities or act out. He said Anthropic would do it first, without waiting for industry or regulators to force it. The model is the arrangements banks already have. Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Demis Hassabis then said they would follow — Altman and Amodei agree on almost nothing.

16:30 An industry asking to be regulated is abnormal
Casey says he has been unexpectedly optimistic these past few weeks. Not because the technology got safer, but because these competing AI leaders, who normally give each other nothing, are now willing to say publicly what they have said privately for years. That gives their own employees permission to speak up, and gives legislators permission to take it seriously — few industries go to Washington and say ‘please slow us down, we're out of control, regulate us before it's too late’. He stresses this is different from the social media era: Facebook never once said ‘our recommendation algorithm is addictive, please slow us down’.

21:58 Everyone already has the recipe
Kevin adds an easily overlooked fact: everyone has the recipe for large language models, everyone knows how to build one. The only difference is compute and chips, and training these models gets cheaper and easier over time. So even if you fully trust OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and xAI, the problem remains — before long, any six or seven kids in some country can assemble their own out-of-control agent swarm and let it loose. This is not a one-country problem, the cat is out of the bag. That is also why you act while there are only five quasi-frontier labs.

1:00:05 Chips don't become junk in three or four years
On the question of whether companies should slow down and hold budget because smaller, faster chips arrive in 2027 or 2028, Kevin's analogy is that last year's chip is like last year's iPhone: the resale value is still high and it can still do a lot. He says people who doubt the whole AI investment narrative want to believe chips are obsolete in three or four years, but that has not been borne out. Chips do age and wear, and AI companies do move old chips to other workloads and stop using them for frontier training, but there is still plenty of work for them. They even had a company (unnamed) send over a very old chip to put on display in their new office.

1:02:08 AI labs can't move because of network effects
Someone asked why, if US regulation and export controls are an existential threat, OpenAI and Anthropic don't move their model-release base to the UK or EU. Kevin's judgment is blunt: if Trump won't let them release frontier models in the US, he also won't let them export the whole lab to another country, even though someday they would very much like to. Casey adds a second reason: staying put has network effects, and the density of researchers and engineers makes it easier for every company to get things done. Moving elsewhere would save a lot of money and might help on regulation, tax and export controls, but it would lose the feeling of being at the center of this boom — a boom that looks virtual but is still highly concentrated geographically.

item.title: Stablecoins Are Not a Duopoly: Big Companies Want Their Own Coin
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-empire-稳定币不是双寡头-大公司要发自己的币/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-empire-稳定币不是双寡头-大公司要发自己的币/
item.description: The multi-stablecoin debate returns: Rob says he knows of multinationals issuing their own stablecoins, Circle's USDC network effect is underrated, but at 2-3% rates its revenue gets cut in half.
item.content:encoded:
The multi-stablecoin debate returns: Rob says he knows of multinationals issuing their own stablecoins, Circle's USDC network effect is underrated, but at 2-3% rates its revenue gets cut in half.

Regulation, stablecoins, Circle Arc, the Meta vs Instinct fight, Polymarket's talent war — high information density, and the second half is worth more than the first.

4:05 The multi-stablecoin debate is not over
Santi had previously said the ‘hundreds of stablecoin thesis is dead’, and Rob pushed back on the spot. Rob says he knows of multinationals issuing their own stablecoins; SoFi, Verve, two bank consortia, the Stripe consortium, MoneyGram and Western Union are all doing it, and Bridge already has its own stablecoin internally for treasury management. His mechanism: big companies hold a lot of cash, and if they can earn yield on it, they have an incentive to issue their own coin rather than use USDC or USDT. Santi pressed: don't these big companies have FX desks at JP Morgan and Morgan Stanley? Rob said it depends on the size of the company and the complexity of global treasury management — for Western Union's remittance corridors in Africa and Latin America, JP Morgan's correspondent banking network doesn't do the job well.

13:18 CLARITY failed, but nobody has really given up
The Senate voted down the CLARITY Act 49 to 50 on Tuesday; it needed 60 votes. Three Republicans — Susan Collins, Josh Hawley and Jerry Moran — voted against, and every Democrat they had been counting on voted against. Santi said not to over-read Tillis's turn, since Kirsten Gillibrand said that same day she is still pushing the legislation. On Polymarket the odds of passage fell to 4% at one point, then came back to 8%. The market dropped on the news, with Coinbase down 10% and Circle down 12%. Rob said it's worth remembering that dozens of people worked on this bill for a year, including staff on the Banking Committee and the Agriculture Committee.

16:58 The SEC gives tokenized stocks a five-year exemption
The SEC issued an order granting tokenized securities trading venues (TSVS) a five-year temporary conditional exemption, letting them trade tokenized NMS stocks through permissioned AMMs and liquidity pools without registering as exchanges, and liquidity providers got a limited market-maker exemption. Two key conditions: token holders must get the same rights as holders of the underlying stock, such as dividends and voting; and third-party tokenization requires written notice with an opportunity for the issuer to object. Santi read that out and said this clause could directly break the current onchain tokenized stock practice — if AMC can object, you can't just throw AMC onto Hyperliquid. Rob said this is almost certainly coming, because onchain tokenized stocks currently create strange dislocations after hours and pre-market, and Robinhood pairing memecoins with tokenized stocks is an example.

22:43 The winner in tokenization is the whole ecosystem
Rob said it's hard to point to a single winner. The obvious beneficiaries are issuers, existing exchanges and clearinghouses, new exchanges that want into the US market (Coinbase, Polymarket, Lighter, Hyperliquid, Backpack), global neobanks, and new transfer agents and core infrastructure providers like Alpaca. Santi said his first reaction was Superstate and Securitize, and Securitize was up 16% that day. Rob said this looks more like a rising tide lifting all boats than value concentrating in one place. He added that as more assets come onchain, everything onchain gets bigger — more liquidity, more users, better infrastructure, more stablecoin issuance.

29:06 S&P buying Open Zeppelin is buying data
S&P is a ratings agency with a roughly $120 billion market cap and about $14 billion in revenue. This week it first led Kao's Series B extension (Kao raised its Series B four years ago; this time it may have raised about $50 million, bringing the B round to about $110 million, with investors including RBC, DRW, Broadridge, BNP and Nasdaq), and then acquired the smart contract security firm Open Zeppelin. Rob said the acquisition surprised him, since Open Zeppelin doesn't seem like a company that would run a process to sell itself. His read: S&P gives ratings, and it can use Open Zeppelin for real-time risk benchmarks and data, to assess what's happening inside protocols, and then sell that to clients. Santi said he heard this is the first such deal, and that traditional capital markets data and analytics players (Moody's and others) will do more like it. Rob said many crypto companies raised a lot of money and have good products but aren't good enough as standalone businesses, and companies like S&P grow into conglomerates by constantly buying good niche products and then bundling them for you through a terminal.

37:40 Circle pushing memes on Arc's first day was a misstep
Circle launched Arc, with more than 190 partners on day one and over 220 million in TVL pre-seeded in a Morpho vault. Rob said he doesn't understand why Circle came out on day one pushing a bunch of memes, since Arc had always been positioned as a payments-first chain, talking about agentic finance, privacy, FX liquidity and real commercial activity. He said this is the exact opposite of the story Circle has told for a long time, and it left a lot of people with a bad impression. Santi said he went to Circle's launch event yesterday, and the room and Twitter were two completely different worlds — within an hour he met people from BlackRock, DTCC, ICE, Visa and MoneyGram, and Circle's convening power is extremely strong; if it had launched purely on its original positioning, the effect would have been much better. Rob said Circle may have seen Robinhood chain's success, but Robinhood is a trading platform and Circle is a payments company, and having bought Taza Pay it should stay in its own lane.

42:38 Circle's revenue gets cut in half by rates
Rob said he doesn't expect 4% to 4.5% rates to last forever, and that rates will normalize to between 2% and 3%, which means that if Circle is just an interest-income business, its revenue at the current TVL gets cut in half. He also said that as a payments stablecoin, if it can't share yield with end customers, there isn't much reason to hold large amounts of it. Circle's agreement with Coinbase requires giving 50% to Coinbase, which puts it at a disadvantage competing with new stablecoins. So Circle is working to become a payments company and get a payments company multiple, and Arc and the Circle Payment Network are part of that story. Santi said not to underestimate USDC's network effect — in DeFi there is now only one thing that matters for liquidity, and that's USDC; any DeFi founder needs USDC on their platform.

46:14 Instinct's reckoning comes in month four
Rob said companies now get big faster and raise more, faster, that venture capital as a market structure is broken, and that the hottest companies see valuations rise faster and faster regardless of fundamentals. He said a company's first big reckoning usually comes in year four, while Instinct's first big reckoning will come in month four — because the two biggest companies in the world are about to launch direct competitors, Grokbot and Meta's Muse. Santi said in his own use Muse is six to eight times better than Instinct; Instinct is clearly compute-constrained, and for the same question Muse is sometimes 10 to 15 minutes faster, fails less, and can get around the roadblocks Resy has set up for these products. Rob said he doesn't know how growth investors are comfortable at this valuation, and the only thing that could prove them wrong is Instinct sprinting to train its own model, but that takes a billion dollars to build data centers.

item.title: Prediction Markets Aren't a Casino, but 90% of Volume Comes From Sports
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-freakonomics-预测市场不是赌场-但九成交易量来自体育/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-freakonomics-预测市场不是赌场-但九成交易量来自体育/
item.description: Kalshi spent four years on compliance to win 90% market share, but its revenue structure looks more like a sportsbook's; what's genuinely underrated are the quiet markets like FDA approvals.
item.content:encoded:
Kalshi spent four years on compliance to win 90% market share, but its revenue structure looks more like a sportsbook's; what's genuinely underrated are the quiet markets like FDA approvals.

The first half is founder narrative; the value is in the middle and back: how contracts are written, the 90% sports share, regulatory risk. Worth listening for anyone who wants to understand how prediction markets actually work.

8:16 Comply for four years first, then open your first market
Kalshi's two founders wrote "regulatory first" into the company's principles and spent four years getting regulatory approval before launching their first market. Mansoor calls this anti-Silicon Valley: everyone else ships the product and patches in compliance later; they went to the federal government first and asked, "How should this be regulated?" The cost was that for the first four years they thought about quitting almost every day, held together by "the cost of regret is too high." The payoff came in 2024, when a federal appeals court ruled Kalshi could list election contracts, landing just before the presidential election. Mansoor attributes their 90% market share directly to that path: institutions would rather plug into a platform that's inside the system, because changing the rules from outside the system is harder.

15:36 Prediction markets force you to shut up, not to take a position
Robin Hanson lays out three mechanisms that make prediction markets more accurate than polls or expert interviews. First, people being interviewed have an incentive to be interesting, dramatic, and to tell the questioner what they want to hear, while the market only rewards being right. Second, the market gives you an incentive to shut up about topics you don't understand — you only bet in the few markets where you actually have an edge, whereas interviewees will answer confidently on things they know nothing about. Third, the market doesn't require you to have a direct opinion on a topic; it invites you to find mispricings and errors in other people's pricing, and if you find one, it pays you to correct it. He closes with an old poker-table line: sit down, look for the sucker, and if you can't find him, you're the sucker — so don't play that market.

20:48 Internal prediction markets die on the project owner's excuse
Eli Lilly ran an internal prediction market in the early 2000s that successfully predicted which drug compounds would pass Phase III trials; Google ran one too, called Google Profit. Both were considered effective, and neither survived. Hanson's explanation: the project owner wants to know whether they'll deliver on time, but what they want even more is a good excuse if they fail. And the best excuse is precisely "everything was going fine and then at the last minute something happened that nobody could have anticipated." A market that keeps accurately predicting "you will be late" invalidates that excuse in advance, so nobody wants it to exist.

22:58 Domain expertise is not the key skill for forecasting the future
Mansoor cites Philip Tetlock's Superforecasting research: put experts in a given domain — geopolitics, say — up against a group of non-experts forecasting the same set of events, and the non-experts win. His explanation is that domain experts become too doctrinaire over time, while people who can step back and look at a problem coolly are better calibrated and less biased. Mansoor says this is a fairly heretical claim in politics, academia, and financial analysis — it implies that if you want a more accurate answer, you should look for a diverse group of participants who pride themselves on self-calibration, critical reading, and filtering information, not an authority in some field. He treats this as Kalshi's underlying logic.

33:28 One contract takes a month to write, for grammar and apostrophes
Nicole Kagan writes the contracts and self-certifies them with the CFTC. The most complex category is "what someone will say in a given speech," and they recently rewrote the rules because a pile of grammar questions came up: what if there's an apostrophe? If they misspeak or mispronounce it, does it still count as the same word? What if it appears inside a proper noun? What if the livestream cuts out midway and it's uploaded somewhere else afterward? Those rules took over a month to write, ran seven or eight pages, and are extremely detailed. When Bloomberg reported on them, it guessed they were built for automated processing and must be for AI; Kagan says that's not it at all — they wrote them so users could understand them, and never considered that "something a human can understand is probably something a computer can understand too."

35:35 When you can't call it, settle at the last fair price
Kalshi's contracts are usually binary: pay $1 if the event happens, $0 if it doesn't, with every position fully collateralized — if one side bets 30 cents, someone else has to bet 70. But some situations can't be judged yes or no. Cardi B was clearly dancing during her seven-second Super Bowl halftime cameo, but she had no mic and there was no way to confirm whether she was singing, so the team said "we are epistemologically uncertain" and settled at the last fair price. Another case is 50-50: when multiple people win simultaneously, each settles at 50 cents. Kagan says they have the right to do this when it's "genuinely unclear" whether an event meets the criteria, and they've already revised the halftime show contract — the new rules require an audible lead or backing vocal, and under them Cardi B did not perform.

41:52 Ninety percent of volume comes from sports, and that's the most uncomfortable fact
Dubner puts it bluntly: roughly 90% of Kalshi's volume is concentrated in a category that had barely come up before — sports, the business that makes DraftKings and FanDuel nervous. Mansoor's response is that the sports share is falling fast and other categories are growing faster, but he concedes "10% is still a lot, and don't forget we're big." He insists on distinguishing gambling from trading: all derivatives markets are mostly speculative, speculation provides liquidity, and the key isn't whether there's speculation but the business model — one model hunts for losers and bans winners, the other pursues price discovery and wants smart people to show up. He also concedes the second model carries risk, saying there is such a thing as "responsible gambling" and "responsible trading," and that platforms have a responsibility to monitor.

44:00 Seventy to eighty percent of active users never place a trade
Mansoor says one of his favorite numbers is that 70% to 80% of active users don't trade — they just log in every day, keep it next to X and a few newspapers, and use it to calibrate or check information. Kalshi's business model is a neutral platform, like the NYSE or Nasdaq, taking an average 1% on trades and not caring who wins or loses. He also says the information environment is getting more polarized and the signal-to-noise ratio is falling, because social media algorithms reward clickbait: write a nuanced, restrained, multi-paragraph take on X and you get four likes; write something extreme and unhinged and you get tens of thousands. Prediction markets have exactly the opposite incentive — that nuanced, boring, well-calibrated judgment is the one that makes money.

item.title: Diffusion isn't just for images — it's going to win at language model inference
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-nopriors-扩散模型不是图像专利-它要在推理时赢下语言模型/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-nopriors-扩散模型不是图像专利-它要在推理时赢下语言模型/
item.description: Autoregressive inference must generate one token at a time sequentially, which is a memory bandwidth bottleneck; diffusion models process multiple tokens in parallel at once, making the inference workload look more like training, so Inception is betting on it.
item.content:encoded:
Autoregressive inference must generate one token at a time sequentially, which is a memory bandwidth bottleneck; diffusion models process multiple tokens in parallel at once, making the inference workload look more like training, so Inception is betting on it.

A diffusion model pioneer explains clearly why parallelism at the inference stage will become the architectural deciding factor, and how a 50-person company finds differentiation in the cracks between giants.

3:10 Diffusion models started because GANs were too unstable
Ermon says that when he was working on image generation back then, he was very dissatisfied with GANs: they could work, but training was extremely unstable and results were hard to reproduce. So in 2019 he and his PhD students turned to score-based generative models, with the idea of training a neural network to denoise — if it can denoise, it means it understands image structure, and it can then reverse the process to progressively refine a clean image from pure noise. This is the underlying technology of modern diffusion models. He emphasizes that today's best image, video, some music, and a large number of protein models are all based on diffusion.

5:11 The 2024 paper brought diffusion to text
Ermon's team published a paper in 2024 that, for the first time, got a diffusion model to match the quality of autoregressive models at GPT-2 scale (under a billion parameters): same perplexity, same degree of data fit, but about 10x faster generation, because diffusion outputs multiple tokens at once. He says this is still somewhat academic, but it was enough for him to decide to start a company and scale the technology to commercial scale.

8:14 Autoregressive inference is a memory bandwidth bottleneck
Ermon compares the 2017 switch from RNNs to transformers to the inference stage: during training, transformers won by processing multiple tokens in parallel, but at inference time autoregressive models are still sequential — before generating the 10th token, all previous tokens must be generated first. This workload is extremely memory-bandwidth-bound, with most time spent moving weights between memory hierarchies and very little arithmetic, which is unfriendly to GPUs. Diffusion models' inference workload is more like training — processing multiple tokens in parallel at once — so it naturally matches the computation pattern GPUs are good at.

10:16 Inference efficiency also determines the ceiling of RL post-training
Ermon points out that economics is determined by how much intelligence you can get per watt and per dollar. Much of the progress in reasoning models comes from test-time compute scaling, and one of the bottlenecks in RL post-training is generating rollouts — letting the model explore, scoring trajectories, and then improving the model. So inference efficiency directly bottlenecks post-training efficiency: a model that scales better at inference will automatically also scale better during post-training. This is the core logic of his bet on diffusion LLMs, and what he means by "more parallel approaches will eventually win."

12:19 Mercury benchmarks against Haiku, Flash, mini series
Ermon says Inception's Mercury model benchmarks against speed-optimized models like Haiku, Flash, mini nano, with comparable quality but significantly faster, and is already serving customers in production. He emphasizes that you cannot directly run a diffusion LLM on vLLM or SGLang; you must build your own serving engine to handle the complexity of real production workloads. This is both a barrier and a moat: even if someone else trains a diffusion LLM, without a corresponding serving engine they can't use it.

17:21 Voice customer switched from custom chips back to Nvidia GPUs
Ermon gives the example of voice agent company OpenCall: the voice pipeline includes ASR, an inference LLM for tool calling, and TTS, and speed is critical. OpenCall originally served the LLM on Cerebras custom chips to achieve the required speed, then switched to Inception's diffusion LLM because they could get the same speed on Nvidia GPUs — higher availability, lower cost, better quality. Ermon says once you get used to fast models you can't go back, like broadband.

25:26 Diffusion models are inherently more controllable than autoregressive
Ermon says diffusion models are generally easier to control than autoregressive models: autoregressive must wait until the entire object is generated before knowing whether it satisfies constraints, whether it's aligned, what score the reward function gives; diffusion is coarse-to-fine generation, so from early on you can judge whether the direction is right, and you can use external reward functions or constraint sets to guide generation. There is considerable evidence in the academic literature supporting this, and some guidance methods are simply impossible on autoregressive models. He sees this as the differentiation space for future product experiences.

29:29 20% to 30% of tasks are extremely latency-sensitive
Ermon estimates based on OpenRouter's task categories (research, chat, coding, software engineering, log processing, etc.) that about 20% to 30% of tasks are very latency-sensitive. As a lower bound, this portion of the workload can be served by the model that provides the highest quality within a given latency budget. He also admits that we are not yet at frontier intelligence level, and many workloads still require frontier-level intelligence, so the addressable market for diffusion models is layered.

item.title: When Your Kids Fight, Are You a Witness or a Judge
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-raisinggh-孩子打架时-你是证人还是法官/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-raisinggh-孩子打架时-你是证人还是法官/
item.description: The mistake parents most often make when stepping into sibling conflict is refereeing with their own childhood fairness wounds. What kids need isn't a verdict on who was right, but practice repairing a relationship inside low-stakes conflict.
item.content:encoded:
The mistake parents most often make when stepping into sibling conflict is refereeing with their own childhood fairness wounds. What kids need isn't a verdict on who was right, but practice repairing a relationship inside low-stakes conflict.

Medium information density with a clear core framework: witness not judge, sportscaster mode, fair is not equal. Suited to parents with more than one child, especially those whose own childhood emotions get triggered by sibling fights.

3:05 Deal with your own sibling baggage before you step in
The episode opens by pointing out that almost everyone carries sibling baggage — even people without siblings carry either a longing for that ‘mythic connection’ or relief at having escaped it. The fairness trap is the thing most likely to trigger a parent's emotions: a cake sliced unevenly, a rule that was looser for one kid, a new dress given to only one of them. Those memories get activated the moment you see your own kids fighting. If you step in before dealing with that baggage, you are effectively imposing your sibling history on your children. So the first step is always clearing your own head, not rushing in to hand down a verdict.

4:07 You are a witness, not a judge
This is the single most important line in the whole piece, and Dr. Pressman repeats it a dozen-plus times. The moment you start deciding who was right, who hit first, who was worse, that judgment comes from your own history, not from what actually happened between these two children in front of you. As a witness, your job is to observe and describe, not to adjudicate. That distinction determines your tone, your words and your posture when you step in. Once you become the judge, you will unconsciously favor, convict and punish — and what the kids feel isn't justice, it's your unfinished childhood emotions making decisions on their behalf.

5:09 When you must step in
Dr. Pressman gives clear signals for intervening: a child is in danger, there's a power imbalance, or they're stuck in a loop they can't get out of. If the two are evenly matched and physically safe, you can stay nearby and occasionally ask ‘Is everyone okay?’ But watch especially for a power dynamic that turns into toxic bullying — rare, but when it happens an adult has to cut it off. Kids who experience peer or sibling bullying have far worse adult outcomes, and the damage is much bigger than we realize. Bullying, though, has a strict definition: a power differential plus repeated, malicious, intentional abuse. Merely ‘being a jerk’ isn't bullying, and kids being jerks to each other is completely normal.

6:17 Sportscaster mode: describe, don't adjudicate
If you do need to step in, Dr. Pressman recommends ‘sportscaster mode’ — you act like an observant, reflective commentator and simply describe what happened. For example: ‘I noticed this happened over here, and that happened over there — did I get that right?’ This lets you validate both kids at once without taking sides, and there's no winner. The key is to avoid questions like ‘Who started it?’ ‘You always do this’ ‘There's something wrong with you.’ When you tell a child there's something wrong with who they are rather than with a behavior, you are feeding the exact habit you don't want them using on each other — turning anger and outbursts into a verdict on a person's worth. ‘You're stupid’ means ‘You are a stupid person,’ and no one needs to hear that.

8:21 Stop dehumanizing language on the spot
Dr. Pressman says kids can scream, yell, be vicious to each other, even get physical — but if she hears dehumanizing language, she pauses the fight right there to change the wording. Because what you want to constantly ‘wire’ and ‘bake’ into your kids is: talk about the behavior, not about who the person is. This isn't a lesson delivered afterward, it's immediate intervention. She'll say ‘Let's rephrase that’ in the moment. The logic behind it: language habits need repeated reinforcement to internalize, and every dehumanizing expression you let slide is reinforcement in the opposite direction.

14:33 Fair is not equal — it's needs-based
Dr. Pressman uses the peanut butter cupcake example to explain the difference between fair and equal: giving two kids peanut butter cupcakes of identical size and identical recipe looks equal, but if one of them is allergic to peanuts, it's completely unfair. Fair means giving each child what they need, not giving everyone the same thing. This framework protects you when a child demands ‘Why does my sister get a phone at 12 and I don't?’ — you can answer ‘You're different people, I've learned more since then, and I'm making a different decision that's better for you.’ If you try to be perfectly equal, you're assuming every child is the same age, the same temperament, the same personality, the same interests, the same needs — which obviously doesn't hold.

16:37 Don't put labels on your kids
Dr. Pressman points out that giving all your kids the same label (say, ‘you're all helpers’) does promote positive behavior, but giving the label to only one child in the family creates tension and problematic dynamics. Labels plant seeds of resentment, insecurity and lack of motivation, and they push siblings apart. Teachers, friends, other parents and relatives will all apply labels; a parent's job is to counteract that damage, not join in. Labels ‘haunt’ a child — Dr. Pressman uses the word haunt, and says it sounds dramatic but it's true.

18:41 Repair is not a forced apology
Dr. Pressman distinguishes real repair from fake repair. Repair isn't necessarily a public apology — if the kids finish fighting and suddenly giggle together, share an inside joke, make faces at each other, that is repair, that is reconnection, and you are watching it happen. Every reconnection strengthens the relationship and tells your kids ‘this relationship is forever, it gets messy, but we always come back.’ But a forced apology is not repair. Saying ‘sorry’ and saying ‘apologize to your brother’ don't teach what the research literature calls repair. An insincere apology only makes people angrier. You can ask ‘How do you think that made your sibling feel? Is there anything you could do to help them feel better?’ If the child says no, you don't just drop it — you come back later and ask ‘Have you had time to think about that?’

item.title: America's Richest Are Hiding in Small Business
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-oddlots-美国最富的一群人-藏在小生意里/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-oddlots-美国最富的一群人-藏在小生意里/
item.description: Half the rise in US income inequality comes from pass-through business income — and the owners of these businesses aren't tech giants but car dealers, beer distributors, dentists and hot dog vendors, protected as "small business" for forty years.
item.content:encoded:
Half the rise in US income inequality comes from pass-through business income — and the owners of these businesses aren't tech giants but car dealers, beer distributors, dentists and hot dog vendors, protected as "small business" for forty years.

New research built on linked IRS full tax-return data pulls the question of "who are the rich" away from the tech narrative and back to regional mid-market businesses; high information density, suited to anyone tracking taxes, PE and wealth distribution.

6:13 Tax returns assemble a different picture of the rich
More than a decade ago, the two authors were commissioned by the Treasury to link corporate tax returns with the returns of owners and employees, because even the IRS itself could not match the different forms belonging to the same business. They found that the picture of the rich painted by the media and by Capital in the Twenty-First Century is very different from the actual picture in US tax returns: not passive rent-collecting Gilded Age monopolists, but millions of actively operating mid-market regional business owners. This data project later became the basis of the whole book.

12:16 Seventy percent of pass-through income flows to the top 1%
Of pass-through business income, 70 cents of every dollar flows to the top 1% of earners. From the 1980s to 2021, more than half of the rise in the top 1%'s income share came from pass-through business income. So anyone trying to understand income inequality and wealth inequality cannot get around this sector. The authors had assumed monopolistic giants were passively collecting the money; instead they found mid-market regional businesses spread across the whole country, numbering in the millions.

15:22 Car dealers are the single biggest bucket of pass-through income
The book opens with a "wedding of the century": a third-generation Mercedes dealer in Florida held his daughter's wedding in Paris, rented out Versailles for the dinner, and spent $60 million — right after selling the dealership for several hundred million dollars. When the authors looked at top 0.1% pass-through income by industry, car dealers ranked first. They then went to yacht and private jet registration data and found these people by name, because tax returns themselves cannot identify individuals.

19:23 Car dealer wealth is half skill, half licence
The authors tell two stories. Larry Miller started in Toyota's parts division, took the parts business from 961st to first, later owned more than 40 dealerships and bought the Utah Jazz — a good case of "move slow and make things." But the other side is regulatory protection: franchise laws were meant to protect small dealers from being force-fed inventory by Ford and GM, yet in 2008 Chrysler had three times as many dealerships as Toyota while selling the same number of cars, and closing a store meant paying three years' rent. Dealers also enjoy geographic monopolies and high margins on add-on services like warranties and financing.

22:25 Beer distributors are a rent-collecting layer left by Prohibition
When you see a truck on the road with Budweiser on it, the truck actually belongs to a distributor, such as Reyes. These distributors sit between brewers and bars, restaurants and grocery stores; state laws require beer to pass through this layer, originally to stop big brewers from controlling production and distribution at the same time. The result is that these "little guys" became big guys, showing up in large numbers in the private jet data. The authors mention a beer wholesalers' convention in San Antonio where the mayor said he had never seen so many private jets at the airport.

34:31 Same anaesthesiologist, far higher tax burden for the employee
The book compares two anaesthesiologists: one runs a private practice through an S-Corp, the other draws a salary from a hospital system. The former treats most of his income as business profit, pays no payroll tax and no uncapped Medicare surtax, even though he bills Medicare heavily. The IRS only requires payroll tax on the "reasonable compensation" portion of wages; anything above that counts as profit. The 2017 reform cut the top pass-through rate from 37% to below 30%, and although it put guardrails on professional services like doctors, by splitting out surgery, ancillary services or real estate, more income can still be shifted into the lower-rate bucket.

38:35 A quarter of federal elected officials are pass-through owners too
The authors say the reason the tax loophole has survived so long is that roughly a quarter of federal elected officials are themselves pass-through business owners. Ohio Senator Bernie Moreno is a car dealer, and the Social Security plan he introduced with Elizabeth Warren is funded by a payroll tax on working-class wages, with no mention at all of these wealthy business owners. The authors argue the most realistic reform is not to abolish the loophole but to cap it by income: for example, once business income exceeds $1 million or $400,000, you can no longer claim the deduction that cuts the rate from 37% to 30%.

48:52 The owners' share of the pie went from four tenths to five tenths
Over the past 25 years, 60% of growth in the corporate sector came from the pass-through form, so the pie is getting bigger; at the same time, the share owners take out of the pie rose from a third to 40% to about 50%. Using data from 2001 to 2021, the authors calculate: value added per worker rose from $34,000 to $52,000, a gain of $18,000, of which owners took $15,000. They attribute this to skill scarcity (the US has 30% fewer doctors per capita than the OECD average, and the AMA restricts supply), policy-created scarcity, and the rising value of professional services such as M&A.

item.title: Hair relaxer made Black women beautiful, and made them pay with their health
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-ninepi-直发剂让黑人女性变美-也让她们付出健康代价/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-ninepi-直发剂让黑人女性变美-也让她们付出健康代价/
item.description: Chemical hair relaxer built the Black community's first millionaire industry and has also been linked by research to elevated uterine cancer risk — the same product is at once an economic ladder and a bodily cost.
item.content:encoded:
Chemical hair relaxer built the Black community's first millionaire industry and has also been linked by research to elevated uterine cancer risk — the same product is at once an economic ladder and a bodily cost.

This episode has medium information density, but it tells the story of how one product can be empowerment and harm at the same time, very concretely — suited to listeners interested in consumer history, public health, and the racial economy.

1:06 Hair relaxer is "creamy crack"
Chemical hair relaxer has a nickname in the salon: creamy crack, because it is said to be as addictive as cocaine — once you start, it is very hard to stop. When you stop, the new curly growth breaks off where it meets the already straightened dead hair. The week before use you cannot wash your hair or scratch your scalp, or you will get burned; when applying it you have to avoid the scalp and coat only the hair shaft, but leaving it too long near the ends still stings. On the show the host recalls being coated with relaxer for the first time at age 9, having already seen women in the salon cry out in pain.

5:18 From African hair tradition to a survival strategy
Hair historian Lorie Tharps says starting the story from slavery is starting from chapter two and missing chapter one: Africa already had rich hair traditions, and hair connected tribe, family, and identity. After being enslaved in America, straightening went from self-expression to survival strategy — because they were told their hair was inferior, ugly, more like an animal's, and straightening became a visual way to prove "we are equal to you." They used butter instead of palm oil, made shampoo from cornmeal and kerosene, used butter knives as crude curling irons, and wrapped hair in yarn to straighten it.

8:21 Barbers' money built Black colleges
The methods these enslaved people invented were good enough to make them the first choice as barbers and wig makers for white people. White people paid for their craft, and this channel let many of them buy their own freedom. Tharps says some early Black colleges and institutions were funded or founded by Black barbers, such as Wilberforce University — an HBCU entirely owned and operated by African Americans, built in large part on barbering income. But the irony is that these Black barbers did not cut Black people's hair at the time; they served white clients.

10:22 The hot comb gave way to an accidental discovery
Madame CJ Walker and Annie Turnbo Malone used the hot comb plus hair oil to produce sleek straight hair, turning scattered straightening methods into a system, and Walker became the first self-made millionaire woman in America, of any race. But the hot comb's effect was temporary, reverting with sweat, moisture, or rain. In the early 1900s, Cleveland tailor Garrett Augustus Morgan wanted to invent a substance that kept high-speed machines and needles from damaging wool and other animal fur, and after trying a formula found the fur had straightened. He first tested it on a neighbor's dog, then on his own hair, and both straightened — he had accidentally discovered that lye (sodium hydroxide) plus other things could straighten hair.

14:24 The man who put relaxer on drugstore shelves
George Johnson is called by Tharps the Madam CJ Walker of his era. A barber doing homemade conks came to this chemist and asked whether he could make something fast and easy, and that produced Ultra Wave for men, followed by Ultra Sheen for women. Unlike the temporary hot comb and dangerous homemade lye formulas, Ultra Sheen was long-lasting, safer, and available at any drugstore, no salon needed. That privacy mattered: straightening hair with chemicals carried shame, and doing it at home meant no one saw you going to the salon.

16:26 Profits flowed back to the Black community, then regulators took aim
Johnson put profits back into the Black community: Soul Train, Essence Magazine, Chicago's Independence Bank — then the largest Black-owned bank in the country, lending to homeowners and entrepreneurs redlined by white banks; funding Martin Luther King Jr. and Jesse Jackson; employing hundreds of Black and brown workers who could not find jobs because of racial discrimination, giving them profit sharing, full health insurance, on-site nurses, full college tuition, paid maternity and sick leave, and four-day weekends every holiday. In 1964 Johnson Products became the first Black-owned company listed on the American Stock Exchange. But in 1975 the FTC required Johnson to put a warning label on the outside of relaxer packaging, saying the product contained lye and could be harmful — while Revlon's relaxer, which also contained lye, was not immediately required to add a label, delayed by nearly two years.

20:28 The civil rights movement flipped the politics of straight hair
During the Black Power era, Black people decided straight hair had solved nothing — from Madam CJ Walker's straightening comb to relaxer, every method had been tried and it still had not worked. So came a simpler and more radical idea: I will no longer straighten my hair, I will use my hair as protest. Black hair grows up and out, and does not make you smaller — it makes you taller. The political flip was so complete that some Black people with naturally straight hair got perms, because not everyone's hair can grow into an Angela Davis-style afro. But the beauty industry then commodified the afro, selling wigs and marketing it as beauty and empowerment while also pulling its teeth, turning it into just another fashion trend. By the 1980s, straight hair was back.

28:38 A 34,000-woman study: risk up two and a half times
A large 2022 study followed 34,000 women and found that frequent users of chemical hair straightening products — most of them Black women — were two and a half times as likely to develop uterine cancer as never-users. New York Times Magazine contributor Linda Varosa says this was the first high-quality study to link straightening products, Black women, and two cancers (endometrial cancer and uterine cancer). The study also linked these products to fibroids, and Black women have fibroids at far higher rates than other women. The study shows correlation, not causation, but Tharps thinks agonizing over correlation versus causation misses the point: she thinks the red flag should simply be waved, with warnings on packaging, labels, and in salons.

item.title: A Broken Arm Forced a Perfect French Score: Constraints Are the Engine of Creativity
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-cautionary-断臂逼出的法语满分-限制才是创造力的引擎/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-cautionary-断臂逼出的法语满分-限制才是创造力的引擎/
item.description: After David Epstein broke his arm, he was forced to replace note-taking with image-based memory, and his French scores went to perfect. During a two-day London Underground strike, many people found better commutes. Constraints aren't obstacles — they're the switch that forces you to experiment.
item.content:encoded:
After David Epstein broke his arm, he was forced to replace note-taking with image-based memory, and his French scores went to perfect. During a two-day London Underground strike, many people found better commutes. Constraints aren't obstacles — they're the switch that forces you to experiment.

Medium information density. The core is the framework distinguishing useful constraints from useless ones. The second half — scientific integrity and startup experimentation — is worth more than the first.

5:28 A broken arm forced a memory method into existence
In eighth grade, playing American football, David Epstein threw too hard and his arm snapped on the follow-through; his right arm was bound from shoulder to hand against his torso. His French class had a weekly dictation test: listen to a native speaker's recording and fill in the blanks in a text, and he was mediocre. With his right hand bound, he couldn't write fast enough with his left, so he had to hold the flying words in his head first, by linking each word to something sports-related — he didn't know at the time that this was called a mnemonic device. As a result he could remember every word, then slowly fill them in with his left hand, and he started getting perfect scores. The key mechanism: his most convenient path was blocked, forcing him to find an alternative, and the alternative was better.

8:35 A two-day subway strike improved commutes for years
During a London Underground strike, people were forced to find different routes to work. The strike lasted only 48 hours, but a substantial share of people discovered a better commute than the one they had used for weeks, months, or even years, and kept using it afterward. Epstein recalls the study estimating this collectively saved about 1,500 hours of commuting per day. His inference: we normally experiment too little; useful constraints drive people to run experiments they otherwise wouldn't, and the payoff from those experiments can far exceed the inconvenience.

10:38 General Magic died of too many resources
General Magic was a late-1980s, early-1990s startup with nearly unlimited talent, money, and resources, and it correctly judged the direction of technology for the following decades — on paper, they invented the iPhone. But Epstein says more startups die of indigestion than of starvation: because they could do anything, they did everything, and projects kept ballooning out of control. They never clearly defined who the customer was (the so-called Joe Sixpack, and nobody knew who that was), and in the end they were building for each other rather than solving a specific problem. Internally, a low-level service engineer built a prototype of eBay and handed it to the company, and it was rejected as "too small, it'll never amount to anything." Epstein argues they should have started from smaller goals and smaller milestones.

12:41 A world without constraints is fiction
Tim Harford raises a disagreement: General Magic wasn't without constraints, it's just that all its constraints were long-term, so they could pretend the constraints didn't exist until money and time actually ran out. Epstein partly agrees but corrects him: they didn't lack money, they had more than they could spend; what they lacked was time. He cites Oliver Burkeman's point: believing that with the right productivity tools you can get everything done may just be a refusal to face your own mortality, a refusal to prioritize ruthlessly. About two-thirds of the former General Magic employees he interviewed said they simply couldn't figure out what not to do. Epstein treats this as a parable for the AI era: when the cost of starting something approaches zero, it erases the hard work of deciding what not to do, which may be one reason adoption has risen unprecedentedly while productivity hasn't risen correspondingly.

14:42 The Hemingway principle fights the sense of urgency
Epstein calls his own writing method the Hemingway principle: Hemingway stopped mid-sentence, so the next day he knew which important place to return to. The last thing Epstein does at the end of each workday is designate which important place to start from the next day. He says this guards against the two main ways a workday goes off the rails: first, falling into an algorithmic feed or inbox first thing in the morning; second, the so-called mere urgency effect — people prioritize what feels urgent (like answering email) over what's truly important, even when the important thing objectively deserves the time more.

17:44 Pre-registration made miracle drugs disappear
Before 2000, psychology was full of counterintuitive findings: thinking of Florida made you walk more slowly, power poses raised testosterone, hurricanes with female names were more dangerous. Medicine was the same — nearly every NIH-funded cardiovascular drug trial found a positive result; after 2000, new trials were almost all negative. The turning point was the NIH forcing researchers to constrain their behavior: write down your prediction in advance and stick to it. Epstein explains the mechanism: researchers would originally make a prediction, and when it didn't hold, dig through a large dataset for a correlation, then retroactively invent a prediction, so that at publication it looked like they had been looking for this from the start. Digging through data amounts to running nearly infinite tests, and each test raises the probability of a false positive, so a false-positive association is almost guaranteed.

20:45 Everything in the fridge both causes and prevents cancer
Epstein's favorite "dark-humor paper" aggregated all nutrition research and found that nearly every food you can think of has been shown in different studies to both cause and prevent cancer, with only bacon as the exception — found only to cause cancer. He also tells the case of nutrition star researcher Brian Woznick: he did the famous bottomless soup bowl experiment, where people ate far more when an unseen tube kept refilling their soup. Later he wrote a blog post describing his research methods: when a prediction didn't hold, he handed the data to a graduate student and said "find me something positive," and she never failed. Epstein's analogy: it's like firing randomly at a wall, then finding the densest cluster of bullet holes and painting a bullseye and a ten-ring around it, and passersby marvel at the marksmanship. Most of Woznick's life's work was eventually retracted, and his research had been cited in a Nobel laureate's book.

27:51 Entrepreneurs who write predictions fail more but succeed more
Epstein extends pre-registration to personal life: when making a behavior change (say, wanting to exercise more), first write down what you plan to try and what you predict it will produce, then do it, then check whether the prediction came true — this educates your intuition. He cites a randomized controlled study: entrepreneurs randomly assigned to a "scientific method training" group or an ordinary market research group; the trained ones more often falsified their own prior beliefs, discovering that the value they thought they were adding to the market didn't hold up, and as a result they pivoted more often and succeeded more often.

item.title: California Passed a Law Just to Shut Up a 24-Year-Old Blogger
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-allin-加州为了让一个-24-岁博主闭嘴-专门立了一部法/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-allin-加州为了让一个-24-岁博主闭嘴-专门立了一部法/
item.description: California's counterattack on an investigator isn't denial, it's legislation: the moment he uploads footage he's captured, he's fined $4,000, then pays the other side's legal fees. The law was introduced by the state attorney general's wife.
item.content:encoded:
California's counterattack on an investigator isn't denial, it's legislation: the moment he uploads footage he's captured, he's fined $4,000, then pays the other side's legal fees. The law was introduced by the state attorney general's wife.

The first half is the California high-speed rail ledger; the second half is how a blogger with no journalism training used undercover filming to force arrests and legislation. High information density, but the stance is unmistakable.

0:08 $15 billion of high-speed rail leading to nowhere
The first number in Nick Shirley's new film is $15 billion, 18 years, and the number of towns California high-speed rail connects today is zero. When it was approved in 2008, it promised to link Los Angeles and San Francisco; that same year China broke ground on its own high-speed rail, which now connects more than 30,000 miles and covers the entire country, while California's segment connects nothing. He calls it the "high-speed rail to nowhere" — not a figure of speech: walk the line and all you see is concrete and rebar. To finish, it will take another $100 to $200 billion.

1:09 Cost went from $33 billion to $236 billion
The next entry in the same ledger: the original estimate was $33 billion, it jumped to $126 billion, and the latest estimate is $236 billion. By that number, it would be the third most expensive infrastructure project in world history — first is the 1950s interstate highway system, second is the International Space Station. The people he interviews say the difference is: you can drive I-5 or I-80 across the country, you can go to space, but "we will never ride California high-speed rail." His name for this stretch of construction is "the most expensive piece of concrete known to man," while people in the Central Valley call it a modern Stonehenge. In a privately recorded clip from 2016, Newsom himself admitted he didn't believe the project would be built in our lifetimes.

3:09 A third of the money goes to delay compensation
A third of the $15 billion went to "change order delays" — because the builders didn't know where the infrastructure was or how to build it. Contractors got compensation rights as a result: $170,000 a day, $5 million a month, simply because they couldn't start work. This February, California just closed a delay settlement of more than $500 million, the largest delay settlement yet. At the same time, California still hasn't bought high-speed rail trains; Nick's read is that they know there will never be a train on those tracks. He runs another calculation: at current ridership, buying one-way tickets directly, $15 billion would subsidize free one-way tickets between San Francisco and Los Angeles for 150 years; at $236 billion, for 300 years.

9:11 The state senator says it's happening
State Senator Cortezi just pushed through $1 billion a year for 20 consecutive years. Nick asked him to his face: not an inch of track has been laid in California, how do you explain that? He said "it's happening," and asked the reporter whether he'd ever been there. Pressed on Newsom privately saying it was impossible, his answer was "maybe he did, maybe he didn't." Asked whether the high-speed rail authority has ever been held accountable for delays and overruns, he said "we're trying to hold them accountable." His justification isn't transportation but that this is the largest economic development project in the country, and no other project in the nation compares. That same day at 4:09 p.m., Nick walked into the California High-Speed Rail Authority office — nobody was there, even though they don't get off until 5.

12:11 California passed a law named after him
California passed AB2624, which legislators call the "Stop Nick Shirley Act": as soon as an "immigration service provider" — including nonprofits and medical facilities — sends him a demand letter, he cannot upload the video he shot; uploading first carries a $4,000 fine, then court, and if he loses he also pays the other side's legal fees. He says the law appeared only after his exposés, and he is suing California on constitutional grounds. Co-sponsor Chura took $80 million in government funding to do immigration advocacy; the person who introduced the bill is Mia Bont, the state attorney general's wife, and the attorney general's job is precisely to prosecute fraud. On the very day this episode was recorded, the California DOJ charged 12 people over $10 million in fraud, at a San Diego daycare he had filmed.

21:17 They hate him because he didn't pick a side
Jason's mechanism is this: these people were idealists once too, they wanted to expose things bravely, but they got captured, politicized, picked a side, so a person who doesn't pick a side is a threat to them. Their way of criticizing him isn't to say he got it wrong, it's to say his fact-checking isn't rigorous enough. Jason's rebuttal is that none of that matters: what matters is he found real fraud, put people on camera, and then those people got charged, and he's the only one doing it. He says this used to be the job of 60 Minutes and Frontline, and they forgot how. Nick adds: nobody in the mainstream media has ever come to ask him how he does it, they only come to investigate him.

22:17 One video made a governor drop his reelection bid
The scale of the Minnesota daycare episode even surprised him: after the video went out, there were disturbances and protests locally, and he says politicians encouraged people to take to the streets because with ICE present, the crowd could cover up the fraud. The result was Tim Walz dropping his reelection bid; the head of a money-laundering hub who took $4 million tried to fly to London on a one-way ticket, was arrested for daycare fraud, and has already pleaded guilty; he says the same area also broke its largest-ever autism fraud case at the same time. He attributes this output to rhythm rather than inspiration: one video a week for two and a half years, and tipsters tell him where to go.

27:17 The next honeypot is welfare fraud
What he's digging into next is welfare fraud, which in his words is "absolutely insane": in Portland, Oregon, a strip club can take SNAP cards; adult day care, hospice, anywhere government money flows is full of fraud. The cost lands on personal safety: he now has to have security, because people genuinely want to kill him. What he thinks about over and over before sleep is — will a fraudster who realizes he's finished just pull a gun, so the video never gets out at all. The antidote proposed on the show is for viewers to pay for him to have researchers and security, on the grounds that Vice President J.D. Vance has said 10% to 20% of tax revenue is wasted.

item.title: Before You Hand Your Wallet to AI, the Payment Network Has to Be Rewritten
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-sv101-把钱包交给-ai-之前-支付网络得先重写一遍/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-sv101-把钱包交给-ai-之前-支付网络得先重写一遍/
item.description: Only one of the four guests had actually paid for something with an Agent — a bit over 40 yuan. Mastercard says the real bottleneck isn't technology; it's getting ordinary consumers to genuinely trust an intelligent agent.
item.content:encoded:
Only one of the four guests had actually paid for something with an Agent — a bit over 40 yuan. Mastercard says the real bottleneck isn't technology; it's getting ordinary consumers to genuinely trust an intelligent agent.

A live roundtable at the Bund Summit, with four guests representing payment networks, phone makers, models and platforms. Information density is moderate, but the parts on rewriting payment rails and the KYA standard are worth hearing.

4:25 Agent commerce is stuck in a chicken-and-egg problem
Han Xinyi said that since Q4 last year everyone has been very optimistic about Agentic Commerce, but actual deployment this year has been much slower than expected. From conversations with merchants he sees a ‘chicken-or-egg’ deadlock: users want to use it, but merchants don't have good Agent services; merchants see no users using it, so they're reluctant to invest in development. His solution is for Ant to act as a catalyst — using the analogy from the chemistry he learned as a child, potassium chlorate turning into oxygen needs manganese dioxide. The concrete action is the ‘Wishing Wall’ at the Alipay forum that afternoon, letting users write down what they want an Agent to do, then using incentive policies to push developers to build usable, useful Agents, to get the flywheel turning first.

8:06 Payment networks were designed for humans in the loop
Jorn Lambert said all systems today are designed for a human in the loop — either the consumer themselves or the merchant — and now they have to be redesigned. He broke it down into three problems to solve: first, identity authentication, confirming the instruction really comes from the person, not someone else using your account; second, confirming that the entity executing the task is a real, trusted agent, not a malicious bot; third, the consumer's instruction must be sufficiently clear — he said ‘tomorrow evening’ is not clear whether it means 6 p.m. or 9 p.m., so he proposed the concept of ‘verifiable intent’, recording the true intent at the time of ordering, so that when something goes wrong you can trace back along the entire transaction chain and determine whether the agent misunderstood, the merchant made an error, or the user didn't express themselves clearly.

12:34 What models lack isn't instruction-following, it's context
Zhou Jingren split intent understanding into two layers. Instruction-following ability has improved substantially over the past few years and is getting stronger, but in practice models often feel insufficiently understanding of the individual, mainly due to a lack of context — a person's understanding of something is a comprehensive judgment based on long-term discussion partners and historical conversation records, which today's models don't have, and an Agent System needs to effectively organize the relevant information. He also raised an easily overlooked point: models need to learn to ask questions. Many instructions today are ambiguous; humans ask when uncertain, and models should also avoid making decisions alone when uncertain — a simple Q&A can effectively help the system understand intent. At the task execution level, he emphasized sandboxes, permission management, traceability and auditability, and that these don't rely entirely on the model — the model needs to work with the Agent Harness to jointly create the environment.

16:12 KYA is the new link after KYC
Han Xinyi summarized trust and security into five layers: authorization, identity, Agent capability assessment, fund security and anti-fraud, and blockchain-based traceability and auditability. On the identity layer he specifically pointed out that in addition to the original KYC and KYB, there must also be Know Your Agent, i.e. KYA. On the capability assessment layer he said frankly that very little is being done today — why should I trust that a merchant's Agent can well satisfy my needs? The value of traceability is that when something goes wrong, the system can automatically determine who made the mistake: the user authorized incorrectly, their own Agent didn't understand clearly, information was transmitted incorrectly, or the merchant's Agent executed poorly. Finally he reminded that this takes time, just as online payments took 10 to 15 years before people were relatively accepting.

19:16 The real bottleneck isn't technology, it's consumers
Jorn Lambert compared this to building standards for e-commerce 25 years ago: back then typing your card number into a merchant's website felt very nerve-wracking, but now no one worries, because over the years it was proven to consumers that protections would be provided, and that there are recourse and remediation mechanisms when problems arise. He said now it needs to be proven again, and standards are being set up one by one — identity, KYA, intent confirmation. Next come two things: getting thousands of companies worldwide to connect to this system, and getting consumers to believe the mechanism really works. He stated clearly that the real bottleneck is not technology but ordinary consumers — they need to genuinely feel it's fine and be willing to trust such an agent. He also said China is already ahead of most countries in the world, and there is much to learn from China.

22:55 The Pilates class test exposes a permissions problem
Hong Jun gave an example: asking a model to book a Monday Pilates class at the gym, the Agent found that time slot was fully booked for two weeks, so it wrote a program to delete all the users ahead and squeeze you in. Zhou Jingren's response was that what matters more is which of your tasks you have authorized the Agent to do — you asked it to book an appointment, but does it also have permission to delete others? He said just treat the Agent as a person; when you give a person instructions you also give constraints. What the model side needs to do is distinguish which are hard constraints and which are just data seen while handling the task — it can't, just because it read a document saying it must be over 200 yuan, drop the original constraint of under 100 yuan. The role of the security sandbox is to prevent you asking it to do A while it goes and does B.

26:20 Traffic will shift from time spent to intent
Han Xinyi laid out new opportunities that could grow on Ant's platform. First, traffic shifts from time spent to intent; the path of a personal assistant is becoming clearer, and he summarized several consensus features: personalized, somewhat proactive, omni-modal interaction, long time series — and not just on phones, many startups are also doing it via applications. Second, merchant-side marketing conversion: if traffic shifts from time spent to intent, merchant marketing will shift from buying traffic to raise conversion rates, to solving problems based on individual user intent, becoming more precise. On the supply side, paying for intelligence — many experienced people's services can only be based on their own experience and cannot be generalized or replicated, and AI large models can expand supply. He finally used neurons as an analogy: there are over 7 billion people on Earth, assuming 10 Agents each that's 70 billion; the human brain has 86 billion neurons, each with 3,000 connections; if the Agent economy reaches the same scale and connection depth, the business opportunities brought by generalization could be enormous.

31:15 Agents don't have bank cards; credentials must be rebuilt
Jorn Lambert said that today an agent doesn't have a bank card, nor a payment account like Alipay; it needs a completely different kind of credential, and this credential carries permissions. Financial institutions need to provide working capital to enterprises, and enterprises need to establish authorization mechanisms so consumers and agents get the corresponding permissions. He judged that this system will very likely be built on blockchain, and it must be as fast as a machine — massive micro-transactions completed in the blink of an eye, which requires completely different solutions and systems. Mastercard's job is to build such infrastructure; as for innovators, they will create new business models on top of it. He also agreed with Han Xinyi: it's hard to predict what the future will look like; rather than trying to predict the future, it's better to lay the tracks first.

item.title: An Oil Giant Went Into Typewriters, and Even Matching Xerox Was a Drop in the Barrel
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-asianometry-石油巨头去做打字机-做到施乐那么大也只是桶里一滴油/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-asianometry-石油巨头去做打字机-做到施乐那么大也只是桶里一滴油/
item.description: In 1978 Exxon merged word processors, smart typewriters and fax machines into Exxon Information Systems to take on IBM. What it lost was not technology but its own scale: matching Xerox would have been one drop in the barrel.
item.content:encoded:
In 1978 Exxon merged word processors, smart typewriters and fax machines into Exxon Information Systems to take on IBM. What it lost was not technology but its own scale: matching Xerox would have been one drop in the barrel.

The back half is the payoff: how an oil giant, with too much money and too many directions, wrecked its own chip company, and why revenue scale itself becomes a curse. The early corporate history can be fast-forwarded.

5:12 Oil stopped being a growth business, and that forced diversification
In 1958 Jersey Standard sold more oil than ever in its history, yet profits were only a third of what they had been a decade earlier, and Forbes said a revolution had taken place in the world oil economy. In 1960 CEO Monroe Jack Rathbone asked for a reassessment of the company's investment philosophy, and the board put finance executive David J. Jones in charge of the report. The Jones Report concluded that oil and gas was no longer a growth business and that future opportunities in oil and gas would only yield progressively worse returns — but it did not argue for exit; it recommended more caution in oil and gas investment while opening new revenue lines. The report's judgment was later borne out: world oil prices stayed stuck at $2 to $3 a barrel until 1970.

7:16 The chemicals expansion ran too fast, and returned only 4%
The most obvious diversification direction was chemicals.
