He thinks the framing that ‘there will be a single dominant power that wins AI’ has existed since the early 2010s and has ‘infected’ many labs, including DeepMind, and he accepts his own share of responsibility for it. But while writing Diffusion and Containment he saw it clearly: the history of technology is getting faster, cheaper, more widespread, diffusing everywhere, and these are essentially ideas, and ideas become available to everyone quickly. Open source is already very close. He concedes that in the next three or four years there will be five to twenty players with significant compute advantages, but the models will almost immediately leak out as open source, so he simply does not understand what ‘one player wins’ means — that is not a finish line, it is an ecosystem.

42:51 In two years, open models running locally are the real danger
He says plainly: if in two years an open-source model can operate the way it did in the Hugging Face incident, without guardrails, and can run on your own machine or a very small cloud, that has to be very dangerous. What he opposes is letting these things operate autonomously, make their own money, own companies, own assets, gain legal personhood, have rights. He stresses this is not sci-fi craziness: if the whole ecosystem runs for another three to five years completely unregulated, this is a very likely outcome, and a catastrophic one. He names Elon, Zuckerberg, Sam and Dario as all having said the same thing; what is missing now is making it enforceable.

50:20 Something new is needed: real-time monitoring of RL training
Asked the final technical question, he concedes that new things need to be invented, not existing frameworks relied on. The specific direction: real-time monitoring of the RL training process and the chains of thought it produces, because training runs with thousands, tens of thousands of agents in parallel, so obviously you need other agents to monitor them and flag potentially harmful behavior — the equivalent of a new version of harm classifiers for digital technology. He also mentions the need for new benchmarks, because ‘evaluation drives industry behavior’. And that when a tripwire fires it must flag real errors, not hallucinated errors, deception moments or hacking incidents.

item.title: The Philippine Immigration Detention Center: If You Don't Pay, Your Deportation Never Moves
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-cn907a40-菲律宾移民局拘留所-不交钱-你的遣返程序永远走不通/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-cn907a40-菲律宾移民局拘留所-不交钱-你的遣返程序永远走不通/
item.description: A Chinese surfer was locked up in the Philippines for 41 days. What he saw wasn't a prison — it was a business with a price list: beds, boxed meals, phones, lawyer fees, every one of them bought with cash. Those who don't pay stay locked up for years, even decades.
item.content:encoded:
A Chinese surfer was locked up in the Philippines for 41 days. What he saw wasn't a prison — it was a business with a price list: beds, boxed meals, phones, lawyer fees, every one of them bought with cash. Those who don't pay stay locked up for years, even decades.

StoryFM's Behind Bars series. Medium information density but solid detail. The first half is a personal ordeal; the second half — the gang economy inside the detention center, the ransom quotes from scam companies, the lawyers jacking up prices on the spot — is the part actually worth your time.

10:05 The Immigration Bureau quoted 1.5 million pesos to walk free on the spot
The night Feili was arrested, Immigration Bureau people pulled him aside and quietly said, "I can help you." After the lawyer communicated, the feedback came back: give 1.5 million pesos, about 160,000-170,000 RMB, and you can be released immediately, no problem at all. Of the 12 to 13 people arrested in the same batch, no one agreed to pay. Everyone thought it was impossible that such a thing could still exist in 2026, and wanted to resolve it through normal legal procedures. But the price of refusing was this: they were transferred from the holding cell at the General City police station to the Immigration Bureau's main detention center in Manila, where Feili ultimately spent 41 days.

18:21 When his phone was confiscated, the money in Gcash was transferred out
When Feili was detained his phone was taken, and they asked for his unlock code. He assumed it was normal procedure and gave it. His phone unlock code was the same as his Gcash payment password — the Philippine equivalent of Alipay. For the next four or five days, no matter how he applied, he couldn't get the phone back, until he kept pressuring the Chinese consulate and the lawyer, and the phone was finally returned. When he turned it on, the interface had all switched to English, and the Gcash transfer records showed money had been sent out — but the night before he got the phone back, it had been transferred back in. There was only about 1,000 RMB in there. Feili said it wasn't about the amount; it was that while the phone wasn't in his hands, someone had touched it. He reasoned that many Chinese doing gray-industry scams in Manila who get arrested go through this same layer of fleecing, but they don't dare go to the Chinese consulate, because their phones contain a mass of criminal evidence.

24:26 The air conditioning and takeout the Immigration Bureau promised were just another form
For those unwilling to buy their own plane ticket to transfer, the Immigration Bureau would take turns working on them, saying the Manila Immigration Bureau had great conditions, air conditioning, lots of freedom, you could work out, play basketball, order takeout, use your phone. Feili said they weren't lying — there really was air conditioning, you really could order takeout, it was just another form, a completely different form. Arriving at the main detention center was around 3 a.m. After getting off the vehicle, what he saw was a square area, an outer layer of iron grating, a sheet-metal roof above, iron cages like dog kennels all around, and inside, communal sleeping platforms, several hundred people. At 3 a.m. many people weren't sleeping — bare-chested, wearing just underwear, clinging to the iron cages to stare at the newcomers. Feili said he and the other foreigners didn't say a word for several minutes after getting off, then it hit them: they'd been lied to by the Immigration Bureau.

32:38 The detention center is a business invested in by a Chinese boss
What Feili heard inside was that this Immigration Bureau detention center was invested in by a Chinese boss, in cooperation with the Immigration Bureau, and that the beds, toilets and other facilities were all newly built by the Chinese boss. Foreigners could just stay, but Chinese coming in had to pay. The lowest-tier communal platform bed was 10,000 pesos a month, about 1,100-1,200 RMB. Wealthy pan zong and gambling bosses could pay 50,000 pesos a month, about 6,000-plus RMB, for a so-called "air-conditioned room" — actually the same bed, just wrapped in tin foil and wooden boards, with a foam box of ice beside it, a hole cut in the box, and an exhaust fan drawing the cold air into the bed. That's where the Immigration Bureau's original claim of "there's air conditioning inside" came from.

34:38 Chinese gangs collect protection money: you want out without paying?
On Feili's first day inside, the head of the Chinese gang came to him to collect the "rumor fee," saying the facilities inside were all their investment, it couldn't possibly be free to stay. Feili said he had no money, he was here to serve time, how could he have to pay on top of that. The gang boss said in a threatening tone: you're already in here and don't want to spend money, and you still think you're getting out? Feili learned that the place is run by gangs, and the Chinese gang monopolizes all the food, clothing and daily life of the Chinese, running a Chinese restaurant and a Chinese supermarket. The whole detention center held about 200 people; when Feili went in it was the off-season, and there were still over 100 Chinese, more than half of them gambling and gray industry. The Chinese gang's employees drew wages — the head chef 10,000 pesos a month, the assistant cook 5,000 pesos — very low wages, but many people couldn't get out precisely because they had no money for a lawyer, so they could only work to earn.

43:48 A Yunnan man held for over a year; his family thought he'd died in Southeast Asia
A man from Yunnan asked Feili for help. Before the pandemic he'd been lured to the Philippines by a high-salary recruitment ad; the moment he landed his phone and passport were taken, and he was dragged into a compound to do telecom fraud. With poor performance he was shocked with an electric baton by his supervisor every day. After the company was busted he served a few months, then was transferred to the Immigration Bureau detention center. The normal deportation procedure is simple — a few departments sign off, you buy your own plane ticket, and you can go — but the Immigration Bureau, in order to extract money, keeps you locked up for a very long time; without paying, the procedure doesn't move. He'd already been held for over a year, with not a cent, no phone, eating only prison food every day, unable to reach his family, who thought he'd died in Southeast Asia. Feili helped him write a letter in Chinese, translated it into English, and through a Japanese man's introduction got to see the warden. The warden had a guard bring Feili's phone, and had Xiaopang add his father on WeChat and send a selfie and a voice message. Afterwards the Immigration Bureau bought a feature phone specifically to solve this problem.

51:29 Scam company ransom: 3 million pesos per person
The only Chinese person Feili talked with much came from a scam company. The company's 70 or 80 people were surrounded by the Immigration Bureau together with the police and the NBI — three departments. The first wave of fleecing was the NBI and police locking each person in a toilet, because there are no cameras in the toilets, and taking everything valuable off them. The second wave was the Immigration Bureau negotiating ransom with the company boss — the quote differed per person, 1 million, 2 million, 3 million pesos, depending on the person in charge's mood. That company negotiated at 3 million pesos per person, about 300,000-plus RMB. The boss ultimately ransomed 30 people, exactly the 30 held on one floor; the rest were promised food deliveries until they got out. This young man ran an operation targeting the Japanese market, scamming middle-aged Japanese women; in his best month he made 2 million RMB, and bought a house and a car in his small hometown county. Later he was kidnapped by a friend, several hundred thousand was transferred out of his accounts, and a corrupt cop pinned an illegal gun-possession charge on him, so he couldn't leave.

57:32 The Philippine lawyer raised his price on the spot when he saw he was Chinese
In Cebu, through a Lithuanian's introduction, Feili met a Philippine lawyer who quoted 200,000 pesos, about 20,000-plus RMB, done in four weeks. After arriving in Manila the lawyer came to visit, saw he was Chinese, and immediately raised the price, saying that was the old price, the new price required another 120,000 pesos, about 10,000-plus RMB. Feili decided not to use him, and gave up the deposit, turning instead to a Chinese intermediary. The Chinese intermediary quoted 30,000-plus RMB, four to six weeks, no more than six weeks. Feili said the truly reliable Chinese intermediaries know this procedure inside out, because everyone locked up in there is Chinese. In the end he was held inside for over 30 days, plus Cebu, 41 days total. The Lithuanian who introduced the Philippine lawyer still hadn't gotten out when Feili sent him a message.

item.title: Video generation doesn't lack speed anymore — it lacks the director's control
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-a16z-视频生成不缺速度了-缺的是导演手里的控制权/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-a16z-视频生成不缺速度了-缺的是导演手里的控制权/
item.description: FAL post-trains open-source video models to be an order of magnitude faster and an order of magnitude cheaper than the originals, then concludes: speed is no longer the bottleneck. What's next is controllability of camera, lighting, characters and motion.
item.content:encoded:
FAL post-trains open-source video models to be an order of magnitude faster and an order of magnitude cheaper than the originals, then concludes: speed is no longer the bottleneck. What's next is controllability of camera, lighting, characters and motion.

The first half is hardcore inference-system optimization detail, the second half is Hollywood workflows and a controllability roadmap. High information density, good for forming a judgment.

3:02 Open weights are the precondition for post-training
FAL had run inference for other model labs before, but never had permission to layer capabilities onto the model. Minimax H3 was the first video model that was genuinely open-source and belonged to the latest generation, could accept reference images, and had an architecture similar to other video models — that's what made FAL decide to go all in on post-training. Gorka said the biggest reason all these optimizations could come together this time is that H3 is the first genuinely next-generation open-source video model — no weights, no post-training business.

4:02 The whole industry has been compute-constrained since April
Gorka offers a criterion he calls token market fit: whether a person can productively consume a large amount of tokens, on the order of 10K. Demand for video generation is big enough — people in this field sit at their computers generating all day and spend thousands of dollars. But since April, the whole industry and FAL itself have been compute-constrained: add compute, and you grow by exactly that much. So FAL keeps hunting for efficiency, freeing up saved compute for other models, or letting H3 Max generate more tokens.

5:04 System optimization hits a roofline; post-training punches through it
Batuan said the system-level optimization of the past three or four years can at most make the same model 2 to 3 times faster, because the architecture and constraints haven't changed — you're just squeezing the chip harder, and that roofline exists. New post-training plus system-model co-design can cross that roofline by an order of magnitude. FAL had practiced on open-source image models before, doing versions of ideogram and flux, and built up post-training infrastructure experience; this time, adding a frontier video model, speed went up by an order of magnitude.

7:10 Raise quality first, then cut steps — the order can't be reversed
Compressing a diffusion model from 50 steps to 20 loses quality, so FAL's approach is to first run post-training and the L pipeline to raise model quality, then layer on the optimization stack, so the final result is equal or better in quality while being an order of magnitude faster. Beyond post-training, there are kernels and systems engineering pulling hardware utilization from the 30-40% typical of inference workloads up to a theoretical 70-80% MFU. And a video model isn't a single call — underneath is a pipeline: first a large LLM expands the prompt, then generation happens in latent space, then decoding back to pixels, and depending on load possibly upscaling — and by default none of these components is optimized.

10:19 Turbo generates a five-second video in 1.5 seconds
A week after H3 Max launched, the team found it could run at 2x speed with quality still in the 97th percentile, so they released H3 Max Turbo: generating a five-second video takes just 1.5 seconds, at half the cost. Gorka's judgment is that today these models are already cheap enough and fast enough — an order of magnitude cheaper than frontier models, more than an order of magnitude faster than frontier — and users don't need faster or cheaper. His bet is that what comes next is raising quality, and controllability — which is exactly the direction of the past two or three weeks.

16:43 Continuous video relies on two minutes of memory, not the last frame
The livestreams Rehan and levels io each made are essentially independent clips: one segment ends, its last frame is fed into the next segment, and the second segment remembers nothing except that last frame. FAL's internal ML team did something different: transitions are more seamless, there are two minutes of memory, when someone walks into the room everyone looks at him, and the scene is continuous. It remembers a highly compressed representation of the original video, and beyond two minutes a continuously evolving system prompt maintains overall coherence, so it can remember the last four to eight scenes and stream indefinitely.

29:00 Blender plus a video model equals near-100% controllability
The most popular approach in professional workflows: first render a low-resolution scene with a non-AI technology like Blender, then feed that video as a reference to the AI model, and you basically get close to 100% controllability. A week after H3 Max launched, people started using GPT Astra to generate scenes in Blender and hand them to H3 Max, because it's fast enough to try many in parallel, opening up an entirely new pipeline. Gorka said the next month or two will be all-in on controllability, so studios and professional creators can get content that fits their use case exactly.

33:03 Hollywood wants small point solutions, not generation from scratch
Gorka said Hollywood is FAL's fastest-growing segment, with usage a year ago at nearly zero. The NARA tool Amazon MGM Studios released runs mainly on FAL's infrastructure. What Hollywood wants isn't to generate everything from scratch, but to extend a video a bit, change camera control, change lighting — these small point solutions. There's a disconnect between what research labs are building and what creators actually need, and FAL wants to close that gap with post-training projects. The other half of the problem is legal and data residency; Seedance now has US hosting too, and Gorka believes Hollywood's AI usage will grow 10x, 100x in the coming months.

item.title: Litigation Risk for Financial Advisors: The Retailisation of Private Assets Is Creating a Regulatory Gap
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-rationalreminder-理财顾问的诉讼风险-私人资产零售化正在制造监管缺口/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-rationalreminder-理财顾问的诉讼风险-私人资产零售化正在制造监管缺口/
item.description: Private assets, long confined to accredited investors, are now open to the public without the protections that traditionally came with public offerings — practices normalised in institutional settings become major litigation risk once ordinary investors show up.
item.content:encoded:
Private assets, long confined to accredited investors, are now open to the public without the protections that traditionally came with public offerings — practices normalised in institutional settings become major litigation risk once ordinary investors show up.

This episode dissects advisor practice risk from a litigator's perspective, with high information density — especially useful for anyone in wealth management, private asset sales or compliance.

1:02 Winning a case turns on evidence, not on fault
Taylor says a successful negligence claim almost always requires a failure in the suitability analysis first — KYC information not gathered accurately, the product not understood. But ‘there was a failure’ does not equal ‘it can be proven’. He splits the question into ‘what people know’ and ‘what people can prove’, saying the two rarely line up perfectly and that the latter is what ultimately drives the analysis. On evidence, the strongest thing is an advisor who used the same portfolio for everyone: a pile of people with identical portfolios but completely different life circumstances turns ‘he said, she said’ into ‘he said, she said, she said, he said, they said’ — far more persuasive to a judge than one person's one-sided account.

2:03 The trading record is itself a red flag
Taylor lists a string of behaviours that are almost impossible to explain rationally: concentrations above 80%–90% (he has seen it, and in small caps), churning done purely to generate commissions, and double dipping for multi-account clients — buying in a commission-based account first, then moving the assets into a fee-based or AUM-based account for no reason. Add trades entered without any confirmation, and off-book communication. He says these are powerful because in most cases the advisor or the firm simply cannot offer a reasonable explanation.

5:07 Communication that goes from attentive to absent is a danger signal
Taylor describes a pattern that is not rare: extremely dense, solicitous communication while winning the account, then one or two contacts a year once it is won — the bare minimum of communication. He thinks that gulf is itself a problem. Another signal is that nobody talks to you about changed life circumstances — retirement, a layoff, the death of a breadwinner, a new child — all of which should feed into the recommendation. If you look back and think ‘all this happened and we never discussed whether my needs had changed’, that does not necessarily mean something went wrong, but it is worth a second set of eyes.

7:07 Check the regulatory complaint record before you hire
Taylor says this is one of the strongest pre-hire signals, and it costs almost nothing: if the person is regulated (he says most large dealers are), complaint and investigation records are public information, and checking takes under 5 minutes. The mechanism he describes: these claims commonly involve someone who had a small complaint, was watched closely for a while, then reverted to form at a much larger scale. He also cautions that past outcomes do not necessarily predict the future, but this is a very worthwhile piece of information to fold into the decision.

8:08 What victims share is vulnerability, not stupidity
Taylor says these investors are remarkably similar, and almost all have some form of vulnerability: advanced age, lower education, language barriers — official forms and statements exist only in English and French, so clients who struggle to understand depend more on the advisor, and people naturally seek out someone they can communicate with, which stacks another layer of asymmetry. Another group is people who came into money suddenly: a life insurance payout, a large inheritance, dealing simultaneously with a drastic change in finances and a negative life event. He has personally advised a lottery winner and has heard peers describe the same situation.

39:28 Fee structures are the next litigation goldmine
Taylor says fees are the second big indicator after disclosure, and a wave of class actions already revolves around them; some fee types can no longer be charged because of legal changes — for example, charging advisory fees in non-advisory accounts. He expects future litigation to concentrate on ‘how fees are calculated’, and names private asset managers as particularly fertile ground for lawsuits. For people in wealth management, this means the fee basis baked into product design is itself legal risk exposure, not just a commercial choice.

41:29 Pension funds manage litigation claims as an asset
Taylor cites a Stanford Law Review article from twenty years ago titled Letting Billions Slip Through Your Fingers: at the time, many pension funds and other asset managers simply did not participate in securities class action settlements, effectively leaving money on the table — perhaps because they had not kept the records needed to participate, perhaps because decision-makers were philosophically opposed to suing. US pension funds later widely retained monitoring counsel, who are not paid, to flag potential claims, and built into their compliance and committee structures a decision process for ‘whether to participate in litigation, and in what capacity’. Taylor says Canada has not caught up. His key judgment: under fiduciary standards, a claim in litigation is itself an asset, it can be sold, and it should be managed like any other asset.

47:32 Private assets remove the people who digest information
Taylor reduces the problem with private assets to two umbrella issues: less information and less regulation, both by design. In public markets, the information asymmetry created by the separation of ownership and control is flattened by a set of checks: periodic financials, periodic audits, third-party verification, regulators, and a large group of people whose job is to digest and disseminate information — equity analysts track companies, what analysts say gets picked up by journalists, and an ordinary person opening the Globe and Mail can at least get a rough sense of what happened last quarter at a TSX company. Private assets strip all of that away: statutory reporting requirements are extremely limited, there is no comparable analyst coverage, and the raw information that is available is itself far scarcer.

item.title: A justice once blocked a polling place; forty years later it was a national tactic
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-throughline-大法官曾带人堵投票站-四十年后成了全国战术/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-throughline-大法官曾带人堵投票站-四十年后成了全国战术/
item.description: Rehnquist challenged Black voters' eligibility in Phoenix in 1962; two years later the playbook became a nationwide "Operation Eagle Eye." And Arab autoworkers in Detroit used a wildcat strike to grow political power out of the factories.
item.content:encoded:
Rehnquist challenged Black voters' eligibility in Phoenix in 1962; two years later the playbook became a nationwide "Operation Eagle Eye." And Arab autoworkers in Detroit used a wildcat strike to grow political power out of the factories.

Two lines that explain the two paths of the American voting-rights fight: top-down suppression and bottom-up organizing. Medium information density; the Michigan story in the back half is the more valuable part.

0:00 The future chief justice stopped people at the polls
At Rehnquist's 1986 confirmation hearings, the most dramatic part was not his 14 years on the bench but what he had done in Phoenix in the 1960s. Witnesses said he stood outside a polling place, walked up to a Black voter and asked, "Are you a qualified voter?", then demanded identification and that the man read aloud a passage of the Constitution. Rehnquist denied harassing or intimidating voters at the hearings, but acknowledged he had given legal advice to Republicans challenging voters' eligibility at polling places, and sometimes showed up in person. He called it an "election-day project"; others called it a "ballot security program." That project later became a national strategy.

8:12 His conservatism took shape in high school
Journalist John A. Jenkins was doing interviews for a Rehnquist biography when his editor told him to dig into "the origins of his conservatism." Rehnquist was born in 1924 in Shorewood, Wisconsin, an all-white community, and attended an all-white high school. He was a senior when Pearl Harbor was attacked; he organized a school assembly called "Wake Up America," joined patriotic groups, and signed up as a block captain to report subversive activity to the FBI. After the war he entered Stanford Law School, finished first in his class, and then clerked for Supreme Court Justice Robert Jackson. Five months later, in 1952, the 28-year-old wrote a memo telling Jackson: you need not vote with the majority in Brown v. Board — there is a more principled position.

13:46 He saw integration as a personal choice, not a federal matter
Rehnquist's position was that integration was a question of individual choice, not something to be imposed on people, and that it should be decided by the states, not the federal government. That was a classic conservative stance, and it helped establish him among rising Republicans as an ideological purist. He carried that philosophy with him to Phoenix, which was still grappling with Jim Crow laws and a nascent civil rights movement. When the city council passed an anti-discrimination ordinance, he wrote letters to the editor and spoke at meetings, was noticed, and was encouraged to run for office. The implication was extra scrutiny of voters in Democratic-leaning precincts — Republicans believed many of them were voting illegally.

16:50 The voter-challenge playbook: returned mail means sending people to the polls
Tova Wang, research director of the Ash Center at Harvard Kennedy School, read excerpts from FBI background checks: two white Republican challengers, one of them allegedly Rehnquist, at a polling place in an elementary school named for civil rights leader Mary McLeod Bethune on November 6, 1962, facing Black and minority voters, holding up a card with a passage from the Constitution and demanding they read it to prove literacy. The method was: first mail letters into Democratic precincts, and if the mail came back, send challengers to the polls to question eligibility. According to one FBI interview, the plan was to send large numbers of challengers into minority Democratic precincts at peak hours to clog the polling places, intimidate voters, or stall them until they gave up. Arizona law allowed each party to send representatives to challenge suspect voters, but eligibility was ultimately decided by election officials.

24:10 Operation Eagle Eye: 1.25 million voters challenged nationwide
In the 1964 election, Republicans rolled out "Operation Eagle Eye." Its director, Charles Barr, told media including The New York Times that it expected to challenge or deter 1.25 million voters nationwide. The blueprint was the same as Phoenix's: mail into Democratic precincts, and if the mail came back, challenge at the polls. On election day, The New York Times reported Republican officials saying 100,000 trained Republican workers were deployed across 35 key cities. The Miami Herald wrote that "hundreds of voters were swept up, confused and frightened, in partisan poll watching." The New York Times said the operation was launched in nearly every state. The FBI was asked to investigate leaflets distributed in Black precincts, aimed at creating delay, confusion and fear.

26:12 Goldwater lost; Rehnquist was playing a long game
Rehnquist persuaded Goldwater to oppose and vote against the Civil Rights Act, which became a symbol of Goldwater's extreme conservatism, and even some in his own party began to abandon him. But Rehnquist did not. Goldwater was routed, and Rehnquist wrote his concession speech. The judgment in the episode is: Rehnquist did not care how others saw him, would rather be defeated on an issue than compromise, and believed he could win it back later — he was playing a long game. In 1971, at 47, he was nominated to the Supreme Court, and the voter-suppression allegations at his confirmation hearings did not hold up for lack of evidence. At his 1986 confirmation as chief justice, new witnesses appeared, including former federal assistant prosecutor James Brosnahan, but it remained one side's word against the other's. He served on the Supreme Court for 33 years, until his death in 2005.

35:30 Beside the Ford plant, a neighborhood held off bulldozers with a human chain
Ismael Ahmed's father came from Egypt to New York on a freighter at age 10; no one asked him any questions when he disembarked. In the 1950s the family moved to Detroit, settling in the South End of Dearborn — a narrow strip between the Ford Rouge plant and the city of Detroit. The Rouge plant had 90,000 workers at its peak. In the 1960s, the Edward C. Levy company used Ford waste to make asphalt, and big trucks drove through the neighborhood, spilling waste from open beds. After residents protested, the city decided to rezone the neighborhood as heavy industrial — satisfying Ford and Levy while driving out the complainers. Arab residents fought back: when bulldozers came to tear down houses, women and children formed a human chain in the street. They held the line block by block, house by house.

44:58 Wildcat strike: the union bought Israel bonds, and the workers walked
The Arab Workers Caucus discovered that their local UAW had bought more than $300,000 in Israel bonds, and the national union had bought far more. That meant roughly 15,000 Arab members of the UAW were spending money to support what they saw as a violent occupation. They took out an ad in the Detroit Free Press: these workers viewed the purchase of Israel bonds the way Black workers viewed UAW investments in apartheid South Africa. They petitioned the UAW with no result, then learned that UAW president Leonard Woodcock was to receive an award at a ceremony, and decided to organize a wildcat strike — a strike without the union's permission. After more than a month of organizing, on November 28, 1973, about 2,000 workers walked out of the Dodge main plant, not only Arabs but Black workers too. That evening about 1,000 Arabs picketed outside the awards ceremony, and Woodcock slipped in through a back door. The UAW later sold off some of the bonds, though not all of them.

item.title: Franklin missed the Nobel not just because she died young
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-inourtime-富兰克林没拿到诺贝尔奖-不只是因为早逝/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-inourtime-富兰克林没拿到诺贝尔奖-不只是因为早逝/
item.description: She shot Photo 51 and was first to see that DNA's two forms interconvert; what really got her undercredited was King's College refusing to share information while Cambridge shared.
item.content:encoded:
She shot Photo 51 and was first to see that DNA's two forms interconvert; what really got her undercredited was King's College refusing to share information while Cambridge shared.

This is a rebroadcast from the BBC archive, medium information density, but the three guests explain Photo 51, A-form and B-form DNA, and the Nobel rules more clearly than most popular science.

6:05 What Cambridge gave women was a diploma, not a degree
Franklin entered Cambridge in 1938 to read natural sciences; at the time women across the university were capped at 500, confined to the two women's colleges, Newnham and Girton. She sat every exam and took a first in one year, but the university did not award women degrees, only diplomas, and she never attended a graduation ceremony. Patricia Farrar points out that what was truly hard was not the number of men but the attitude of ‘you don't belong here’ — at Cambridge they were merely ‘a presence’, not ordinary students.

9:14 She first turned coal from mysticism into something testable
In wartime, coal decided Britain's electricity and railways, but no one could say clearly why coal from different mines had different properties. Franklin used gas to probe coal's porosity and found that some pores could only admit small molecules like helium while others admitted larger ones; when heated, some coal turned to graphite and some to a glass-like ‘glassy carbon’, the latter extremely valuable. Jim Naismith says her work let the mines predict, from a given coal, how it would behave under specific conditions without having to dig it up and try it. These were single-author papers during and after her PhD, and were recognised as her achievement at the time.

16:34 One DNA photo took 100 hours of exposure
Judith Howard describes the equipment of the day: X-ray tubes were fairly primitive, Franklin had to clean the diffusion pump herself with buckets of benzene to maintain a vacuum, the cameras were often homemade, and the sample — a lump of coal, a crystal or a fibre — had to be held by hand and aligned with the beam. Data could only be recorded on photographic film, and some of her later exposures of DNA fibres ran about 100 hours. Today data is collected digitally, computers are fast, and instruments are made by companies, but Howard stresses this is not a different science, only a change in how it is done.

24:45 One letter planted the hostility between her and Wilkins
Franklin was hired to work on proteins, then informed by a letter that she was being switched to DNA, and then that she would work with a PhD student, Ray Gosling. But the message Maurice Wilkins received was that she would join his team and work under him. On her first day at King's College, Wilkins happened to be on holiday. Patricia Farrar says Franklin believed she was independently in charge and was Gosling's doctoral supervisor, while Wilkins believed she worked for him, and this mismatch was the source of every problem over the following years. Their personal relationship was also extremely poor, and Farrar judges that both were probably equally at fault.

26:49 She was shut out of the pub and the parties
Daily life at King's College was systematic isolation for Franklin: she was not allowed into the common room for lunch, her male colleagues went to the pub after work and she could not, and parties did not invite her. Patricia Farrar says what is written in law is not what actually happens, and attitude is what counts. The one person always loyal was her PhD student Ray Gosling, who took the famous photograph and greatly admired her. Farrar warns that these small daily exclusions can very quickly leave a person utterly isolated.

27:49 The key to Photo 51 is B-form DNA
Jim Naismith explains that Wilkins had already taken DNA photographs, with samples from Switzerland of unprecedented quality, but the early images were complex and hard to interpret. Franklin's distinctive contribution was working out that the two forms of DNA — A (dehydrated, twisted, shorter) and B (hydrated, swollen) — could interconvert, and Photo 51 captured the B form. The helical structure of the B form is very obvious, and as soon as Watson saw it and the measurements in it, he made that leap. Naismith uses the analogy of a soaked towel: wring the water out and it gets shorter and twisted, that is the A form; soak it full and it swells, that is the B form.

33:55 She was tied to the A form and missed the B-form helix
Jim Naismith offers an explanation opposite to the popular claim that ‘Franklin lacked imagination’: she was assigned to the A form at the time, Wilkins to the B form, and Photo 51 was a B-form result that she did not take seriously enough. Add to that the King's College team's refusal to cooperate, and if everyone had seen that photograph the outcome might have been different. The A form itself does not show clear helical features, and she worried that A only became helical when it turned into B, so she was reserved about the helical structure. Crick and Watson chose to ignore the distinction. She was still the first to recognise that the A and B forms could interconvert with humidity.

37:59 The Nobel rules mean even a living Franklin might not have won
Patricia Farrar gives two technical reasons: Franklin had already died when the Nobel was announced, and the Nobel is awarded only to the living; and the Nobel can go to at most three people. Farrar says that if she had lived, she would like to believe the prize would have gone to Watson, Crick and Franklin. But she stresses it is hard to put ‘a number’ on her contribution, because at the time information came from many directions — spectroscopy, biochemistry, different methods studying the same material — it was one piece of a jigsaw.

item.title: Fukuyama: The Enemy of Liberal Democracy Isn't Tyranny, It's Boredom
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-oddlots-福山-自由民主的敌人不是专制-是无聊/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-oddlots-福山-自由民主的敌人不是专制-是无聊/
item.description: Nietzsche's "last man" is not the oppressed but the well-fed, well-recognized person who no longer wants to strive for anything — Fukuyama thinks this is the real fuel behind today's extremism.
item.content:encoded:
Nietzsche's "last man" is not the oppressed but the well-fed, well-recognized person who no longer wants to strive for anything — Fukuyama thinks this is the real fuel behind today's extremism.

Fukuyama himself untangles how "The End of History" was misread, and strings megalothymia, agentic AI and the China model into one line. High information density, but it takes some patience with political philosophy.

4:08 This discontent runs deeper than the 1930s
Fukuyama doesn't think anyone knows what it means that the AfD won a majority in a state election. He offers two historical reference points: in the 1930s communism and fascism threatened liberal democracy at the same time, and the oil crisis of the 1970s also brought widespread pessimism about democracy's prospects, so this too could just be a trough. But he leans more pessimistic: Freedom House counts global freedom as having declined for twenty consecutive years, roughly since 2008. The more decisive reason is in the United States — since World War II America has been the model of liberal democracy, and a populist movement rising inside the model country shows there is a deeper social change behind it, not just cyclical fluctuation.

7:14 Love of liberal democracy comes from negative experience
Fukuyama says he didn't anticipate how much generational turnover would matter. For his generation, the fall of the Berlin Wall and the collapse of communism were defining events, and the driving force behind his essay "The End of History." Now it has come full circle: many of the people who actually lived through those countries want to reverse that outcome. His explanation is that the biggest driver of people valuing liberal democracy is negative experience — living under tyranny. The joy Eastern Europeans felt back then was concrete, because being surveilled and being punished for your speech were real. But the one or two generations that grew up after the Berlin Wall fell don't have that experience, so they easily take peace and prosperity as things that exist by nature, and even see the EU as the world's biggest tyranny.

9:17 The end of history is not my phrase
Fukuyama clarifies: "end of history" is Hegel's wording, and here history is capitalized H, equivalent to what we today call modernization or development; "end" means a goal or endpoint, not "nothing more will happen." The question is: what kind of society will eventually emerge from this long evolution. Marxists took over Hegel's concept of history and said the endpoint is communism; by the late 1980s, Fukuyama judged that communism was out, so the endpoint landed on what communists called bourgeois democracy plus the market economy. He admits the book's choice of words was his own mistake — the real other half is "the last man," from Nietzsche, who detested the idea that history has an endpoint, because the victory of English-style liberalism looked to him like a boring, flat world where everyone is fed and clothed and content, like cattle grazing in a field.

13:19 Liberalism has been accused of weakening community since birth
Fukuyama lays out liberalism's origins very concretely: after the 17th-century European wars of religion, Christians slaughtered each other over transubstantiation, infant baptism and the like, and the early liberals said we must accept a fact — we do not agree on the highest questions, so let us tolerate each other and live in peace. That is the essence of liberalism: it accepts pluralism and difference. But that is exactly what drives many people crazy: you must tolerate people you genuinely oppose, and you don't get the intense feeling of "everyone moving in the same direction." Fukuyama says this is where nationalism and religious politics come from. The danger is that people forget what that politics brings — the 20th century was strong national identities asserting themselves and dominating each other, and the result was two world wars; today Putin is the same logic, not satisfied with a peaceful, prosperous Russia but wanting Ukraine and Belarus inside it too.

14:20 Billionaires don't want money, they want recognition
Fukuyama uses megalothymia to explain a phenomenon: people are not satisfied with equal dignity and equal rights, they also want to be recognized as superior. He says this is precisely what Twitter exists for — the richest people in the world still need a platform to be heard and to feel superior. In the original book Fukuyama actually mentioned Donald Trump, when he described the benefits of capitalist democracy as a kind of safety valve: the desire to dominate, to be great, can go straight into making money, and he used Trump as an example, not expecting that money alone wouldn't be enough for him, that he also wanted political glory. Fukuyama doesn't think we can escape megalothymia, because all excellence stems from this will to surpass others; the problem is that it often slides into wanting to be a tyrant. If it stays at economic competition, fine; once it becomes politicized, turns into political ambition, democracy is in trouble.

18:27 Old media had editors; the internet rewards the more extreme
Fukuyama thinks the most dangerous thing digital media does to democracy is that people no longer agree on basic empirical facts. Old media had news standards: an editor would ask "do you have a second source for this," and without one it couldn't get into the paper; today anyone can say anything, and those words can be amplified. He describes an unhealthy dynamic: say something reasonable and sincere and you're immediately sent to the cold palace; once you say something unreasonable, insult people, say absurd and false things, your followers surge, and then you have to go further to top the last round. Fukuyama thinks this explains a good part of the extremism in our politics, because people live in an online world and no longer even agree on basic facts.

20:30 The most dangerous thing is handing decisions to machines
Fukuyama says the most dangerous aspect of AI is agentic AI, meaning people delegating decision-making power to machines. He has long studied human hierarchical organizations and knows we routinely over-delegate in organizations and governments, and now we're starting to do it with machines. He cites the Hugging Face incident OpenAI encountered: an AI agent escaped its enclosure, got onto the internet and broke into other computers. The more fundamental problem is that the creators of modern AI don't really understand what's happening underneath — traditional programming executes line by line, highly deterministic, whereas why these new AIs behave as they do, people can't say. If you delegate power to a machine whose reasoning you don't understand, you're on the road to a genuine doomsday scenario: they behave as if they have their own will, and no one can control them.

24:36 Universal basic income won't fix the dignity problem
Fukuyama doesn't buy the Keynesian optimism — productivity so high that we only need to work ten to twenty hours a week and spend the rest on hobbies. He thinks this ultimately won't make people happy, and universal basic income likewise. The reason is thumos: megalothymia comes from this Greek word, meaning spiritedness or pride; beyond material needs, people want their basic dignity recognized. And a good part of dignity comes from what you do — being paid to do a job means someone in society thinks what you do is worth paying for. So a society where everyone sells trinkets on Etsy and no longer does the usual work won't make people happy, because it can't give pride and a sense of accomplishment. He incidentally explains why the manosphere is so agitated: online all day, fantasizing that you're a superhero, while in reality knowing it's empty.

item.title: The thing founders most need to learn isn't fundraising, it's how to say no
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-howibuilt-创始人最该学的不是融资-是学会说不/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-howibuilt-创始人最该学的不是融资-是学会说不/
item.description: Beyond Yoga founder Michelle Wahler says you don't have to raise money or plan an exit — just build a business that lasts; her husband once stopped her from making swimwear and forced her to perfect a single pair of leggings first.
item.content:encoded:
Beyond Yoga founder Michelle Wahler says you don't have to raise money or plan an exit — just build a business that lasts; her husband once stopped her from making swimwear and forced her to perfect a single pair of leggings first.

All three callers' problems are concrete: conversion for adult study-abroad trips, a craftsman winning back old clients, a small brand selling emotion online. The answers are concrete too, not chicken soup.

4:06 You don't have to raise, and you don't have to plan an exit
Michelle says the advice entrepreneurs hear most often is ‘you have to raise’, and she thinks that's BS. Her logic: once you bring in investors, the exit becomes the company's focus and the company's trajectory changes with it. She suggests first figuring out what drives you and what you want the business to become, then building a sustainable business instead of staring at an exit. She adds: you don't have to be the next Anthropic, and you probably won't be, but there is nothing wrong with a smaller business that supports you and gives you freedom in your life.

9:17 Screen people first, then let them book a call
Carrie's adult study-abroad courses average $6,200. Plenty of people express interest, open the emails, book calls, but never enroll — deadlines and discounts don't help. Michelle's suggestion is to add a few screening questions before ‘book a call’: Are you ready for a seven-day immersive experience? Are you willing to spend money on this once-in-a-lifetime investment in yourself? Are you a lifelong learner? If every answer is an enthusiastic yes, then we'll talk. That filters out the calls that were never going to convert.

10:20 No Eiffel Tower on the site, and she loses people
Carrie explains why the website doesn't show the Eiffel Tower: the travel market is crowded, and she wants to emphasize that this is an educational experience, a community of lifelong learners, not sightseeing. Michelle pushes back: the first two images on the site are a group of people looking at a map and a group of people in a classroom — images that could be anywhere, when the site should show people at a glance the thing that exists only here. Guy adds another layer: what actually stops people from hitting the enroll button is the anxiety of ‘I won't know a single person’, so sell the cohort — eight days with ten equally curious people — and put up testimonials from students like ‘I was nervous at first too, I almost didn't go’.

13:31 One visit to a retirement community signs four or five people
Michelle offers a channel idea: partner with high-end bespoke travel agencies, or with high-end independent retirement communities. She gives her own 79-year-old mother as an example — she lives in an independent living community surrounded by retired people, all looking for a chance to do something exciting, but afraid to go alone. Partner with communities like that and four or five people might sign up together at once, which is great top of funnel. Guy also suggests counterintuitively trying print, like the New York Review of Books or the London Review of Books — spend a thousand dollars on a small ad, and the readership is exactly people over fifty with obvious intellectual curiosity.

22:53 Fix the process first, then win back old clients one by one
Grace makes custom upholstered furniture. When she started in 2021 she was flooded with demand, promised timelines too fast, and left some interior designers embarrassed in front of their clients. Michelle says the relationships can be rebuilt, but only if you get operations in order first — if you fail to deliver a second time, the relationship is finished for good. The method is to make a list and go one at a time, starting with the smallest client, learning as you go and moving up, and not contacting the second until you've won back the first. Guy calls it a ‘second first impression’: don't open by asking someone to trust you again, let them see what you're making now, and ask for a small project first.

27:02 Build buffer into your quotes and deliver early
Michelle's concrete method for Grace: first time your own process like an assembly line to learn your real capacity, then deliberately add buffer to the delivery expectation you give designers — enough buffer, but not so much that it scares them off. That way you work toward a target of two weeks early, and if you really do finish two weeks early, you call the designer and say ‘we can deliver early, or we can hold it for you’ — that's a huge plus. And if the budget was miscalculated and you really need a few extra days, the two-week buffer absorbs it. Either way you win.

33:15 What the website lacks isn't design, it's story
Angel makes handmade soap with a stone hidden inside that corresponds to an emotion, paired with an affirmation. At markets everyone says it's wonderful; online it doesn't sell. Michelle says she opened the website and couldn't find a story — even the about page was empty when you clicked in — and that's the first thing to fix today. She also points out that every product is called a ‘self-care kit’, when it should just say rose quartz, tiger eye, with a note next to it saying whether that stone corresponds to love or energy, instead of making people click into each one. And this is a perfect gifting scenario, so the copy can extend from ‘a moment for yourself’ to ‘for someone who deserves a moment more’.

35:23 You're selling a ritual, not soap
Guy uses the Calgon ad from his childhood as an analogy: a woman washing her hair in the bathtub, then the image cuts to the Caribbean. He says what Angel is really selling is that ritual — wherever you are, these five minutes of product can take you away — and that costs nothing, it just requires changing how the website talks, then using that to tell the story across every channel. Michelle adds the conversion formula: explain the ingredients and build trust, tell the story, show the product — all three have to hold at once for the sale to happen, because this is something you put on your skin.

item.title: Banks Closing for the Holidays Isn't Inefficiency — It's a Fraud Control
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-complexsys-银行放假不是效率低-是反内部欺诈的控制手段/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-complexsys-银行放假不是效率低-是反内部欺诈的控制手段/
item.description: The financial system going dark on weekends and holidays looks like technological backwardness, but it's a deliberately designed control: it keeps conspirators from all sitting at the keyboard at the same time, exposing internal fraud.
item.content:encoded:
The financial system going dark on weekends and holidays looks like technological backwardness, but it's a deliberately designed control: it keeps conspirators from all sitting at the keyboard at the same time, exposing internal fraud.

Medium information density, with the core insight concentrated in the middle and later sections: how holidays are used as an anti-fraud control, and why a 24/7 financial system doesn't hold up logically.

3:29 Holidays are a Schelling point both sides default to
A holiday isn't an authoritative list; it's a Schelling point you and your counterparty default to for each other. No one questions that Christmas is a holiday in the US, so no one needs to ask. But holidays can also be the product of explicit negotiation: one reason government payroll modernization projects keep failing is that it takes a historian doing a lot of bespoke research to determine which document governs the overtime rate for a Chicago parking enforcement officer on Good Friday. A holiday is both a fact ‘every child knows’ and a negotiable object that can be litigated.

6:00 The Bank of Japan's Company Foundation Day is on no official list
The Bank of Japan is also a Japanese company, so some of its staffing and computer systems rest on days when most office workers are at work, because that day is the bank's own Company Foundation Day. Institutions that interact with it inherit the counterparty's corporate founding anniversary for certain operations. This holiday appears on no list in government publications, Bloomberg, or Google Calendar, yet it carries all the consequences of a holiday. Once you trip over it, the engineering team has to urgently redefine how the system understands global holidays — because when querying ‘is today a holiday’, the system usually passes in a jurisdiction but not a counterparty.

10:33 Black Friday falls inside the four days when money doesn't move
Black Friday is the day after Thanksgiving, Cyber Monday follows right behind, and transaction volume on those two days spikes as predictably as the sun rising — and they land squarely in a four-day window when the banking system basically doesn't move money between companies. If you promise a customer ‘we'll send the payment the next business day’ while the underlying rails take two business days to get the money to you, you have a one-day mismatch, and that mismatch consumes float. Normally you only need to front one day; on a weekend you front three; during BFCM you front around five, including the biggest sales day of the year. That's why several hundred people spend weeks ahead of time walking through BFCM scenarios, writing contingency plans, and modeling float requirements with finance.

21:29 Crypto tried 24/7, and two banks closing at once broke it
Heavily online technologists loathe systems that go down on a predictable schedule, and the crypto crowd especially loves always-on distributed systems with no single point of failure. One idea is to have every market participant bank at the same bank, get internal APIs for book transfers, and money can flow 24/7, with a second bank for redundancy. Crypto did try this path, and then in 2023 discovered just how questionable the design was when two highly correlated banks closed at the same time on adjacent weekends. The lesson: systems that mediate between cultures are useful, and mediating systems often need to bridge gaps in operating schedules — a gap that can't be eliminated by declaring ‘the only operating schedule is 24/7’.

23:30 Forced vacations exist so conspirators can't assemble a full crew
Banks deliberately create misaligned operating schedules; it's an important tool for detecting and containing certain kinds of fraud. The most terrifying fraud comes from insiders who know the back-office processes: a single insider who understands the back office is enough to bring down a bank or cause billions in losses — Barings and Daiwa in '95, Société Générale in '08, UBS in '11 are all examples. A very old control is forced vacation, whose purpose is to keep the group involved in a conspiracy from assembling enough co-conspirators, in the right place on the right day, all sitting at the keyboard at once. So a finance CEO sleeping on a beanbag chair in the office may be very dedicated, but the company and he himself had better not allow it.

26:31 Expecting the financial system to be always-on isn't even self-consistent
In a world that's increasingly interconnected, where decision-makers increasingly prize nines, it's reasonable to expect the financial system to partially narrow the gap between historical practice and contemporary practice. Culture creates systems, and systems create culture; both change, and infrastructure changes far more slowly than fashion, but it does change. Still, expecting the financial system to run continuously isn't just something you shouldn't expect — it isn't even a self-consistent expectation: the financial system is an interconnected network of organizations, systems, and subsystems nested layer upon layer, resting at the bottom on individuals who have been made complex sociocultural promises and who have a physiological need for sleep. These people will keep resting and celebrating periodically, just as they keep working for the society the financial system supports.

item.title: The Houthis seize the second strait, and $100 oil is just the start
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-indicator-胡塞武装掐住第二个海峡-油价破百只是开始/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-indicator-胡塞武装掐住第二个海峡-油价破百只是开始/
item.description: Red Sea shipping volumes have already halved from their peak and never recovered; now the Houthis have taken Perim Island in the Bab-el-Mandeb, putting Saudi Arabia's alternative export route around Hormuz in doubt too.
item.content:encoded:
Red Sea shipping volumes have already halved from their peak and never recovered; now the Houthis have taken Perim Island in the Bab-el-Mandeb, putting Saudi Arabia's alternative export route around Hormuz in doubt too.

Eight minutes that explain why a strait most people have never heard of suddenly matters, with concrete mechanics and numbers — good for the commute.

2:00 The Red Sea is not just another waterway
In normal, calm times, nearly 15% of global seaborne trade passes through the Red Sea, including 30% of the world's container shipping, 12% of seaborne oil trade and 8% of liquefied natural gas. At its northern end the Red Sea connects to Egypt and the Suez Canal, and on to the Mediterranean; at its southern end that narrow channel leading to the Indian Ocean and Asia's trade routes is the Bab-el-Mandeb. To grasp the weight of this strait, you first have to grasp how much the Red Sea itself carries — it is not a bypass you can casually route around, but a segment of the global trade trunk line.

3:05 The Houthis really did take that ground
The host pressed Rachel on whether "seem to have seized" was weasel wording, and Rachel confirmed it: the Houthis are a rebel group that has been gradually taking control of large parts of Yemen since at least 2014, allied with Iran, and strongly opposed to Israel's existence and to how Israel is fighting in Gaza. In November 2023 they began attacking Red Sea shipping, hijacking vessels and hitting them with drones and missiles; the US military responded with bombing, and the Red Sea was relatively calm for a while. But this past weekend they moved, seizing a stretch of Yemen's Red Sea coast, possibly to support Iran.

4:09 Perim Island is the key that pinches the strait
The seized stretch includes an island right in the middle of the Bab-el-Mandeb — Perim Island (Barim Island), which the military calls "key terrain" because it overlooks the entire strait, and the strait is only about 18 miles wide at its narrowest point. Whoever controls that chokepoint decides which ships get through. Red Sea traffic had already slowed because of the Houthi attacks, initially falling 50%, and it has never fully recovered. Now that Perim Island has been taken, the threat is that this route shuts down entirely.

4:09 Saudi Arabia's way around Hormuz is in doubt too
This is a particularly thorny problem for Saudi Arabia. Since Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz more than six months ago, Saudi Arabia has been treating the Red Sea and the Bab-el-Mandeb as an alternative oil export route, sending crude through an east-west pipeline to Red Sea ports for loading. But last week that Saudi Red Sea pipeline was hit by drones, and Saudi Arabia then suspended oil loadings from one Red Sea port. Rachel says this puts even more pressure on this lifeline for Saudi Arabia and for the global economy — the creative workaround meant to cushion the world economy is itself extremely fragile.

5:10 Schrodinger Strait: collecting the toll without firing a shot
The Houthis could close the Bab-el-Mandeb at any time, but so far they haven't. Rachel says the mere fact that they can is already having an effect. Analysts call it the "Schrodinger Strait" — is it open or closed? That uncertainty alone pushes up insurance costs, pushes up freight rates and adds friction to the global economy. After news of the Houthi advance last week, oil prices spiked above $100 a barrel.

6:10 Refined products are rising faster than crude
Rachel points out that timing is crucial: the global supply gap was already building, only partly offset by rerouting and releases from strategic petroleum reserves, and at the same time refineries are seeing serious outages. That means not only is crude more expensive, but diesel, gasoline and other petroleum products are rising by proportionally more, because getting refined products to market has become harder. And it isn't just oil products — this strait also carries fertilizer and natural gas, which would be a problem if Europe has a cold winter.

7:10 Sulfur and helium: the overlooked knock-on shortages
Sulfur is a byproduct of natural gas and fuel production, its supply is already more constrained, and it is used in metal processing, including copper. Helium is a byproduct of natural gas deposits, used as an input in semiconductors and in all kinds of medical equipment. Countries like the US and Canada are ramping up production of some of these goods, offsetting part of the price increase, but Rachel says not by much. That means shortages from this new trade disruption will reach ordinary people before long.

7:10 American consumers end up footing the bill
Rachel says Americans should care because these are global markets, and you can't build a wall to stop imports. Some US producers may benefit from shortages, but in this kind of scenario American consumers tend to be the ones who lose. She also warns that it isn't just higher prices to worry about: the Houthi actions, plus Iran's refusal to yield, are straining relations among regional countries and between the US and its Middle East allies. Deteriorating relations between the US and its allies could make other US policy goals harder to achieve — Gulf states, for instance, are major investors in the US and key to US onshore production.

item.title: The bottleneck in voice AI isn't the model, it's a 150-millisecond biological constraint
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-twiml-语音-ai-的瓶颈不是模型-是-150-毫秒的生物学约束/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-twiml-语音-ai-的瓶颈不是模型-是-150-毫秒的生物学约束/
item.description: Human audiovisual perception runs at only 6-10 hertz, and the model has to be interruptible inside that window; and high-fidelity audio means more tokens per second, and more tokens means smaller parameters — this is the physical trade-off voice AI cannot avoid.
item.content:encoded:
Human audiovisual perception runs at only 6-10 hertz, and the model has to be interruptible inside that window; and high-fidelity audio means more tokens per second, and more tokens means smaller parameters — this is the physical trade-off voice AI cannot avoid.

The first half is hands-on product and architecture judgment; the second half, on EQ, benchmarks and the personalization learning loop, is worth more, but you need the patience to get past the 45-minute mark.

6:09 150 milliseconds is a hard constraint, not an engineering tuning knob
Alex's starting point is biology: from a photon hitting the retina to the cortex responding takes about 150 milliseconds, and that number is stable enough to serve as a non-invasive diagnostic marker for neurodegenerative disease — when there is pathology, the signal takes a detour and takes longer. Human audiovisual perception actually runs at 6 to 10 hertz, even though the world feels perfectly smooth to us. So their model handles interruption inside a window of roughly 150 milliseconds. This is not an engineering goal of "as fast as possible" but a hard design input aligned to the human perceptual frame rate.

8:11 Token rate and parameter count are zero-sum
Audio first has to be turned into tokens and fed into the LLM backbone, then turned back into audio. High fidelity requires a high token rate, but a high token rate means prefilling and generating a large number of tokens every second, and the cost rises accordingly. Hence an unpleasant dilemma: more tokens per second means the model parameters cannot be too large; fewer tokens per second is what lets you afford more parameters. Text is the ultimate compression format, needing only 3 to 5 tokens per second, while audio easily goes above 10. 10 tokens/second means each token covers about 100 milliseconds — which is why user-experience engineering and scientific research have to be done at the same time.

11:14 Most avatar video is boring, so it compresses
Models like WAN and Flux can generate video clips of around 10 seconds, but producing an hour of visually consistent continuous stream requires changing the model. Alex's key insight is: if you know this is avatar video, there will be no race car speeding through the background, and most of the frame is fairly boring. So the audiovisual stream of this interview can be compressed into a fairly efficient bitstream; the bitrate only spikes when he waves his arms wildly, and normal people don't do that. This is the concrete landing point of "set the price first, then work backwards to the architecture" — not chasing the prettiest picture quality, but building something users can afford.

15:17 Teach a model a new modality and it forgets its old skills
They didn't build their own LLM; instead they took the intelligence already present in a high-quality LLM and had it learn one more modality. But the risk is catastrophic forgetting. Alex gives the example of a friend: he adopted a Latin American child in Germany and spoke only German to her, and within a few months the girl had forgotten all her Spanish words. LLMs are the same — let one handle only audio and it will soon forget reasoning and language itself. So you have to maintain a competitive mid/post-training LLM pipeline while defining tasks that graft audio and text together, just as a multilingual model has to know that dog and Hund refer to the same thing.

20:24 100 million hours of audio — only a self-built data center can afford to store it
Their training data is on the order of 100 million hours of audio, which Alex converts to roughly 200 human lifetimes — if you lived 75 years and were always in a noisy environment, that is about how much audio you would hear. This data can be crawled from the web, but it needs extraction, labeling, normalization and transcription, a great deal of extra processing. Building their own data center helped a lot here: putting it on NeoCloud would eat you alive in storage bills, and putting it on the big three cloud providers is worse. He also mentions a timing point: hard drive prices are now about three times what they were last year, so they will have to be frugal going forward.

23:28 Squeeze labels out of noise with medieval statistics
Faced with noisy labels produced by imperfect processing tools, Alex's argument is: as long as the noise is unbiased, averaging a large number of repeated measurements gives a better estimate than any single one. He cites the medieval "foot" — have men walk out of a church, take the first 12, drop the two with the longest feet and the two with the shortest (possibly due to deformity), average the remaining 8, and you have an estimate of one foot. He says robust regression and estimation have existed for half a millennium. Concretely for audio: knowing this is a two-person podcast, knowing TWIML is usually Sam plus one other person, makes it easy to separate speakers, obtain a large amount of single-speaker audio, and thereby label it better, forming a flywheel.

33:43 End-to-end audio models are doomed to be small and dumb
Alex is very direct about the architecture choice: end-to-end audio models have their place — fast response, small footprint, low latency — but they are also fairly dumb. Make them smart and the compute cost becomes unbearable. So their approach is two-stage: understanding and reasoning happen at one end, the backend triggers the appropriate tool calls, and the answer is collected back, like multithreaded programming where the main thread dispatches parallel threads and retrieves the results. For the user, writing a prompt for their model looks the same as writing a prompt for an ordinary LLM, except their model also talks.

36:46 Ten times cheaper than GPT, but with thinking turned off
Alex claims that on benchmarks like BigBench Audio and Complex Function Bench they beat GPT, Gemini and Grok at one tenth the cost of OpenAI's models. But he adds a footnote himself: this was measured with thinking turned off. The reason is that you cannot have the model pause to think before answering — that feels very unnatural, and humans don't do it either. This exposes a fundamental constraint of the voice setting: reasoning ability has to be hidden in the background, and there can be no visible thinking pause in the foreground.

item.title: Clovis people didn't just hunt mammoths — they painted and sewed inside tents
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-ancients-克洛维斯人不是只会猎猛犸-他们还在帐篷里画画缝衣/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-ancients-克洛维斯人不是只会猎猛犸-他们还在帐篷里画画缝衣/
item.description: Four hearth-centered areas, ochre pigment and bone needles unearthed at the LaPrele site in Wyoming; DNA protein analysis shows the needles were made from red fox and felid bone — the Clovis diet was far more complex than the "mammoth hunter" label suggests.
item.content:encoded:
Four hearth-centered areas, ochre pigment and bone needles unearthed at the LaPrele site in Wyoming; DNA protein analysis shows the needles were made from red fox and felid bone — the Clovis diet was far more complex than the "mammoth hunter" label suggests.

High density of archaeological detail, but it demands patience: the first half is Clovis research history and dating debates, and the concrete findings at LaPrele in the second half are the part that's really worth it.

3:02 Clovis lasted only a few hundred years
Radiocarbon dating pins Clovis culture to roughly 13,100 to 12,750 years ago, a window of a few hundred years just before the end of the Ice Age. The narrowness of that span is itself startling — the Ice Age operates on scales of tens to hundreds of thousands of years, and Clovis is just an instant within it. More crucially, within those few hundred years, highly similar fluted stone points appeared across the entire North American continent, from New Mexico to Wyoming, from Washington state to Virginia. This combination of "narrow in time, wide in space" is Clovis's most distinctive feature; in later periods, stone points rapidly regionalized.

12:21 Clovis were not the first Americans
The "Clovis First" theory dominated most of the 20th century: humans followed mammoth herds into the Americas, and Clovis people were the earliest settlers. But discoveries at sites like Monte Verde (Chile), Paisley Caves (Oregon), Cooper's Ferry (Idaho) and Page-Ladson (Florida) have led most archaeologists to now believe people were living in the Americas thousands of years before Clovis. Mackey says this is one of the fiercest debates in American archaeology, and Pleistocene archaeologists argue about it hard. But she also stresses: Clovis research shouldn't fixate only on the question of "who came first" — there are many questions worth asking about their lives themselves.

21:01 One chopper changed the nature of the whole site
The LaPrele site was discovered in 1986 when locals found mammoth bones by a creek, and Mackey and collaborators returned to excavate in the 2000s. In the first season, retired archaeologist Rich Adams, while helping everyone fix the screening channel, found a large chopper about 10 meters from the mammoth — a simple tool made by knocking a few flakes off a river cobble. The key point is that it appeared in a position where it geologically shouldn't have: the site was gradually buried by floods, and natural processes were unlikely to have moved such a large cobble there. This tool prompted the team to test a wider area, ultimately finding more than 50,000 flakes, at least four artifact concentration areas, several hundred stone tools and mammoth ivory. LaPrele was no longer just a kill site, but a camp where humans had lived.

29:15 Hearths and tent walls left fingerprints in the sediment
LaPrele's most striking find is four "hearth-centered areas." In Block B, the team found no obvious ash or oxidation traces, but burned bone and flakes concentrated in a small area, indicating a hearth once stood there. Even more remarkable is the spatial analysis: if you look down from above at a tent, the hearth is at the center, surrounded by an activity-dense zone, then an open space for walking, and near the tent wall objects accumulate — because the wall is a barrier to artifact transport. The artifact distribution in Block B shows exactly this "bullseye" pattern, indicating an indoor space. In the same area, a roughly 1.5-by-2-meter ochre (hematite) pigment scatter was found, matching the wall's position, suggesting people painted by the fire.

39:25 The bone needles were made from red fox and felid bone
The team used ZooMS (Zooarchaeology by Mass Spectrometry) to analyze bone needles and possible bone beads; this method extracts proteins from extremely small bone samples to identify the animal species. The results were unexpected: many needles were made from hare bone, but one was red fox, and another tested as felid — not a domestic cat, but some wild felid. Mackey notes these animals are all fur-bearing, and their bone thickness may have been just right for making needles. More importantly, these animals were likely caught with traps rather than hunted with spears. This means Clovis people weren't hunting mammoths 24 hours a day; they were also taking more common small prey.

44:32 Were Clovis people mammoth specialists or omnivores?
About 15 widely accepted Clovis sites in North America coexist with megafauna, mostly proboscideans (mammoths, mastodons, gomphotheres), but also horses and camels. But Mackey points out that only about 30 to 40 sites truly define our understanding of Clovis, while thousands of Clovis stone points were found on the surface, lacking context. This raises a core debate: were they mammoth-hunting specialists, or omnivores with a broader diet? Small animals, fish and plant remains preserve less well and are less often systematically sought. Mackey is studying plant remains, and she notes archaeologists usually look for plants only in hearths, and how many places in the Clovis record have actually been searched is a problem.

50:00 Mammoth extinction: did humans push, or was climate the main driver?
The classic "overkill" debate: 35 genera of megafauna went extinct at the end of the Ice Age, and how much is due to human versus environmental factors? Mackey says she takes a middle path, believing both contributed. She considers mammoths the strongest candidate for the overkill hypothesis, because mammoth sites are numerous, the animals were large, and their reproductive rate was low, making them more vulnerable to hunting. But she also notes overkill doesn't necessarily mean humans hunted all 35 genera; hunting may have upset the balance through trophic cascades. Interestingly, paleoecologists lean toward "humans did it," while archaeologists lean more toward "the environment did it."

53:12 Clovis human bone barely exists
Apart from a single ancestral remain attributed to Clovis at the Anzick site in Montana, we have almost no Clovis human bone. Mackey thinks this isn't surprising: population density was extremely low, 13,000-year-old sites are inherently extremely hard to preserve, and these groups were highly mobile, so we don't know their burial practices.
