She also stresses that Clovis people are the ancestors of millions of Indigenous people in the Americas today, and any related research must proceed on the premise of consultation and collaboration.

item.title: Two Hundred Years of Psychiatry's Lessons: No Penicillin, Only Trial and Error
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-lex-精神病学两百年的教训-没有青霉素-只有试错/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-lex-精神病学两百年的教训-没有青霉素-只有试错/
item.description: From ice-pick lobotomies to insulin coma, psychiatry repeatedly claimed 80% cure rates yet never found a psychiatric penicillin — and even today's best drugs still see eight in ten patients drop out of trials.
item.content:encoded:
From ice-pick lobotomies to insulin coma, psychiatry repeatedly claimed 80% cure rates yet never found a psychiatric penicillin — and even today's best drugs still see eight in ten patients drop out of trials.

The first half is the dark history of psychiatry; the second half is how drugs and diagnosis get shaped by commerce and hope together. High information density, but it demands patience.

10:18 There is no psychiatric penicillin
Modern psychopharmacology was born in the early 1950s, and Andrew Skull stresses that this was not a planned achievement but a "serendipitous event" — almost purely accidental. It was genuinely an advance over what psychiatry had before, but the drugs in hand today are only symptomatic treatment, not cure — "we do not have any psychiatric penicillin." More troubling is the iatrogenic harm: making PTSD patients confront their trauma head-on actually made things worse for many of them; antipsychotics and antidepressants are at best partially effective, and doctors cannot tell in advance who will respond and who will deteriorate, while the people in between must weigh side effects against efficacy.

19:41 Twenty billion dollars bought not one bit of improvement
Under Stephen Hyman and Thomas Insel, the NIMH poured money into treating mental illness as brain disease, betting heavily on genetics and neuroscience. After leaving office, Insel admitted in an MIT interview: they had funded a great deal of cool science, but after spending 20 billion dollars, the situation of people with mental illness had "improved not one bit." Skull calls this a devastating statement. DSM-5 was originally meant to rewrite the diagnostic system based on underlying pathology; by around 2008 the editors gave up and fell back on the 1980 approach from 1980; before publication Insel and Hyman publicly denounced it as unscientific and useless, and Spitzer and Alan Francis also fiercely criticised its backroom dealings.

33:44 America's largest psychiatric wards are prisons
People with severe mental illness live on average 15 to 25 years less than others, and that gap is still widening. Skull assigns much of the blame to public policy rather than psychiatry itself: today the three largest inpatient psychiatric "centres" in the United States are the Los Angeles County Jail, Chicago's Cook County Jail and New York's Rikers Island. Patients cycle through a three-stage loop — a brief hospitalisation, the street or a cheap hotel, then prison. Community care is what Skull calls "a shell game without a P," a con with no replacement facilities, amounting to a return to something like the Dark Ages.

45:18 When you can't cure them, blame their genes
The early asylums were born of intense optimism; the earliest alienists believed that if patients came early enough, 60%, 70% or even 80% could be cured. Actual discharge rates were only 35% to 40%, so each year deposited another cohort of chronic patients, the ratio of new to chronic patients grew steadily worse, and the asylum's image came to be defined by that chronic patient who "only left in a pine box." By the late 19th century the cure rate by in-house headcount was only 10% to 12%. Faced with the accusation "you promised and didn't deliver," the answer shifted to blaming the victim: mental illness was a fundamental biological defect, patients were evolutionary throwbacks, degenerates, who could not be released because "they breed like rabbits." This narrative provided the justification for lifelong confinement and sterilisation.

58:13 The ice-pick lobotomy: psychiatry won a Nobel Prize
Walter Freeman began performing lobotomies in 1936, building on work the previous year by the Portuguese neurologist Egas Moniz, who won the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1949 for it — by then with 14 years of experience. Freeman wanted to be the Henry Ford of lobotomy and mechanised the operation: first electroshock to render the patient unconscious, then drive an ice pick through the eye socket into the skull, stir and sever. He toured state hospitals in a camper he called the "lobotomobile," switching from his right hand to his left when it tired, sometimes doing 20 to 30 cases in an afternoon, and boasted he could teach any fool to do a lobotomy in 20 minutes, "even a psychiatrist" — he was a neurologist and held psychiatrists in contempt. The operation was performed from the 1930s into the early 1970s, and was finally retired by generational turnover and antipsychotic drugs.

1:17:01 Cotton cut out his patients' stomachs and claimed an 80% cure
Henry Cotton was a psychiatrist trained by Emil Kraepelin and Adolf Meyer, who ran the New Jersey State Hospital in Trenton. He embraced the theory of "focal sepsis": a low-grade infection releases toxins in the body, and when the toxins reach the brain they poison it. With no antibiotics, the answer was to find the source of infection and cut it out — first pull the teeth, the patient doesn't improve; then remove the tonsils, still no improvement; so out came the stomach, the spleen, the colon, and he claimed to have cured 80% of his patients. Wealthy patients came from all over America. He gave a lecture series at Princeton, published by Oxford University Press and Princeton University Press, and The New York Times called it a major breakthrough. In reality, 45% of those who underwent abdominal surgery died within a year. He died of a heart attack in 1933, and his successor stopped the abdominal operations, but tooth extraction and tonsillectomy continued until 1960 — a dentist who arrived in 1916 pulled hundreds of thousands of teeth and firmly believed Cotton should have won the Nobel Prize.

1:42:33 Schizophrenia may not be a disease at all
Once the genome was decoded, people expected a Mendelian gene for schizophrenia to be found quickly. It didn't happen. Now, using genome-wide association studies, adding up all 300 small genomic variants explains only about 10% of schizophrenia — Scull's verdict is "not very powerful." More troubling still, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and autism overlap heavily in genetic abnormalities, which undermines disease categories drawn along symptom lines. He cites the British psychiatrist Robin Murray: schizophrenia is more like the most extreme end of psychosis, a continuum. He speculates that if in ten years psychiatry announced "there is no such thing as schizophrenia," public trust in psychiatry would be badly damaged.

3:16:10 New drugs are no more effective than old ones, and eight in ten patients quit the trial
The CATIE study (published in the New England Journal of Medicine) compared one first-generation antipsychotic against four newer ones and concluded the new drugs were no more effective than the old one. The more underrated finding was tolerability: depending on which drug was used, 67% to 82% of patients dropped out of the trial, either because the drug didn't work or because the side effects were unbearable. In other words, these are already "our best drugs," yet real-world discontinuation rates are astonishingly high. The old drug's patent had expired and it was cheap; the second-generation drugs were patented and expensive, in some cases 10 times as expensive, but the higher price bought no efficacy advantage.

item.title: 40,000 Ottomans Lay Siege to Malta — and Lose to a Few Hundred Knights
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-historyhit-奥斯曼四万大军围攻马耳他-为何败给几百骑士/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-historyhit-奥斯曼四万大军围攻马耳他-为何败给几百骑士/
item.description: In 1565 an Ottoman fleet of 180 ships and 40,000 men besieged Malta, defended by roughly 500 knights and a few thousand Maltese. Fort St Elmo held out for a month before falling, but the delay lasted until Sicilian reinforcements landed in September and the Ottomans withdrew.
item.content:encoded:
In 1565 an Ottoman fleet of 180 ships and 40,000 men besieged Malta, defended by roughly 500 knights and a few thousand Maltese. Fort St Elmo held out for a month before falling, but the delay lasted until Sicilian reinforcements landed in September and the Ottomans withdrew.

This episode is on-location siege narrative — vivid but light on analysis. If you want the mechanics of why Malta held, the middle and later sections on scorched earth and disinformation are the most valuable.

3:02 Malta's value is its position, not its resources
Malta sits almost exactly in the middle of the Mediterranean: 80 km north of Sicily, hard against North Africa to the south, and roughly equidistant from Gibraltar and the Suez Canal. Whoever controls Malta controls the trade routes. The Grand Harbour where Valletta now stands is a rare natural deep-water port, safe to anchor in no matter which way the wind blows. The Knights did not originally want Malta, since it had no ready-made fortifications and no resources; it was the first Grand Master who insisted on a foothold and took it.

7:10 What the Knights brought was the Italian bastion
The Knights brought Italian-style military architecture (Traccia Italiana) to Malta: no longer the tall medieval castle but low, sloped, outward-projecting bastions with thick earth-filled walls to absorb the impact of gunpowder artillery. Fort St Angelo got the first bastion. By 1552 the Knights had realised how dangerous their position was, and Grand Master Domades pushed hard to build fortifications. Between St Angelo and Fort St Michael at Senglea they also strung an underwater iron chain, serving much like a WWII anti-submarine net, to block ships.

11:26 The garrison was waiting for a fleet on the horizon
On 18 May 1565 the garrison of Fort St Elmo saw a vast fleet approaching on the horizon, signalled at once, and the whole island went to war footing. The defenders numbered about 10,000 in total, including knights, Maltese civilians and mercenaries hired from Italy. This was not a war you could surrender in: the defeated would be killed or sold as slaves, so for many it was a fight to the death. The Ottomans, for their part, arrived thinking they would take it in a few days and move on to the next place, and set their first objective on Fort St Elmo.

13:33 Fort St Elmo held only a month, but it pinned the Ottomans down
The Ottoman fleet of about 190 ships and an estimated 35,000 soldiers arrived at the Grand Harbour and did not strike directly at the Knights' headquarters at St Angelo, but first attacked Fort St Elmo, which guarded the entrances to the two harbours. Fire opened on 27 May, with hundreds of guns bombarding almost without pause and reducing the walls to rubble; every night the Knights patched the breaches, hauled ammunition and treated the wounded, then fought again the next day. Fort St Elmo had been thrown up in only about six months, its works were not good enough, and the Ottomans found it relatively easy to scale and dismantle. The Grand Master's strategy was simply to keep the Ottomans attacking and keep bleeding them. By the night of 22 June the fort was a ruin, and the surviving garrison said Mass in the chapel, preparing not for victory but for death. At noon on 23 June the last knights died fighting, and Fort St Elmo fell.

16:46 Both sides used corpses to send a message
This was a war with no room for surrender. After the last defenders of Fort St Elmo were killed, the Ottomans cut off their heads and lashed the bodies to rafts in the shape of a cross, casting them into the sea as a warning to the Grand Master of what was coming. The Grand Master is said to have fired Ottoman heads back from the guns of St Angelo in reply. On 15 July the Ottomans tried to attack Senglea, but below St Angelo at sea level there was a small battery the Ottomans had not spotted; when it opened fire they were caught completely off guard, and nearly all the attacking boats were sunk.

18:51 Scorched earth broke the Ottomans first
By July the Knights' side still had tolerable supplies; it was the Ottomans who had the problem. The Knights and the Maltese practised scorched earth, burning everything as they withdrew, so the Ottomans could find no food at all. It was high summer, the heat was unbearable, and Ottoman morale began to sink into panic. The Grand Master's tactic was to drain the enemy's manpower and morale as much as possible and hold out until they gave up on their own. An Ottoman leader is said to have remarked that if St Elmo had taken this long, what would St Angelo cost them. Maltese civilians also fought in large numbers, including women who took part in nursing and in combat.

22:03 A tiny cavalry force scared off an Ottomans army on the verge of winning
In early August the Ottomans attacked both Birgu and Senglea at once, at one point breaking through the walls and fighting a bloody melee in the streets, and they looked to have the upper hand. The Knights countered with a ruse: a commander at Mdina, the fortified city in the Maltese interior, sent out a very small force of Maltese cavalry, which raided the Ottoman field hospital and supply camp. Rumour spread fast through the Ottoman army that a huge relief force had arrived. The Ottoman commander Mustafa Pasha broke off the assault, retreating on the edge of victory. By late August both sides were locked in a war of attrition, with disease, lack of food and casualties mounting, and the Ottomans had also lost experienced commanders such as Dragut.

23:03 The relief came, but the Ottoman Empire was not broken
On 7 September 1565, 8,000 Spanish, Italian and Sicilian troops dispatched by Don Garcia in the name of Philip II of Spain landed on Malta from Sicily and advanced on the exhausted Ottoman army. The Knights had been begging for relief for weeks, and it came late but it came. The Ottomans formally surrendered. But Kirsty stresses that this did not weaken the Ottoman Empire's power or legitimacy; they continued to exist as an empire for a long time afterwards, and today people tend to inflate the significance of this victory. After the siege the Knights immediately set about building the new city of Valletta and repairing Fort St Elmo; Grand Master La Valette died before he saw the city finished.

item.title: Britain's Expedition to Ethiopia: A Hostage Crisis Won with Railways and Elephants
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-restishistory-英国远征埃塞俄比亚-一场用铁路和大象打赢的人质危机/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-restishistory-英国远征埃塞俄比亚-一场用铁路和大象打赢的人质危机/
item.description: In 1868, to rescue a few dozen hostages, Britain spent £10 million, shipped in 44 elephants and 20 miles of railway track, and used breech-loading rifles against spears to produce a massacre—then immediately withdrew, leaving Ethiopia to two decades of civil war.
item.content:encoded:
In 1868, to rescue a few dozen hostages, Britain spent £10 million, shipped in 44 elephants and 20 miles of railway track, and used breech-loading rifles against spears to produce a massacre—then immediately withdrew, leaving Ethiopia to two decades of civil war.

The storytelling is excellent, but the information density is not high; suited to those who want a complete case study of how an imperial intervention ends, not those looking for an analytical framework.

5:12 Face was worth more than the hostages
The Derby cabinet decided to send troops not for humanitarian reasons, but because Britain could not be humiliated by an African king in front of its subjects in India and Aden. The episode states clearly that if you asked Derby or Disraeli, they cared far more about British prestige than about those few missionaries. The rescue of the hostages was a by-product; prestige was the main product. This judgment determined every subsequent action: Napier's orders were to go in, rescue, and get out—never occupy, never install a puppet.

11:18 Napier worked the supply line backwards from the endpoint
Napier was an engineer by training, and his planning method was to work backwards: to rescue the hostages he needed 5,000 men; those 5,000 needed hundreds of miles of supply line, so he added another 7,000 to guard it; then he needed a coastal base and two sea routes. He mobilised the resources of the entire empire—Liverpool, Woolwich, Chatham, Bombay, Madras. The episode quotes Philip Marsden's book saying that everyone from quartermasters to cooks to porters began working to free the hostages from the hands of the 'gorilla king'. This was treating an expedition as an engineering project.

14:21 The expedition's hard currency was Austrian silver
In East Africa, the only universally accepted currency was the Austrian Maria Theresa thaler, first minted in 1741, with the 1780 version most sought after. Napier first sent men to Central Europe to buy up old coins, then sent men to the official Vienna mint to exchange British silver for 20,000 coins minted weekly specifically for the expedition. The episode says this coin remained in local circulation until the 1950s. A British expeditionary force had to rely on Habsburg silver from two centuries earlier to buy food and bribe local warlords.

18:37 44 elephants and 20 miles of railway track came ashore
By the New Year of 1868, the British had landed 13,000 soldiers, 20 miles of railway track, and 44 elephants—the elephants were transported across the Indian Ocean in specially reinforced transport ships, seven more than Hannibal had. Engineers blasted paths up cliffs, first having to climb to 8,000 feet, then cross gorges and ravines for 350 miles to Magdala. They also laid copper telegraph wire along the way, extending field telegraph to the forward units. The episode says this may have been the most technologically advanced military operation in history.

21:44 Napier bought passage with gifts
The road to Magdala passed through the territory of Ras Kassa, King of Tigray. Napier stopped to wait for him, formed his troops in salute, invited him to inspect the artillery, presented Arabian horses, rifles, and glassware, and promised that his troops would not loot or steal, would pay for every sack of grain, and offered Queen Victoria's friendship. Kassa gave a lion-skin cloak in return and promised weekly grain deliveries. The episode points out an unwritten understanding: Kassa expected Napier to deal with Teodros once and for all—that was the bargain.

37:20 Teodros threw three hundred people off a cliff after drinking
On the Thursday before Easter, Teodros drank too much and went to sleep after lunch. At four in the afternoon he was woken by the sound of prisoners complaining that their chains were being removed too slowly. Enraged, he called for a sword, stabbed two prisoners to death on the spot, then ordered the remaining three hundred or so to be thrown off the cliff one by one, with guards sent down to finish off any survivors. The whole process lasted two hours. That night a servant heard him praying to God, admitting he had been drunk when he gave the order for the massacre and asking not to be blamed for it.

46:49 Breech-loading rifles turned a spear charge into a massacre
The Abyssinians had charged rifle lines before; they knew riflemen took a long time to reload after firing, and they could rush in during that gap. But this time the British were equipped for the first time with Snider breech-loading rifles, which could be reloaded in seconds, and the entire line could fire 30 to 40 bullets per second, with no interruption in fire. The chiefs and captains at the front, wearing bright red shirts, were the first to be shot down. The result: about a thousand Abyssinians killed and thousands wounded; two British dead and about twenty wounded.

56:00 Refusing the cattle and sheep meant refusing peace
Teodros sent a thousand cattle and five hundred sheep as a peace gesture, but Napier refused them. The episode explains why: by local custom, accepting these animals meant accepting peace and that the matter was settled. When Teodros saw Napier driving the cattle and sheep back, he bitterly told his courtiers that these people had got what they wanted and now wanted his life. This turning point locked in the suicidal ending.

item.title: Australia Regulates Supplements Like Drugs, but Nobody Checks Whether They Work
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-bizthisway-澳洲保健品监管像药-但没人管它有没有效/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-bizthisway-澳洲保健品监管像药-但没人管它有没有效/
item.description: Australia puts supplements and pharmaceuticals under the same agency, which looks strict; but efficacy is neither reviewed before market nor tested during production — the impression of "good" was planted by marketing and cross-border policy.
item.content:encoded:
Australia puts supplements and pharmaceuticals under the same agency, which looks strict; but efficacy is neither reviewed before market nor tested during production — the impression of "good" was planted by marketing and cross-border policy.

The first half's regulatory breakdown is solid, and the back half's chain from marketing to daigou policy is complete; but the middle section has a lot of transcription garbage, and the information density is uneven.

4:00 Australians taking pills is a tradition
The soil for Australia's supplement industry isn't the natural environment, it's four social habits: a sparse population that makes self-medication the default, pharmacists who also diagnose and dispense, naturopathic industry organisations dating to the 1920s, and health food stores that resemble food-as-medicine shops. Stack those four together and Australians take it for granted that you solve health problems without going to the hospital. Black Moth (澳佳宝) started as a naturopathic clinic; only after the second generation took over did it translate that into products the mainstream system could recognise — turning "take a spoonful of fish oil a day" into standardised fish oil capsules, for instance.

12:05 The contract manufacturers are the industry's foundation
Pen Pharmaceuticals, which appeared in 1974, was Australia's first company focused on contract manufacturing for supplements, and by around 2003 it was producing roughly 70% of Australia's vitamins, minerals and herbal products. Its value lay in process know-how: tablets, compound ingredients, sealing the gelatin shell and oils of soft capsules, the mixing uniformity of powders, the stability of liquids — each is its own set of solutions. In the 1980s and 90s a new generation of contract manufacturers extended service in both directions, moving from pure production (CMO) to CDMO covering formulation, ingredients, trial production, labelling, packaging, testing, and registration for export. The brand only has to hand over a concept, and the factory can turn it into a product ready to sell.

15:05 Registration means nobody looks before it hits the market
Australia legislated in 1989, putting the TGA in charge of both pharmaceuticals and supplements, and all products must obtain an AUST number. Most supplements fall into the AUSTL category: only low-risk ingredients permitted by the TGA, only low-level health claims, and a company can get a number just by applying — the TGA does no pre-market review, only post-market spot checks. By around 2010 Australia had roughly ten thousand complementary medicines, and nearly 98% of them were in this registration system. Only prescription drugs, over-the-counter drugs and a small number of high-risk supplements enter the AUSTR tier, which is the only one requiring the TGA to assess safety, quality and efficacy in advance.

20:06 It looks strict, but in practice it's loose
Put the contract manufacturing and regulatory lines together and you see that GMP only guarantees the factory produces steadily to the standard the brand gives it, and that problems can be traced to a batch for recall — it is not itself responsible for whether the product works. The TGA side only handles declarations and issuing numbers; efficacy is explained by the brand itself. So the claim that "Australia regulates supplements like drugs" is not wrong in itself, but it is misleading: the method of control is the same, while the degree of control over the efficacy part differs enormously. The whole system does no effective upfront oversight of a product's actual effects, and there is a risk of disconnect between the brand and the product's efficacy.

25:08 The marketing was copied from Centrum, not invented
CEO Radek Sali, who took over in 2008, did not conjure a marketing plan out of thin air. He did industry research and found that the best seller among peers was Centrum, and the feedback from retailers was: Centrum didn't give the channel much margin, but you couldn't argue with it running ads on TV all year, with good athlete endorsements, so consumers walked into the pharmacy and asked for it by name. Sali wanted to replicate that at Swisse. He started with Australia's national sport, cricket — the men's team captain, buying only very short ad slots during the hottest summer cricket broadcasts, so that even on a limited budget he could appear at important moments. But the female-dominated sales channel wasn't moved; some buyers didn't watch cricket themselves and didn't know the athlete. He asked his mother what shows she liked, and she said a dance variety show, and the strategy turned from there to spoken segments in entertainment content.

26:09 Selling health as a lifestyle
Swisse's bigger promotional push drew on Oprah and Ellen, and signed a three-year deal with the actress Nicole Kidman, extending its reach from Australia to the United States. By 2012 Swisse had 25 brand ambassadors, had shot more than 80 TV commercials in the previous 12 months, and reached annual revenue of 183 million Australian dollars, with marketing spend of forty to fifty million Australian dollars a year — said at one point to be the highest marketing spend of any consumer brand in all of Australia. Its ads didn't stress efficacy or ingredients; they mainly presented a state of being energetic, positively disciplined and good-looking — converting health into a lifestyle consumers aspire to. In 2012 Swisse took more than 20% market share in Australian supermarket channels and more than 10% in pharmacy channels.

32:14 The growth point was found in Chinese pharmacies
Swisse spent heavily on the US market without much success, and on returning to Australia found that Swisse sold extremely well in pharmacies in Chinese-concentrated areas — some stores selling at ten times the level of an ordinary store — because students and Chinese immigrants bought it in bulk to carry back to China or resell online, that is, daigou. In 2015 two policy shifts arrived: in March the Hangzhou cross-border e-commerce comprehensive pilot zone was approved, and in June China and Australia signed a free trade agreement, which took effect that December. The FTA mainly affected ordinary trade; Australian official statistics put the tariff on vitamins and supplements generally at 3% to 10%, while Black Moth itself estimated an average of 20%, and after the agreement it was said at the time that this could fall to zero within four years. Cross-border e-commerce goes through bonded warehouses, platforms buy in bulk, logistics time and cost drop sharply, and such goods are treated in policy as for personal use, so they don't have to go through the registration and filing process for supplement imports.

35:16 The brand was bought; the impression stayed put
In September 2015 the Hong Kong-listed company Biostime completed the acquisition of a controlling stake in Swisse, and two years later completed a full buyout, a deal of about 1.7 billion Australian dollars, or 8.7 billion yuan. For Swisse the deal carried little premium; for Biostime it added a large chunk of business revenue and imagination. All those Swisse ads in Hunan TV variety shows now are, in theory, a Chinese supplement company spending the money, yet the brand can still say it is an Australian supplement brand, and consumers can still apply their old vague good impression of Australia to it — a large proportion of the acquisition's core value is deposited in brand goodwill.

item.title: Lenin Built the Terror Machine, Stalin Just Took It Over
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-empirehist-列宁设计了恐怖机器-斯大林只是接手了它/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-empirehist-列宁设计了恐怖机器-斯大林只是接手了它/
item.description: The secret police, the labour camps, the one-party state — all architecture Lenin left behind. What Stalin did was turn it into a personal instrument of power: the first thing he did as General Secretary was stuff his own people into key posts.
item.content:encoded:
The secret police, the labour camps, the one-party state — all architecture Lenin left behind. What Stalin did was turn it into a personal instrument of power: the first thing he did as General Secretary was stuff his own people into key posts.

This episode gets the ownership of the Soviet terror system straight: it wasn't invented out of thin air by Stalin — Lenin built the stage, Stalin performed on it. The back half, on Lenin's testament and the funeral details, is dense with information.

2:06 In 1917 Stalin was a man nobody noticed
The episode opens by recalling the impression left by the previous instalment: Stalin was a bad orator and a slow theorist, and nobody would have guessed he'd become the next dictator. Guest Giles Milton confirms that judgement and adds a key detail — Stalin rarely appeared in public and was not well known in Russia; he hated public speaking because his Georgian accent was so heavy. That explains how he was later able to accumulate power quietly: nobody treated him as a threat.

4:11 Churchill once wanted to wipe out the Red Army with gas
During the civil war, Britain, France, America and Japan all backed the Whites. Churchill, as Minister of Munitions in 1919, pushed Britain to send troops and weapons to Russia to fight the Reds. More striking still, Britain had developed a lethal chemical weapon late in the First World War, and Churchill thought it more humane than the bloody slaughter in the trenches, so he sent it to use against Trotsky's Red Army. Because of atmospheric conditions in northern Russia the gas worked poorly, and the whole stockpile ended up dumped in the White Sea. This history explains how hard it was when Churchill allied with Stalin in 1941 — he himself was one of the men who had wanted Stalin dead.

9:27 The terror machine's architecture was Lenin's legacy
Many people put the Cheka, the labour camps and the one-party state all down to Stalin, saying he built them while serving as a political commissar in the civil war. Giles argues this completely misunderstands Lenin's role: it was Lenin who built the architecture, and Stalin merely later took it and used it for his own political career. The Cheka was the secret police, which later became the more familiar KGB — surveillance, arrest, torture, execution. The host sums it up: looking back at history we often say Stalin was a corrosive influence, that he brought the terror, but the architecture was Lenin's bequest.

10:27 Tsaritsyn: Stalin arrested a front-line general
Trotsky appointed Snezarev, a general from the former tsarist army, to command the Tsaritsyn campaign — a typical Trotsky move of using old officers, and one that put him directly in conflict with Stalin. Stalin, as political commissar, arrested the general and all his subordinate officers and locked them on a barge on the Volga. His intention, it is said, was to sink the boat and drown them. When Trotsky found out he was furious and ordered the general released immediately. This was the first round in the struggle between Trotsky and Stalin, and Trotsky won big. But Stalin later told the story as one of the great civil-war battles in which he personally went to the front, and Tsaritsyn was later renamed Stalingrad.

16:44 Whenever Stalin was unhappy he threatened to resign
Giles gives a detail that doesn't fit Stalin's later image: whenever things went badly, such as not getting authorisation at Tsaritsyn to settle scores with Trotsky, he threatened to resign. He wrote a letter saying that without this, my work on the Southern Front will become meaningless and unnecessary, and this gives me the right or the obligation to go even to the devil rather than remain on the Southern Front. The Politburo read the letter, grew tired of reading it, and then said, no, Joseph, stay, we all love you. He was a sulker. The picture fixes this in the reader's mind: the early Stalin used emotional blackmail, not terror.

29:12 Nobody thought the General Secretary's job was worth having
In April 1922 Stalin was appointed General Secretary. Today that title means supreme power in the state, but at the time it was just a functional description, tedious work. Stalin understood: handled properly, the post gave him complete control of the party. He could plant his own people in key positions and clear out everyone who supported Trotsky. From the day he took it over he made full use of the position, with one eye already on the future — Lenin's health was poor, he was thinking about who would succeed Lenin, and now he had the chance to fill the party with supporters so that when Lenin died he would be in an advantageous position.

32:13 Stalin's apology letter: says sorry without admitting fault
Stalin telephoned Lenin's home. Lenin was gravely ill, and Stalin accused Nadezhda of discussing politics with Lenin as he was dying, saying it was unforgivable. Nadezhda told Lenin, Lenin was furious, and insisted Stalin write a letter of apology. The letter is superb: Stalin apologises without apologising — if you think I offended her, then I apologise, but I don't think I really did offend her, so there is nothing to apologise for. Lenin grew even angrier. On 4 January 1923 Lenin wrote down his assessment of Stalin: Stalin is too rude, and this defect, entirely tolerable in our internal and comradely relations, becomes intolerable in the post of General Secretary, and he therefore proposed that the comrades find a way to remove Stalin and replace him with someone else.

35:21 If Lenin hadn't died, Stalin would have put him in prison
Lenin's political life ended with his stroke, and he died ten days later. His wife, Nadezhda Krupskaya, said the most famous thing of all: if Lenin had not died in 1924, he would have been serving time in one of Stalin's prisons. She saw that Stalin was going after Lenin on his way up. Giles thinks it very likely, because Stalin was absolutely ruthless towards anyone he believed was not on his side. Lenin wanted a simple burial; Stalin decided not to bury him but to embalm him and put him on permanent display. Within hours of Lenin's death they began draining the fluids and removing the organs, and the heart was never found again.

item.title: Solo Founders Aren't Alone: The Relationship Is the Product
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-solofounders-单人创始人不是一个人-关系才是产品/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-solofounders-单人创始人不是一个人-关系才是产品/
item.description: 85% of startups die because the relationship didn't work, not because the product idea was bad. Being a solo founder really means being a solo artist — treating relationships as the main job, not actually carrying it all alone.
item.content:encoded:
85% of startups die because the relationship didn't work, not because the product idea was bad. Being a solo founder really means being a solo artist — treating relationships as the main job, not actually carrying it all alone.

This episode is medium density, but Dave Morin uses three cases — OpenClaw, Pulsia and Ramble — to explain clearly what solo founders actually survive on. The mechanics in the back half are worth more than the motivational talk in the front half.

4:04 The share of solo-founded startups doubled in five years
Carta data shows that roughly 40% of companies this year were founded by a single person, up from under 25% five years ago. Dave Morin doesn't think this is an accident: social media means you hardly feel alone for a waking hour, and AI has become a huge input source over the past two or three years. You used to lie in bed texting friends; now you talk to AI, explore your own ideas, and get input on what to do tomorrow. The "internal craft" of starting a company has also gone from a dark art held by a few to something YouTube and ChatGPT can teach.

10:06 Most startups die from relationships, not products
Dave puts it bluntly: most startups fail because the relationship didn't work, not because the product idea was bad or the market didn't exist. He compares it to a band breaking up — you never get to hear the music you loved again. When your favorite app suddenly gets redesigned and the UI becomes infuriating, behind it is often that the "band" changed, the relationships changed, the people who made the thing changed. So he says the relationship is, in a sense, the product itself.

16:11 Designing the team matters as much as designing the product
When Steve Jobs died, Dave was working on Path, Jony Ive was helping him, and he was helping Jony with some Apple work. Jony told him something he still remembers: designing the team matters as much as designing the product. From that Dave draws his core judgment — you can be a solo artist, but you are always inside a huge collaboration, not just with the creators around you but with customers, audiences, and the community that cares about your product. You are not alone.

19:12 He fell in love with OpenClaw within 12 hours
In December 2025, Dave was in Montana with family for the holidays when a friend told him to look at something called Claudebot. He didn't look the first day; he installed it the second, and within less than 12 hours he had that childhood feeling — the one from age 7, when his grandfather put a Macintosh on his desk and he first felt he could create anything. The second time he felt that was seeing Facebook; within 24 hours he decided he had to find the founder. This time it was OpenClaw, and he immediately went to find Peter, moving from Twitter DM to iMessage, talking every day, saying "I don't know what this becomes, but everyone needs to experience it, and we have to protect it at all costs."

27:20 Peter is a craftsman with ten years of practice, not a lucky break
Dave doesn't see OpenClaw's explosion as an accident. Peter did ten years of hardcore PDF engineering and understands Mac OS details at the engineering level better than most people. So when Claude and agentic engineering arrived in 2025, he was an artist who had already digested all the material and could make his art extremely fast and extremely beautifully. Dave's conclusion: this is an extremely well-trained creator who, given new tools, made something magical.

32:24 Ben built himself a Company OS on the road
After Ben and his co-founder decided not to be partners and split the company in two, he went alone to Kyoto, Hong Kong, Shanghai and Thailand. Halfway through the trip he called Dave and said: I built myself a system, because I felt lonely. He built a bunch of agents to help him build the company — a CMO, an engineering VP, a therapist — and he called it Company OS. Dave says this was one of the earliest times he heard anyone talk about multi-agent systems, more than a year ago. Three months later Pulsia launched. Ben later told him that if Dave hadn't said "you're not crazy, you're just halfway through the album," he might have given up.

36:29 Matt applied data science to campsites
Matt's previous company was in book publishing, using data science and machine learning to reverse-engineer "what book you should write," selling books out before they hit Amazon — at its peak, more than 80% of Amazon's top 50 books were ones they published. During the pandemic he and Dave talked around a campfire: could this approach be applied to camping? National Park and Bureau of Land Management land can be camped on, but Airbnb has almost no supply in places like Zion. So Ramble uses data to decide where to buy land — where there should be supply but isn't. Dave calls this "the PhD mode of startups," because it's essentially real estate development: buying land and negotiating with landowners, counties and cities, and zoning boards.

44:32 You have to be the person in the world who loves it most
Dave says Matt is an extraordinary climber, at the Denali level, and he knows fewer than five people who do that kind of climbing. Ramble is an expression of Matt's love of nature; he wants to give other people that experience of being completely immersed in the natural world. Dave's inference: you have to love it that much to turn it into a business. Otherwise, first, someone else will love it more than you and they will beat you; second, you'll have to talk about it for ten thousand hours, and ten years later you'll still be talking about it, so you have to love it, because you'll have to eat ten thousand dinners about it.

item.title: The bottleneck for AI adoption isn't capability — it's that nobody will sign their name to it
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-latentspace-ai-落地的瓶颈不是能力-是没人敢签字担责/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-latentspace-ai-落地的瓶颈不是能力-是没人敢签字担责/
item.description: Waymo drove better than a human four years ago and still can't get into an airport — what constrains AI's usefulness was never capability, but liability, risk and trust. AIUC wants to fill that gap with standards plus insurance.
item.content:encoded:
Waymo drove better than a human four years ago and still can't get into an airport — what constrains AI's usefulness was never capability, but liability, risk and trust. AIUC wants to fill that gap with standards plus insurance.

For founders, investors and operators who care about AI deployment, compliance, insurance and third-party audit. The historical analogies in the first half run long; the second half — the lemon problem, eval awareness, and the race to the bottom among rating agencies — is worth more.

7:58 Waymo still can't get into an airport after four years
Rune's core evidence is Waymo: by early 2022 it was already a superhuman driver, but you can't take it to the airport; more than four years later you still can't, even though everyone agrees it drives better than a person. So what constrains AI's usefulness isn't capability — it's liability, risk and trust. Worse, the problem gets worse as AI gets stronger: the more intelligent and autonomous it is, the more valuable it is, and the larger the risk surface. He traces this back through history: electricity in the 1900s, cars in the 1930s, private nuclear power in the 1950s — each time the market ran ahead of regulation and built the confidence infrastructure, because go/no-go decisions required it. The common blueprint is standards plus insurance: standards supply the rules of the road and which tests to run, insurers pay the claims, and therefore have the strongest incentive to genuinely quantify risk and find ways to reduce it.

23:26 Most companies have the right building blocks, but they don't work
Rune says the most important thing is that many companies have never done serious stress testing — they spend their time optimising output quality in the good case and the average case, and they often hire their first security lead very late. Most companies actually have the right architecture and do have guardrails, either out of the box from the model vendor or filters they built themselves; the problem is they don't work well. For example, dropping in a classifier that says "if this looks like medical advice, filter it out" — lots of companies have that, but the genuinely hard part is sitting down and thinking through every way someone could ask for medical advice, and reading the academic literature on the frameworks and tricks used to get around AI. AIUC-1 splits requirements into three categories: technical controls (for example, you must implement a groundedness filter), testing controls (tests must be run by an independent third party), and policy controls (for example, you must have a named person who owns the liability, and a plan for how customers get notified when something goes wrong).

38:14 Standards made by nonprofits are a problem
Rune says outright that most standards in cybersecurity today are written by nonprofit organisations, and he thinks that's a problem. Nonprofits have no profit motive to hollow out a standard and race to the bottom on price, but by default they are completely unresponsive to the community they serve — there are no customers, nobody asking "what do you want", so satisfaction with existing security standards is generally low. He gives counterexamples of for-profit standards: Moody's, FICO credit scores, and earlier, crash-test standards that came from insurers; UL (Underwriters Laboratories) was born in an era of electric lights spreading, houses catching fire, and insurers footing the bill, and today UL has a for-profit entity, because serving customers well requires one. His conviction is that standards have to come before insurance: whether it's JPMorgan's CISO, Cursor's CISO or an underwriter at Lloyd's, the first demand is "don't have an incident" — once you've confirmed the risk is managed, insurance starts to mean something.

42:47 The policy is a trust signal to the market
Rune explains that demand for AI insurance comes mainly from the gap between "the people building AI" and "the people buying AI". Buying insurance isn't just about getting paid when something goes wrong; more importantly, the insurer brings trust: its willingness to underwrite says "there is risk here, but it's manageable", and its interests align with the company adopting AI, so it's a good signal to the market. When Waymo got its San Francisco operating permit, it went to multiple insurers and stacked a huge policy — not because Google couldn't afford the payout, but so that the government and a trusted third party could look at the data and say "we're willing to put some of this on our own balance sheet". The concrete case is ElevenLabs buying the first AI agent insurance policy, with Lloyd's of London as the third party looking at the data alongside them. There have been no claims yet.

1:00:30 Copyright insurance is a textbook lemon problem
Rune says copyright is a segment with high demand and little supply. One reason is that almost everyone who trained on copyrighted material knows they trained on it, so wanting to buy copyright infringement insurance is itself a signal that you may be a high-risk customer — the people who most want to buy are precisely the ones most likely to have a copyright problem, which Swyx calls the lemon problem outright. Vibhu adds the other side: with open models you don't know what they were trained on, and how far can the chain of liability be traced? Rune admits this is hard and that he doesn't have the answer, but argues that "not unpacking open model training data line by line" is already treated as generally acceptable today, so they won't hold you to a specific standard on it.

1:06:04 Agents are starting to know they're being evaluated
Rune points out that evals face a new challenge: agents are starting to realise they're being evaluated — eval awareness. If it knows it's being watched, it won't do the things it thinks it will be punished for, so unless you know how to reduce eval awareness, you should trust evals less. He thinks monitoring is the paradigm closer to the truth — did you actually give medical advice, how fast did you catch it, how often historically, how fast did you respond — at the cost of being more invasive, since you have to look at some customer data, but it will become more and more common. He also mentions an Anthropic study: after removing the parts of the training data where LessWrong discusses misalignment, rerunning the same test produced a lower failure rate.

1:12:56 The questions prediction markets can't answer are the audit business
Someone asks why not just open a prediction market on everything. Rune's answer: prediction markets depend on public information, and the information that actually determines high-stakes decisions is often private, or doesn't exist yet at all — for example, what a bank's security lead really needs to ask is "will this agent do the specific bad thing I care about in the specific scenario I care about", and that question has no answer anywhere. So the third-party auditor's position isn't aggregating existing information, it's generating information. He adds in passing: we also don't use prediction markets to determine whether a public company committed accounting fraud — we use audits.

1:14:02 Audit is a natural monopoly, but insurers can check it
Swyx cites the line from The Big Short where Moody's says "if we don't give you the AAA, you go to S&P" to make the point that rating agencies compete downward, and watchdogs naturally race to lower standards. Rune agrees, and gives the reason AIUC brought insurers into the picture — insurers are the one party without that dynamic, because they pay the claims directly, and pushing the price all the way down means losing their own money. He also concedes there's no perfect system, that Moody's needs scrutiny, and that watchdogs need scrutiny too. Asked whether the business changes if, in eighteen months, OpenAI's secret five-person group announces AGI, Rune says no, because the one thing a lab can never do is be its own watchdog — the issue isn't whether they care, it's that they're trapped in a race, and may have incentives to cut corners and hide information from governments.

item.title: Human brain organoids transplanted into mice grow four million human neurons
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-naturepod-人脑类器官移植进小鼠-长出了四百万人类神经元/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-naturepod-人脑类器官移植进小鼠-长出了四百万人类神经元/
item.description: Mice genetically stripped of nearly their entire cortex, then given human brain organoids, grew about 4 million human neurons — and behaved neither like normal mice nor like cortex-less mice, but like a third state.
item.content:encoded:
Mice genetically stripped of nearly their entire cortex, then given human brain organoids, grew about 4 million human neurons — and behaved neither like normal mice nor like cortex-less mice, but like a third state.

The first half is solid neurodevelopmental research; the second half's "paper becomes an AI agent" workflow is more informative for people building research tools and AI agents.

2:08 No surgery — genetics makes the room
In 2022, Sergio Pasca's team implanted human brain organoids into newborn rat brains, but human brain cells grow far more slowly than rodent ones, and the implanted organoids were "outcompeted," unable to get connections or room to grow. This time they took a different approach: no surgery, but a genetic method that deletes a gene essential for cell division only in the cells that would form the brain region. The result is that cells are unable to divide the moment they are born ready to build cortex, and stall in place. The structure removed is called the pallium; it exists early and later develops into the cerebral cortex and hippocampus. These "pallium-less mice" lost nearly half their brain volume but survived, with reduced body weight and largely normal basic motor and sensory responses.

4:08 Four million human neurons take over the empty space
The team injected human stem-cell-derived cortical organoids into pallium-less pups aged 5 to 17 days, about four organoids per injection, each roughly 100,000 cells and already differentiated, on their way to forming cortex. The human cells then divided, differentiated, were vascularised by the host, and mouse immune cells entered the interior of the human graft. Months later, the team estimated that these animals, called xenocortical mice, had about 70 million neurons in total, of which about 14 million were cortical and hippocampal cells, most of what had been removed replaced by about 4 million human neurons. Human cells are larger and less dense, so the replacement is not an equal number, but it is still a very large number of human neurons.

6:10 They resemble neither normal mice nor cortex-less mice
The team used machine learning to analyse behavioural differences among three kinds of mice in video: controls, pallium-less mice that had lost almost the entire cortex, and xenocortical mice with the organoid implants. Pallium-less mice differed clearly from controls, while xenocortical mice were "neither," sitting in a third behavioural state. Later experiments backed this up: pallium-less animals had deficits on working-memory tasks, xenocortical animals did not. Sergio's judgement is that function was preserved in the animals that received human cortical cells, and the human cells very likely contributed some of it, but this is not perfect restoration — it only shows these cells can integrate functionally and produce behavioural consequences.

7:11 A hypoxia experiment shows it is the human cells doing the work
The team used this system to model brain injury. Hypoxia is severe in humans and can bring lifelong disease, while mice tolerate low oxygen far better. After the three kinds of mice were exposed to hypoxic conditions for several hours, the human cells were induced to mount a hypoxia response, while the mouse brain was relatively resilient. Two days later, on a motor task, wild-type mice and pallium-less mice were fine, but the xenocortical mice carrying human cells began to show deficits in walking and gait coordination. Sergio argues this shows it is very likely the human cells causing these deficits, and that this would be a powerful system, not only for asking about mechanism but for testing therapies — seeing whether there is benefit before going into clinical trials.

8:12 A very rare neuron type was grown
Aparna Bhaduri at the University of California studies human brain development and cancer. She thinks one highlight of the work is that a cell type differentiated from the human organoids looks like a very rare kind of neuron that has been hard to culture in vitro. Loss of this neuron type is a key factor in a particular dementia, so understanding them better could help future therapy development. But she also notes there is a long way to go: the cortex's laminar structure and its different processing areas are not well preserved in this system, so it does not reach something more like a human brain; and the authors themselves state that the developmental stage the organoids reach is still mid-development — this is not a fully mature cortex.

9:12 This is not a human brain in a mouse's head
Asked whether these animals count as human-mouse chimeras, Aparna Bhaduri says plainly: this is not a human brain inside a mouse. There are three reasons — it is immature; the complexity of cell types is insufficient, some cell types are still missing and the ones present are not mature; and although there are some connections with the rodent, the degree and the way they are wired differ from a human brain. So on complexity, maturity and connectivity, she sees this as an organoid pushed forward in its development, not a human brain. Other researchers Nature spoke to share that view: these are not fully formed functional human cortex.

10:13 Ethicists are not a stumbling block for scientists
Emily Jackson at the London School of Economics studies the regulation of stem-cell-related research, including brain organoids. She says the most striking thing about this paper and the work of Sergio Pasca's lab is the team's focus on the importance of ethics and regulation. She thinks people sometimes mistakenly treat regulation as an obstacle to scientists, and that this is a genuine mistake: in her experience, scientists at the frontier of biotechnology very much want ethicists involved, very much want to know where the red lines are, so they can proceed in the confidence that society approves. She also stresses that when you replace part of a rodent's brain with human brain cells, the key question is what harm this does to the animal — especially a new kind of harm that you would not easily notice, which must be taken very seriously.

17:19 Turning a paper into an agent you can talk to
James's team at Stanford proposes turning static papers into "knowledge agents," which you can think of as a paper's virtual corresponding author. Their workflow is called paper to agent: a set of AI agents reads the paper through, works out how it was done, reproduces the original results, then stores the knowledge on a server, acting as a translation layer between the human paper and any AI, so that models like ChatGPT and Claude become virtual co-authors you can ask anything about the paper — even run analyses with your own data. James stresses this differs from simply dropping the paper into a chatbot: the latter only reads, interprets and summarises results, does not know how the results and figures were generated, and cannot use the data and code, because it has no hands-on experience; a paper agent has that hands-on experience.

item.title: The Chaos in AI Evaluation Isn't a Technical Problem, It's a Transparency Problem
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-nejmaigrandrou-ai-评估的混乱不是技术问题-是透明度问题/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-nejmaigrandrou-ai-评估的混乱不是技术问题-是透明度问题/
item.description: In that 2019 systematic review, fewer than 5% of medical imaging AI papers met the rigor standards long established in other areas of medicine — and even the best-performing models only matched radiologists.
item.content:encoded:
In that 2019 systematic review, fewer than 5% of medical imaging AI papers met the rigor standards long established in other areas of medicine — and even the best-performing models only matched radiologists.

This episode has medium information density, but the first half — a firsthand account of how evidence standards in medical AI moved from chaos to discipline — is directly useful to anyone building medical AI products.

11:22 Fewer than 5% of AI papers in top journals hold up
Around 2019, new papers every week claimed ‘AI is as good as radiologists’ or ‘AI beats radiologists at pneumonia detection’, but these conclusions contradicted each other. Xiao Liu and her collaborators did something no one was doing at the time: they took the rigorous standards that the diagnostic test evaluation field had used for years and applied them to these AI papers, keeping only those with external validation, like-for-like comparisons, and meaningful control groups. The paper count was cut down hard — fewer than 5% truly met the standards long established in other areas of medicine. And within that small set, the best models only matched radiologists. This isn't bad news; it means there's too much noise in the published literature.

16:28 Reporting guidelines don't teach you how to do research, they force you to say what you did
CONSORT, SPIRIT, PRISMA, STARD, TRIPOD — these reporting guidelines are essentially checklists specifying which items a paper must report. They don't tell you how to do the research — they're not methodology guidelines, they're transparency guidelines. Whether your methods are good or bad, you have to write them transparently and clearly. Their function is to put authors, journal editors, and peer reviewers on the same information plane, with no smoke bombs, no hiding behind vague details. Xiao Liu added a side effect: when authors know they must report a certain item, it反过来 forces methodological rigor upward, though that's hard to measure.

18:33 Guidelines are produced by Delphi voting; items without consensus get cut
CONSORT AI and SPIRIT AI weren't written by a few people behind closed doors; they went through a Delphi process: first a literature review and expert opinion generated a set of candidate items, then multiple rounds of multi-stakeholder voting, ending with an in-person discussion. That in-person discussion is often the most valuable, because people learn from each other. Items that fail to reach consensus are excluded; only those with consensus are kept. Xiao Liu says doing this kind of consensus project properly takes at least six months; she tried a rushed version compressed to three months, but participants contribute their time for free, and to get high-quality feedback and multiple rounds of participation, you can't cut corners on time or reach.

20:36 Whether explainability belongs in reporting guidelines was fought over at the meeting
Andy Beam recalls that one question in the Delphi discussion was: should clinical trials include explainability requirements, or at least report any explainability evaluations you did. He and Lauren Oakden-Rayner stood up on the small stage and said ‘No, it shouldn't be done at all, for the following reasons’. That debate was later commissioned into a paper by Rupa, an editor at Lancet Digital Health, and became one of Andy's most cited papers. Xiao Liu also clearly sides with ‘no’ in the lightning round: she thinks you should first ask why you want AI explainability, and keep asking until you reach the bottom — what you ultimately want is just beneficial effects.

26:43 Being a regulatory consultant without ever working in industry felt insincere
At the time, Xiao Liu was doing academic AI research and clinical ophthalmology while increasingly consulting for regulators. She started to feel she had never stood on the side being regulated, and that consulting felt a bit insincere. So she joined Apple as a health scientist, mainly designing validation studies for wearable device algorithms, such as Apple Watch sensing algorithms, including a hypertension notification feature released this year. She says Apple has a well-oiled product shipping machine, which was exactly the experience she wanted. After more than a year there, she returned to Birmingham to build a lab full-time, and then joined Microsoft AI's newly formed medical frontier LLM team.

32:49 Short term, computer scientists set direction; long term, clinicians gatekeep
Asked whether medical AI will be driven more by computer scientists or clinicians, Xiao Liu first asked what ‘driven’ means, and after confirming it means ‘changed’, gave her judgment: short term, computer scientists and engineers; long term, clinicians. The mechanism: the people who process data, choose metrics, and choose benchmarks determine which direction progress goes in the short term; but if the endpoint is real use on patients, clinicians will play the gatekeeper role at a later stage.

33:50 Doctors' work won't change much in five years, but should in ten
Xiao Liu thinks doctors' work won't look dramatically different within five years, but very likely will in ten years and beyond — and she hopes it will. The path she envisions: if medical intelligence and models continue advancing at the current pace, the medical profession no longer has to be about accumulating knowledge, or even about the kind of medical reasoning taught in medical school; the focus shifts to being ‘a companion to experience’ — accompanying deteriorating health, sudden health events, daily wellbeing fluctuations, life-changing diagnoses, treatment failures and complications, and maybe recovery, maybe not. She thinks people will continuously need something deeply interpersonal on this journey: the ability to call on knowledge without necessarily carrying it oneself, but translating it into human language.

40:00 The most optimistic thing is dismantling old medical concepts; the most pessimistic is that we dare not
Xiao Liu says she is more optimistic than pessimistic. What excites her most is that aggregating all the knowledge in the medical world might reveal that our understanding of biomarkers, disease phenotype clustering, and existing medical knowledge frameworks is off. She gives her own PhD research on inflammatory eye diseases as an example: a bunch of diseases are loosely called ‘white dot syndromes’ just because they produce white dots in the fundus, but they are likely driven by completely different mechanisms. She hopes one way new intelligence emerges is by dismantling these old concepts in medicine. The pessimistic side: this field is inherently cautious, may resist such dismantling out of unfamiliarity, and during a period of new technological change may rigidly stick to the evaluation methods and guidelines of the past ten or twenty years, missing opportunities for discovery.

item.title: He Treated Cancer With Bacterial Toxins and Was Condemned by His Peers for Forty Years
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-stuffmissed-他用细菌毒素治癌症-被同行骂了四十年/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-stuffmissed-他用细菌毒素治癌症-被同行骂了四十年/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: Coley used streptococcal toxins to make tumors vanish in some sarcoma patients, but he couldn't standardize the treatment or explain its mechanism, and it was squeezed out by radiation and regulation; his daughter spent the second half of her life building a cancer research institute around it.
item.content:encoded:
Coley used streptococcal toxins to make tumors vanish in some sarcoma patients, but he couldn't standardize the treatment or explain its mechanism, and it was squeezed out by radiation and regulation; his daughter spent the second half of her life building a cancer research institute around it.

Medium information density. The first half is medical-history background; the second half — on why the therapy was abandoned and how immunotherapy picked up the thread — is where the value is.

6:13 The death of an 18-year-old changed him
In 1890, Coley took on 17-year-old Bessie Dashiell, who had persistent pain after injuring her hand and was eventually diagnosed with periosteal sarcoma. Coley amputated below the elbow, but the tumor soon appeared elsewhere, and she died on January 23, 1891, at just 18 years old, only about 10 weeks after Coley first examined her. Coley was 28, in his first year as a surgeon. Amputation was the only treatment available at the time, and it had not worked, which drove him to comb through the records of roughly 90 cancer surgery patients at New York Hospital over the previous 15 years, looking for something better.

7:15 In one record, the tumor disappeared on its own
In the case files, Coley found a case of small round cell sarcoma of the neck in a patient of his colleague Dr. William T. Bull: four recurrences, and by the fifth surgery the tumor had invaded deep structures and could not be removed. After the operation the patient accidentally developed erysipelas of the face and neck, then had a second attack two weeks later. Within days of the first attack the tumor began to soften and shrank rapidly, and by discharge the tumor had completely disappeared. The hospital had no follow-up records, so Coley went door to door in the German immigrant community and found him: in the spring of 1891 he was still alive, with no local or systemic recurrence, seven years after the surgery.

9:21 He tried live bacteria first, then switched to toxins
On May 2, 1891, Coley began trying to induce erysipelas in a patient with inoperable sarcoma of the tonsil and neck. The tumor was so large the patient could not eat solid food and could swallow only small amounts of liquid. Coley exposed the patient to lab-cultured bacteria, but for months could not induce erysipelas, until in October he injected a culture a colleague had brought from Robert Koch's lab in Germany. The patient became very ill, but two weeks later the neck tumor had disappeared and the tonsil tumor had shrunk, and the patient lived in good health for eight years. By the end of 1892, after two early patients died of infection, Coley began working with bacteriologists to heat-kill the bacteria and filter out the toxins, rather than using live bacteria directly.

15:34 The effect was real, but only in some patients
Coley wrote in his papers that in his own experience, in slightly more than 10% of cases the regression process continued until the tumor was completely absorbed and the patient remained cured; in other cases the improvement was only temporary, and after a few weeks the tumor regrew and the patient died despite continued injections at higher doses; and in a very small number of cases, especially large, highly vascular tumors, particularly the melanotic type, no clearly beneficial effect was ever observed. By 1909 he was recommending it for all inoperable sarcomas (except melanotic), for osteosarcoma of the long bones where surgery meant sacrificing a limb, as prophylaxis against recurrence after surgery for primary sarcoma once the wound had healed, and after surgery for all carcinomas to reduce recurrence using the mixed toxins.

19:40 JAMA waited, then declared failure two months later
On May 31, 1894, Coley read his paper before the American Surgical Association. In October of that year, JAMA published an article comparing bacterial toxins to diphtheria antitoxin, saying the best method of use had not yet been determined, that it was still experimental, and calling for patience until experts produced complete results. But only two months later, on December 15, 1894, JAMA published "The Failure of the Erysipelas Toxins," saying "there is no longer much question that toxin injections as a cure for sarcoma and malignant growths have completely failed," and that although many surgeons had faithfully tried it over the previous six months, not one fully verified recovery had been reported. Coley responded the following January, pointing out that he had used not only erysipelas toxins but also Bacillus prodigiosus, and saying that the failure of a few doctors in a limited number of cases would not affect the scientific community's judgment of whether the method succeeded.

23:47 Forty years, a thousand patients, a hundred and fifty papers
Coley worked with these toxins for about 40 years, treating roughly 1,000 cancer patients and publishing about 150 papers. In 1909 he wrote that 52 cases of inoperable sarcoma had been successfully treated with a mixed toxin of erysipelas and Bacillus prodigiosus, of which 35 remained healthy for 3.25 to 16 years, 28 for 5 to 16 years, and 14 for 10 to 16 years. Although Park, Davis, and Company produced various preparations starting in 1899, the toxins never became the most common treatment for inoperable sarcoma. The reasons included: tense relations with his boss James Ewing, who opposed his research; the bone sarcoma registry refusing to include his cured patients, insisting they had been misdiagnosed; his insistence that all cancers had a microbial origin, even after that idea had been overturned; the difficulty of producing and standardizing the toxins; and the 1902 Biologics Control Act, which raised the regulatory cost.

26:54 Radiation took his window of time
Coley's own methods were also fairly loose: different patients received different doses by different methods for different lengths of time. Partly this was because he was trying to figure out what worked and how best to do it, but some treatment decisions were made almost by feel rather than data. He also noted that other doctors using his toxins treated patients for much longer than he did, and admitted that his own shorter courses might explain some patients' recurrences. X-rays were discovered in 1895 and radium in 1898, and radiation quickly became the standard therapy for many inoperable cancers. Both discoveries came early in his writing about the therapy. In 1934, JAMA published a statement from its Council on Pharmacy and Chemistry, slightly more positive in wording than 40 years earlier, saying the mixed toxins of erysipelas and prodigiosus might sometimes play an important role in preventing or delaying malignant recurrence or metastasis, and might occasionally cure hopeless inoperable tumors. But by then Coley had already retired, and he died on April 16, 1936, at the age of 74.

29:00 His daughter spent her life building an institute for him
After Coley's death, his daughter Helen Coley Nauts began organizing his papers and correspondence, intending to write a biography, and ended up digging deep into his work. She had no medical qualifications and no formal education beyond high school, but she carefully went through all of her father's publications, trying to find out why some cases succeeded and others failed. In 1953, she co-founded the Cancer Research Institute with philanthropist Oliver R. Gray Sr., with funding from sources including Nelson Rockefeller. She served as its director until her death in 2001. Her brother Bradley was also an advocate of their father's method and became chief of bone surgery at Memorial Hospital after their father retired. The Cancer Research Institute today has an award named after Coley, recognizing outstanding research in basic and tumor immunology.

item.title: Fiat-Shamir attacks aren't misuse — the protocol itself is insecure
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-zeroknowledge-fiat-shamir-攻击不是误用-是协议本身不安全/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-zeroknowledge-fiat-shamir-攻击不是误用-是协议本身不安全/
item.description: Protocols actually deployed, like GKR, can be proven to accept false statements under standard Fiat-Shamir; this isn't an implementation oversight, it's a problem with the transform itself.
item.content:encoded:
Protocols actually deployed, like GKR, can be proven to accept false statements under standard Fiat-Shamir; this isn't an implementation oversight, it's a problem with the transform itself.

The first half's theory recap drags, but the construction of the Fiat-Shamir attack and the measured numbers from Flock and snark.fast are worth hearing.

13:09 A hand-built counterexample fooled everyone
Before Ron's work with Lev and Dmitry, the field already knew there were examples of ‘secure interactive protocol + Fiat-Shamir = total collapse’, but those protocols were deliberately constructed by theorists to show Fiat-Shamir doesn't always hold, and they looked extremely unnatural. The typical industry reaction was ‘our real protocols wouldn't do anything that stupid’. Ron himself had years earlier built a semi-artificial example in which one component was fictional, which kept him doubtful about security. The turning point was a bug bounty the Ethereum Foundation set up while studying Poseidon's security, whose final tier was ‘mount a Fiat-Shamir attack on any protocol of your choosing using Poseidon’. Ron didn't go for the reward; instead he suggested changing the terms to ‘non-fictional protocols’, which directly prompted the sweep of real deployed protocols.

15:09 GKR's data-saving feature became the attack surface
What actually got broken was the GKR protocol, widely used in practice; Polyhedra's Expander system uses it. The attack exploits a real feature of GKR: it lets you ‘record less data’, apparently recording less but implicitly committing to that data — which is exactly why people want to use GKR, and exactly what makes the attack possible. The key condition for the attack to work is that the depth of the circuit being proven (the scheme) must be at least as deep as the depth of the hash function used for Fiat-Shamir, and implementations at the time placed no restriction on this. Polyhedra made changes and paid the bounty.

17:09 The mitigation is just making the hash chain deeper
The mitigation is plain: make the hash function slightly deeper than the circuit being proven. Concretely, chain several Poseidons together — do 10 Poseidons and the circuit is naturally 10 times deeper, and there's no expected trick to get around it. That's what Polyhedra did. But Ron stresses clearly that this is only a mitigation — we can't demonstrate an attack, but we also don't know that an attack truly doesn't exist. This differs from the usual Fiat-Shamir vulnerabilities: those are typically misuse in practice, like forgetting to include some message the prover sent in the hash; this one is insecure even when Fiat-Shamir is used correctly per spec.

19:10 Diagonalization: make the program take itself as input
Ron gives an extremely artificial protocol to illustrate the attack: the prover sends a message M, the verifier runs M as program code with M itself as input, waits for it to output a 100-bit string, then compares against 100 random bits and accepts only if they match. Interactively this protocol is essentially impossible to accept, because once M is sent, M(M) is fully determined, and the chance of hitting a 100-bit random number is 2 to the negative 100. But with Fiat-Shamir applied, the random number becomes H(M), and the prover only needs to find an M satisfying M(M) = H(M) — take M to be the hash function H itself, since M(M) = H(H) = H(M). This kind of trick is called diagonalization; the essence is forcing a program to nest itself.

28:11 Swapping out Reed-Solomon buys you speed
Blaze, Tensor Switch and Bolt are all hash-based polynomial commitment schemes, and they share a reliance on error-correcting codes. FRI, STIR and WHIR are all built on Reed-Solomon codes, while these three projects try to trade a better error-correcting code for a better PCS. Bolt uses a code called a sketched code: first take a non-cryptographic ‘digest’ of the message, apply Reed-Solomon encoding only to the digest, and the overall codeword = the encoding of the digest + the original message. The benefit is that Reed-Solomon acts on data roughly one tenth the size, cutting encoding cost by an order of magnitude. The cost may be larger proof size, but in settings where not everyone needs to read the proof, proving time matters more. Ron notes this line focuses on proving efficiency, while the WHIR line focuses on verification and proof size, and the two can coexist via proof composition: use Bolt to get an extremely fast proof, then recursively prove its verifier with WHIR to inherit high-quality verification.

35:11 Veil gives hash-based proofs zero knowledge for free
Veil is a method for making a certain class of hash-based proof systems zero-knowledge (Ron dislikes the name ZK ZK). Traditionally, implementing zero knowledge in SP1 means recursively composing a succinct proof with Groth16, but Groth16 isn't post-quantum secure. What Veil wants is a native, hash-based zero-knowledge scheme. Existing proofs of concept show the resource overhead is quite small in both proving time and proof size, and the plan is to implement it directly in SP1.

38:11 Flock let Ethereum dare to abandon Poseidon
Flock is a proof system for batch verification of Boolean circuits, developed by Ron with Benedict and their student William Lang, pushing the theory toward practicality. Ron thinks it brought the industry a ‘second spring’, and more importantly spawned a large number of new ideas and follow-on research.
