One direct consequence is that the Ethereum Foundation decided to move from Poseidon to some kind of Boolean hash. Before Flock appeared, it wasn't clear this could be done efficiently; Flock, plus Binius's important earlier influence, proved it feasible. Ron attributes the shift to two things happening at once: first, the new attacks shook people's confidence in Poseidon, and second, what a year earlier would have seemed surprising, traditional hash functions turn out to be quite efficient to use in proofs.

44:12 Swapping the prover breaks soundness not at all, only threatens completeness
snark.fast is a collaboration between Zcash, Igalia Labs (leading), the Ethereum Foundation and Espresso, with the idea of keeping the Plonk verifier unchanged and replacing only the prover, to see how much faster it can get. Ron distinguishes two properties: soundness means no one can convince you to accept a false statement, so no matter how fast a prover you build, false statements can't be proven — in that sense there's no security problem; completeness means true statements must be provable, which is harder to guarantee, and snark.fast only guarantees that proofs are still accepted on random inputs. A more ambitious approach is to prove that the changes don't alter the prover's input-output behavior, which is what ZK-Golf and Kobe and others are after, with stronger completeness guarantees. Ron also worries that these fully AI-driven projects, lacking oversight, could have AI slip malicious code into the prover.

item.title: Government Doesn't Just Waste Your Money — It Wastes an Hour of Your Week
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-tyler-政府不只浪费你的钱-还浪费你每周一小时/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-tyler-政府不只浪费你的钱-还浪费你每周一小时/
item.description: Plenty of countries file taxes for their citizens; the IRS is legally barred from doing it for you. The time tax hits the poor, immigrants and the formerly incarcerated hardest — and AI may not save them.
item.content:encoded:
Plenty of countries file taxes for their citizens; the IRS is legally barred from doing it for you. The time tax hits the poor, immigrants and the formerly incarcerated hardest — and AI may not save them.

Medium information density, but the "time tax" frame itself is valuable: it reprices the administrative friction of the welfare state as a kind of regressive levy. The confession in the back half about her shifting UBI stance is worth hearing.

0:58 The IRS is legally barred from filing your taxes for you
Lowrey's core example: in Japan, salaried workers never touch the tax process at all; many countries mail you a pre-filled return and you just correct the errors. The US could do exactly this — nine in ten households take the standard deduction, their tax situations are fairly simple — but the IRS is not legally permitted to. This isn't a technical problem, it's an institutional choice. She defines the "time tax" as the portion of cost government shifts onto individuals as administrative labour, and unlike a monetary tax it works differently: you can earn more money, you can't earn more time.

1:02 The worst program is TANF, not the IRS
Lowrey names TANF (cash welfare) the single worst program in government: nominally it exists to address child poverty, in practice it doesn't move the child poverty rate, its compliance burden is extraordinarily heavy and punitive, and its $16.5 billion a year is essentially wasted. She offers a rule — programs aimed at high-income Americans are a far better experience, safety-net programs are generally bad, and welfare is the worst. That yields a counterintuitive judgment: the quality of government service is inversely proportional to the political power of the beneficiary.

6:08 Pandemic fraud isn't something the time tax can prevent
Cowen raises a common objection: after deregulation in 2020 fraud exploded, so maybe the time tax is just the necessary cost of fraud prevention. Lowrey rejects it outright: that fraud came mainly from criminal rings and fake small businesses, plus the fact that UI systems themselves run on ancient COBOL infrastructure. Her mechanism is misaligned incentives — governors have no incentive to upgrade UI systems when unemployment is low, so every recession replays the same conversation. The conclusion: building state capacity and agile digital systems prevents fraud; pushing the work onto individuals does not.

11:19 Large-scale fraud is almost entirely on the supply side
Lowrey points out that Medicare and Medicaid fraud is almost entirely on the provider side: nursing homes, clinics and hospital systems defrauding the government. The ceiling on individual fraud is low, because the money you can extract from government is limited; to commit large-scale fraud you have to process a lot of paperwork. So her policy ordering is: reduce administrative overhead in other programs, concentrate enforcement resources on criminal organisations and legitimate providers, rather than loading burdens onto the 99.9% who don't defraud anyone. She adds a piece of political economy: fraud narratives are often used to make programs look illegitimate, so voters tolerate cuts.

13:25 Fifty hours per person per year, and highly unequal
Lowrey's quantitative estimate comes from the American Time Use Survey: total bureaucratic time is roughly 50 hours per person per year, close to an hour a week. She concedes the number is understated — ATUS can't capture multitasking (cooking while on hold only gets recorded as one thing), and time taxes are scattered across categories and never totalled. Who pays the most? People entangled with the criminal justice system, immigrants, the poor. The rich can "skip the line" with staff and accountants — with one exception: permits to renovate a house in San Francisco, where no amount of money spares you a 500-day wait and multiple rounds of public review.

22:57 AI can fill out forms, but it can't fill a urine test
Cowen asks whether AI agents could handle all of this within five years. Lowrey says probably, but raises two caveats: first, the users of the most burdensome programs are low-income, and whether they know about or trust these agents is unknown; second, much of the burden isn't paperwork at all — it's mandatory interviews, urine screening, data that's hard to collect. She gives SNAP as an example: benefits are calculated by household, and government has no stable definition of "household", so you have to explain how you and your co-residents split food costs — the kind of question AI struggles to answer for you too. She notes she was originally sceptical, but a civic technologist who has worked in this field for years is convinced AI will help enormously.

31:18 Disability insurance is already hard enough to apply for
Cowen presses with data: disability insurance rolls roughly quadrupled between 1990 and 2014 while workplace deaths kept falling — shouldn't the bar be raised? Lowrey doesn't accept the inference. She offers two alternative explanations: population ageing and the rise of obesity-related chronic illness. Then the counter-evidence: 5% of applicants have to submit more than 1,000 pages of medical material; 11,000 Americans die each year while waiting for a disability determination. She admits she worries about both directions — about paying people who don't need it, and about denying people who genuinely do — so she doesn't think this is the moment to add more paperwork.

38:28 The research moved her off her UBI position
Lowrey's previous book, Give People Money, was pro-UBI; here she says plainly that the research findings are "sobering" and that she has updated her priors: the knock-on benefits she expected cash to deliver didn't materialise. Her defence is that the point of giving people money is to give people money to buy things, and that rationale still holds; life improving less than expected isn't an argument against the policy. On AI and UBI, she admits she was extremely dismissive of the claim that "AI will force UBI", and won't go that far now — but if GDP and productivity surge while unemployment rises at the same time, that would be very strange, and you'd have to start considering UBI-type policies.

item.title: After Tome Hit 25 Million Users, He Tore It Down to Build a CRM
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-a16z-tome-做到-2500-万用户后-他推倒重来去做-crm/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-a16z-tome-做到-2500-万用户后-他推倒重来去做-crm/
item.description: Keith Perez walked away from Tome and its 25 million users because his own team didn't like the product; he judged that the CRM battle isn't about making salespeople do more work, but about whether you can fully model a company's customer reality.
item.content:encoded:
Keith Perez walked away from Tome and its 25 million users because his own team didn't like the product; he judged that the CRM battle isn't about making salespeople do more work, but about whether you can fully model a company's customer reality.

The first half is a rare post-mortem of deliberately shutting down a growing product; the second half is dense with operational detail on pricing, expansion and org design.

3:01 They killed a hit not because of the data, but because they didn't like it
Tome launched around the same time as ChatGPT and reached 2 million users a month — so many that inference compute ran short and people had to queue. But Keith says what actually made them decide to stop wasn't some metric, it was that "none of us liked the product." Concretely: they couldn't see a path where a discerning, high-quality presentation maker would treat Tome as indispensable, nor one where investment banking or consulting people would use it to write memos. Their conclusion was that what the models lacked at the time wasn't general reasoning ability but context about who the presenter is, who the audience is, and what relationship holds between them — and that gap wasn't going to close just by waiting for models to get stronger.

6:04 Follow the heat first, then discover the real problem is data
The Tome team dug through their own user base and found B2B users clustered in sales and marketing, so they ran free pilots with 12 large companies. The original idea was helping sales build new-business decks and proposals, but customers started asking: can you also do research, help us qualify leads, help us understand which companies are worth expanding into. They followed that heat, asking customers to open up access to CRM, call recordings and data warehouses — and found the hardest part wasn't doing that work, it was that the data in these systems contradicted each other: the reality in call recordings and the reality in the CRM often didn't line up. Keith says reorganizing that data started to look like the most important work, so they concluded: if you can reorganize a company's reality into something both machines and people understand, that's more worth doing than the original path.

8:11 Nobody wants your four-month-old CRM, so pay them to use it
What they built first was a go-to-market assistant that AEs used every day but that they couldn't charge for — because the data wasn't theirs, and ten other companies were chasing the same thing. So they cut headcount, rethought the CRM from scratch, worked in stealth for four months, and then discovered nobody wanted a four-month-old CRM. The only asset left was a huge office they couldn't get out of, so they posted on X and LinkedIn: use our CRM and we'll let you sit in our office for free. That's "negative pricing." The 10 startups they brought in were there every day, complaining about slowness and missing features, but giving feedback in Slack every two hours. Keith says this was the exact opposite of Tome: a barely working product that users were inside every day, and that they cared about enough to give feedback by the hour.

11:21 The core of a CRM is relationships, not fields
Three of Lightfield's five founders came from Facebook. Their plain judgment was that the most important thing in a CRM is modeling relationships, so they borrowed directly from the Facebook timeline and built an activity log first — when you first made contact, what you said, what they replied, which meetings happened, which documents went back and forth — eventually extending to what the other party did inside your product and how they paid. All the traditional CRM field updates and stage progressions are triggered from that log, but underneath there is always a canonical relationship log. They also tried going fully unstructured and found queries too slow — a needle-in-a-haystack problem — and landed on semi-structured: stuff a large amount of unstructured data into the activity log and let the system infer causality from the log.

15:26 Get the data model wrong and sales will never go back and fix it
They interviewed a lot of CRM consultants, asking what they actually do for clients, and found the highest-consequence thing is the data model: set your stages and fields wrong and you can't send sales back in time to fill in the data — it's over. So Lightfield chose to be "schema-less" — connect email, drop in a call recording, hook up the data warehouse, and the system assembles the relationship in real time; fields can come later, and if you change your mind, it traverses the activity log and refills. Alex Rampell summed this up as "intelligence is greater than schema," and contrasted it with the old era: back then, to save space, every column in a table had to have a predefined varchar length, like name varchar 25 — now they don't even want a schema.

17:28 Someone used it to find cutting-edge treatment for an Alzheimer's patient
Because it supported fully arbitrary schemas, custom objects and custom relationships from the start, Lightfield attracted a set of customers with very strange business models. Keith's example is Power: on one side it serves pharma companies, helping them find clinical trial participants; on the other it's a marketplace aggregating patients with hard-to-diagnose conditions and seeking cutting-edge treatments. They modeled both the B2C and B2B sides in Lightfield, wrote automations to scrape the FDA and clinicaltrials.gov, built a world model of "every ongoing clinical trial in the world," and then matched patients to pharma companies. The result: Lightfield actually helped an Alzheimer's patient find cutting-edge treatment within days.

23:37 Win the founders and engineers first, then wait for the sales VP to come around
Alex points out something often overlooked: the sales VP a greenfield company hires was trained by Salesforce and will say flat out, "I don't use that." Lightfield's design principle is to win first the founders, engineering leads and product leads — the people willing to use frontier technology to understand customers — while making every sales-led capability free for anyone in the company to use. That both helps the company understand what engineering, support and finance are doing and creates real intra-company network effects that make replacement harder. By the time that senior sales VP arrives and finds engineering, finance and support all using it for customer understanding and account scoring, the company pushes him to try it — and that's when they get their opening.

32:00 Pure seat-based and pure consumption pricing both crashed
They tried pure seat-based pricing first; acceptance was decent, but top users consumed 10,000 times what the tail did, which wasn't sustainable long term. Then they tried pure consumption pricing, turning everything into credits — and within three weeks nobody touched any feature. Keith says those were the company's worst three weeks: lots of signups, no usage. Finally they split it into four kinds of work: everyday CRM work (logging meetings, filling fields, updating tasks) goes into a platform fee or seat fee, because customers don't want to budget annually for "the margin of error on core CRM"; pipeline generation is charged by consumption, because there's alpha there and it turns into revenue; workflow automation is charged separately — say someone requests a demo on your website and Lightfield decides this is a deep tech company that should go to Henry and that's a health tech company that should go to Matt; and finally intelligence and prediction, which Keith considers Lightfield's most under-explored part, where customers will pay for the alpha.

item.title: Are bad teeth the number one reason kids go to A&E? The number got misread
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-moreorless-儿童看急诊第一原因是牙-数字被念错了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-moreorless-儿童看急诊第一原因是牙-数字被念错了/
item.description: A British MP said teeth are the number one reason children end up in A&E. The actual figure refers to 5-to-18-year-olds hospitalised for tooth decay — not the same thing, and the decay rate is actually drifting down.
item.content:encoded:
A British MP said teeth are the number one reason children end up in A&E. The actual figure refers to 5-to-18-year-olds hospitalised for tooth decay — not the same thing, and the decay rate is actually drifting down.

Four fact-checks strung into one episode: fast pace, medium information density. The teeth and medicines segments have the most solid numbers; the NEET and P-Doom segments work better as thinking exercises.

1:01 Teeth are the number one reason for A&E visits — that's wrong
Leila Moran, a Liberal Democrat MP and chair of the Health and Social Care Committee, said on Radio 4's The World at One that teeth are the number one reason children go to A&E. Chris Venatza, a consultant in paediatric dentistry at Newcastle University, flatly rejected it: she very likely conflated two sets of numbers. What actually ranks first is "hospital admission for tooth decay treatment" — the number one reason 5-to-18-year-olds are admitted to hospital. A&E attendance has all sorts of causes, and there is simply no data showing whether dentistry ranks high or low among them. Moran's office later confirmed Chris was right, and that she had meant the hospital admission figure, not the A&E figure.

3:09 So many hospital tooth extractions because the rules changed in 2001
When children are hospitalised for their teeth, it is usually not for a filling but for an extraction. Extractions are harder for a child to endure, so children who cannot cooperate for an extraction in a dental clinic may need general anaesthetic. There is an institutional turning point here: the rules changed in 2001, and ordinary dental practices were no longer allowed to administer general anaesthetic, so anyone needing it had to go to hospital. A large share of the hospital admission numbers are therefore general-anaesthetic extractions. That explains why "hospital admission" and "A&E" are two entirely different measures — one is a surgical arrangement pushed into hospitals by the rules, the other is an unplanned visit.

4:10 The admission rate is actually falling, not a crisis
Chris gives the admission rate per 100,000 population: about 320 in 2015, down to 270 before the pandemic, and 250 now. Host Tim Harford's reaction was that this doesn't look like a crisis, and the trend is even rather encouraging. Chris concedes that falling before the pandemic is a good thing, but stresses that even so, a large number of children are still having general anaesthetics and dental treatment in hospital, which is not good in itself. He adds one more thing: for the past decade, dental causes have been the number one reason for hospital admission, unchanged for ten years — so the "number one" position is stable, but the absolute level is heading down.

5:10 To see the decay rate, look at school surveys, not admissions
Chris says there is a better dataset for understanding the real state of children's tooth decay: the government sends dentists into schools to examine five-year-olds. The latest survey found 22% of five-year-olds already have decay reaching the dentine layer — close to a quarter. A quarter of the population having a disease that needs treatment, he says, is not a good state of affairs. Over time: about 30.9% in 2008, down to 23% in 2017-2018, then a plateau, with the latest survey slightly down again on the 2022 one. Longer-run data comes from a survey run once a decade since 1973: 72% of five-year-olds had decay in 1973, down to 43% in 2003 — roughly halved.

8:15 25% of UK medicines come from Israel — off by two orders of magnitude
US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee said on the Today programme that 25% of the medicines Britain uses are made in Israel. Lizzie McNeill checked the latest ONS import data: in 2025 the UK imported £10m of medicines from Israel, against total UK medicine imports of about £28bn, so Israel accounts for just 0.04% — one twenty-fifth of 1%, not 25%. She also ruled out several possibilities: active pharmaceutical ingredients come mainly from India and China, and the more upstream raw materials mainly from China; and medicines supplied by Israeli companies (the largest being Teva) are mostly not made in Israel but in European plants in Hungary, Croatia and elsewhere. Teva estimates it supplies one in eight generic packs in the UK, equivalent to one-ninth of all prescription medicines, but the other Israeli companies are all too small to push the total to 25%.

13:29 Blame Gove for rising NEETs, and Wales dismantles the case
Education Secretary Lucy Powell wrote in The Times that a million young people have been left behind by the education system Michael Gove led. Daisy Christodoulou rebuts with a natural experiment: Wales and Scotland took the opposite path to Gove's reforms. Wales's NEET rate for 16-to-24-year-olds rose from 14% in 2019 to 17% in 2025, while England's rose from 11% to 13% over the same period — similar levels, similar trend, and Wales's rise slightly larger. If Gove is responsible for England's rise, then Wales must be responsible for Wales's rise, yet the two places had completely opposite policies. She says the NEET rate sits on top of economic structure, the minimum wage, tax, regulation and far too many other factors — not just education.

17:51 Teen mental health is declining, and not only in England
Against the criticism that Gove's reforms increased academic pressure and damaged mental health, Daisy turns to the WHO's Health Behaviour in School-aged Children survey, which reports England, Scotland and Wales separately. It shows average life satisfaction among teenagers falling in all three places this century (2000 to 2022), but also falling across Western Europe and many other regions, so it is not specific to England. Then the share of 15-year-olds who "like school a lot": about 10% in England, about 9% in Scotland, about 7.5% in Wales — all low, but essentially the same across the three. The share of 15-year-olds feeling overwhelmed by academic pressure is high in all three, with no big difference.

19:59 P-Doom is a subjective probability, and nobody can supply a model
Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned, warning that Anthropic and OpenAI are irresponsible on AI safety. Anthropic's Evan Hubinger responded on X: he personally thinks the probability that AI kills all of humanity within the next decade is greater than 10%. Alexander Mark Koch, an assistant professor of global risk and resilience at Cambridge, explains that P-Doom is shorthand for "the probability AI causes human extinction", and that it is almost always one individual's subjective estimate. The issue, he says, is extraordinarily complex: it involves regulatory capacity, system resilience, where large-model capabilities are heading, autonomous weapons and biotech tools, whether AI can self-improve into an exponential loop, funding, rules, what China will do, and disaster scenarios ranging from science fiction to "a rogue state using a large model to learn to build bioweapons".

item.title: Sequoia's Former Boss on Reading People: What Happens Before 14 Sets the Core
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-ilt-红杉前掌门看人-14-岁前发生了什么-内核就定了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-ilt-红杉前掌门看人-14-岁前发生了什么-内核就定了/
item.description: Digging into his own refugee family's history, he found that the imprint you absorb unconsciously from your parents before you're 12, 13, 14 stays with you for life; what changes afterward is the external intensity, not the core.
item.content:encoded:
Digging into his own refugee family's history, he found that the imprint you absorb unconsciously from your parents before you're 12, 13, 14 stays with you for life; what changes afterward is the external intensity, not the core.

Not an investing lesson but a retrospective on origins, reading people, and writing. The back half — on structural changes in venture and the great man view of history — is the most valuable; the family history up front is more personal.

7:23 The grandfather who waited for the situation to pass vanished
Moritz's two grandfathers were two reactions to the same catastrophe. His maternal grandfather was a lower-court judge in Bavaria, had fought at Verdun in World War I, believed in the state's durability, and had a pension he was unwilling to give up, so he delayed leaving and was ultimately sent east with his wife and disappeared from history. The other grandfather was nearly blind, supported his family alone by trading cattle, had no pension to wait for, and left with his wife 72 hours before the war broke out — three days later and they too would have died. Moritz says the lesson he draws is not a moral judgment but that you must always have a bolt hole to hide in, and never too many passports.

21:03 His most effective question makes people cry on the spot
When he interviews people he always asks one fixed question: looking back, if there were one thing, one action you could have done differently, what would it be. He remembers a person interviewing at Sequoia bursting into tears when asked — the son of Latino immigrants who, at around 12, stole candy from a corner grocery with a friend; the shopkeeper told his father, who dragged him back to the store by the ear and made him apologize and empty his pockets. Years later, asked that question, the first thing he thought of was still the shame he had brought on his family. Moritz says many people conducting interviews aren't really listening to the answer.

26:03 He sorted everyone he knew on Zoom
Inspired by a series about a French village in World War II, he divides people into three categories: resisters, the silent, and collaborators. During the pandemic, in those Zoom meetings with a dozen little windows, he would stare at each person he knew and think: if these people had lived in a 1940s French village, who would stay silent, who would resist, who would collaborate. He says resisters are always a tiny minority, because bad things happen in a country precisely because most people stay silent. Asked how many of the people he has invested in would be resisters, he says he would like to think so, but he isn't sure.

38:04 The painter took one day off a year
Frank Auerbach was a refugee from Nazi Germany, and Moritz calls him a total monomaniac: apart from one day off each Christmas at Brighton Pier, he painted every single day. His models were a small fixed group of people, the same few faces painted for decades; one model living in Venice flew to London once a week to sit for him. His wife's house sits on the English coast, and Moritz asked if he went there; he answered: I have never been to that house. From this Moritz discusses the cost of monomania — the cost to relationships is almost inevitable, but sometimes great things come out of exactly there.

43:04 He bet on something beyond the résumé
Around 1985, Moritz was still a journalist and wrote to five small funds looking for a job. Everyone except Don Valentine told him he had no technical background, no engineering degree, no experience at a tech company, and suggested he go into PR or marketing. Don was willing to take the risk, for a direct reason: he had seen several people with operating backgrounds at large tech companies move into investing and fail, and he had also seen several who succeeded — an actuary, and the one he cited most, Arthur Rock: an investment banker by background, with nothing in his résumé that predicted success. Don didn't believe in teaching people; he believed in throwing them in the deep end and seeing whether they drowned.

46:15 Venture's old advantage was imperfect information
Moritz says doing venture in the 1980s and 90s had several advantages that have now disappeared, the first being imperfect information: before the internet, unless you were close to something you didn't know what was happening, whereas now the whole world basically gets the same information. The second is that the early market has far too many participants — individuals, two- or three-person funds, giant mutual funds — too many middlemen, and it is no longer possible for investors to build the kind of real, close relationship with founders they once had. He therefore says a moderately smart, mentally agile 14- to 16-year-old could have done venture in the mid-80s; he isn't sure he could still do it well today.

52:57 He believes in the great man view of history without apology
Asked whether great individuals or enduring institutions shape the course of history, Moritz's answer is blunt: he is a firm believer in the great man theory. From Lee Iacocca to Steve Jobs, from politics to the battlefield, what matters is great leaders; and of course also tyrants who cast a shadow over tens of millions of people for decades. In his work at Sequoia and in writing Ferguson, he cares about the same thing — how an organization stays alive across decades. And on Elon, he says he is completely staggered by the scale of his achievements across so many different industries, and thinks he may be the greatest industrialist in American history.

58:40 The more AI writes, the more a human voice is worth
Moritz says that because AI can easily produce vast amounts of text, excellent writing that cuts through the garbage is actually appreciating; his definition of excellent writing is ‘a voice you can hear that cannot be mistaken for anyone else's’. The hardest thing for a writer is to get close enough to your own inner feeling and voice that it outweighs the weight of others' expectations — he quotes Joseph Campbell: the privilege of a lifetime is being who you are, and that is also the hardest thing. He doesn't consider himself a technologist and says AI is rarely discussed at home; on employment he is optimistic: people predicted doom when the nuclear bomb went off, and predicted a genetic revolution creating humans in the 1970s, and neither happened, and this time he thinks more jobs will be created than destroyed.
